Superalgebra deformations of web categories: Finite webs Thanks: The second author was supported in part by Simons Collaboration Grant for Mathematicians No. 525043.
Nicholas Davidson, Jonathan R. Kujawa, Robert Muth, Jieru Zhu

Abstract
. Let 𝕜 \mathbbm{k} be a characteristic zero domain. For a locally unital 𝕜 \mathbbm{k} -superalgebra A A with distinguished idempotents I I and even subalgebra a ⊆ A 0 ¯ a\subseteq A_{\bar{0}} , we define and study an associated diagrammatic monoidal 𝕜 \mathbbm{k} -linear supercategory 𝐖𝐞𝐛 I A , a \mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I} . This supercategory yields a diagrammatic description of the generalized Schur algebras T a A ​ ( n , d ) T^{A}_{a}(n,d) . We also show there is an asymptotically faithful functor from 𝐖𝐞𝐛 I A , a \mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I} to the monoidal supercategory of 𝔤 ​ 𝔩 n ​ ( A ) \mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A) -modules generated by symmetric powers of the natural module. When this functor is full, the single diagrammatic supercategory 𝐖𝐞𝐛 I A , a \mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I} provides a combinatorial description of this module category for all n ≥ 1 n\geq 1 . We also use these results to establish Howe dualities between 𝔤 ​ 𝔩 m ​ ( A ) \mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A) and 𝔤 ​ 𝔩 n ​ ( A ) \mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A) when A A is semisimple.



1.
Introduction

1.1.
Generalized Schur algebras

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be an integral domain and let
A=A_{\bar{0}}\oplus A_{\bar{1}}
be a unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra which is free as a
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule. The prefix “super” means that objects are
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}=\mathbbm{Z}/2\mathbbm{Z}
-graded and one should take graded versions of the usual definitions; see
Section

2.1
for details. While our results hold and are already interesting for ordinary
\mathbbm{k}
-algebras (i.e., when
A_{\bar{1}}=0
), the grading plays an important role in several of our motivating examples.

For a fixed
n,d\geq 1
, let
V_{n}=A^{\oplus n}
and let
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
be the wreath product superalgebra of the symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
and
A
. There is a right action of
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
on
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
where
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
acts by place permutations,
A^{\otimes d}
acts by right multiplication, and where both actions depend on the
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-grading. Here and elsewhere
\otimes=\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}
. The
generalized Schur superalgebra
of
A
is defined to be

S^{A}(n,d)=\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right).

Also associated to this data is the Lie superalgebra
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
of
n\times n
matrices with entries in
A
and the Lie bracket given by the graded commutator. This framework includes a variety of interesting algebras. When
A=\mathbbm{k}
this gives the general linear Lie algebra
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(\mathbbm{k})
and Schur algebra
S(n,d)
. When
A
is the group algebra of a cyclic group of order
r
,
C_{r}
, then
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr C_{r}
is a complex reflection group and
S^{A}(n,d)
is the cyclotomic Schur algebra. When
A=k[t]
or
A=\mathbbm{k}[t,t^{-1}]
,
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
is a current or loop algebra, respectively. More generally, if
A
is the coordinate ring of a variety (or scheme), then
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
is the corresponding map algebra. If
A=\operatorname{Cl}_{1}
is the Clifford superalgebra on one odd generator, then
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
is the Lie superalgebra
\mathfrak{q}_{n}(\mathbbm{k})
and
S^{A}(n,d)
is the type
Q
Schur superalgebra. If
\Lambda
is the exterior superalgebra on one odd generator, then
\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\Lambda)
acts on sutured annular Khovanov homology
[
25
]
.

There is a refined version of the generalized Schur algebra which recently came to prominence. Fix a unital subalgebra
a\subseteq A_{\bar{0}}
which is a free
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule with a free direct complement. To the pair
(A,a)
there is an associated full rank
\mathbbm{k}
-subalgebra,

T^{A}_{a}(n,d)\subseteq S^{A}(n,d),

which is sometimes called the
Schurification
of
A
. Note that
S^{A}(n,d)
is not lost since
T^{A}_{A_{\bar{0}}}(n,d)=S^{A}(n,d)
.

Given a ring extension
\mathbbm{k}\subseteq\mathbbm{K}
one can extend scalars to define
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
and
S^{A}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
. These will, in general, be non-isomorphic
\mathbbm{K}
-superalgebras of the same rank. Both algebras are interesting, but
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
is now understood to play an especially significant role in representation theory. Namely, if
\mathbbm{K}
is a field of positive characteristic, then for a suitable zigzag superalgebra
\bar{Z}
and subalgebra
\bar{z}\subseteq\bar{Z}_{\bar{0}}
, Evseev–Kleshchev proved the algebra
T^{\bar{Z}}_{\bar{z}}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
is Morita equivalent to weight
d
RoCK blocks of symmetric groups
[
20
]
— thereby proving a conjecture of Turner
[
41
]
. In particular, this means that via the derived block equivalences of Chuang–Rouquier
[
13
]

T^{\bar{Z}}_{\bar{z}}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
can be viewed as the “local” object for a block of the symmetric group with non-abelian defect group. It is expected other choices of
(A,a)
will give similar results in other settings. For example, it is conjectured that for certain explicit pairs of Brauer tree algebras
(Z,z)
and
(Z^{\prime},z^{\prime})
the algebra
T^{Z}_{z}(n,d)
will be Morita equivalent to the weight
d
RoCK blocks of Schur algebras
[
32
, Conjecture 7.58]
and
T^{Z^{\prime}}_{z^{\prime}}(n,d)
will be Morita equivalent to weight
d
spin RoCK blocks
[
28
, Conjecture 1]
.

The algebra
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
also seems to be better behaved than the more naively defined
S^{A}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
. For example, Kleshchev–Muth showed if
A
is based quasi-hereditary, then
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
is again based quasi-hereditary whenever
n\geq d

[
30
]
. This need not be true for
S^{A}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
. Similarly, under suitable assumptions, if
(A,a)
is symmetric or cellular, than so is
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
. See
[
3
,
19
,
30
,
31
,
32
]
for details.

1.2.
(A,a)
-webs

Our goal in this paper is to show the language of diagrammatic supercategories can naturally be used to describe
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
,
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
, and
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
and their representation theories.

Let
(A,a)
be a pair of unital superalgebras as above. In fact, in the body of the paper we will work in the greater generality of a locally unital superalgebra
A
(or equivalently a small
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory). While this level of generality is needed for applications, for ease of exposition we focus on the unital case in the introduction.

To the data of
(A,a)
we associate a strict monoidal supercategory defined by generators and relations,
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
, which we call
(A,a)
-webs
. The objects will be tuples of nonnegative integers with concatenation of words providing the monoidal product. The generating morphisms of
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
are given by the diagrams:

for
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
z\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}
, and
f\in A
if
z=1
and
f\in a
if
z\geq 2
. Our convention is to read diagrams from bottom to top. Composition is given by vertical concatenation and the monoidal product is given by horizontal concatenation. Morphisms in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
are then linear combinations of diagrams built by repeated concatenation of generating diagrams, subject to a fairly simple set of local relations. See
Definition

3.1.1
for details. In particular, there the reader will see if
A
is locally unital, then the strands are colored by the distinguished idempotents and there is an additional family of “crossing” morphisms as generators. In the body of the paper the results described below are usually proven in this greater generality.

The category
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
generalizes a number of web category constructions. In particular when
A=\mathbbm{k}
we recover the symmetric webs for
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(\mathbbm{k})
, which are non-quantized versions of those which appear in the literature in
[
11
,
35
,
37
,
40
]
, and are isomorphic to categories defined in
[
8
,
15
]
. When
A=\operatorname{Cl}_{1}
is a rank one Clifford algebra, our constructions recover those of
[
6
]
, which are a non-quantum version of those given in
[
5
]
.
See
Section

13
for more details on these and other examples.

1.3.
Main results: Webs

Our first set of results study features of the monoidal supercategory
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
. If we view
V_{n}=A^{\oplus n}
as row vectors of length
n
, then
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
acts on the right by matrix multiplication. Thanks to the cocommutative coproduct of the universal enveloping algebra
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
and the permutation action of
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
, for all
d\geq 1
there are
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
and
S^{d}V_{n}
, the
d
th tensor and symmetric power, respectively. The category of right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules is a monoidal supercategory. Let
\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{S}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
be the full monoidal subcategory of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules consisting of objects of the form

S^{x_{1}}V_{n}\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{x_{t}}V_{n},

where
t\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 1}
and
x_{1},\dotsc,x_{t}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
.

In
Theorems

5.5.1
and
6.6.2
we establish the following result.

Theorem A
.

For all
n\geq 1
there is a functor of monoidal supercategories,

G_{n}:\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{S}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A),

which is essentially surjective and is asymptotically faithful in the sense that for any fixed morphism space the functor defines an injective map for
n\gg 0
.

We call this the
defining representation
of
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
.
A fundamental tool in understanding a category given by generators and relations is explicit bases for the morphism spaces. To this end, in
Propositions

6.5.1
and
6.6.3
we use the defining representation to give bases for the morphism spaces of
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
.

1.4.
Main results: Schurification and wreath products

In
Section

7
we relate
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
to the Schurification
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
. Taking
\Omega(n,d)
to be the set of
n
-part compositions of
d
, there exists a set of orthogonal idempotents
\{\xi_{\mathbf{x}}\mid\mathbf{x}\in\Omega(n,d)\}\subseteq T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
which sum to the identity. Therefore,

\displaystyle{\mathbf{T}}^{A,a}:=\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}n,d\geq 0\\
\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega(n,d)\end{subarray}}\xi_{\mathbf{y}}T^{A}_{a}(n,d)\xi_{\mathbf{x}}=\bigoplus_{n,d\geq 0}T^{A}_{a}(n,d)

may be considered as a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory with objects indexed by
\Omega(n,d)
and composition of morphisms given by multiplication in
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
. In fact, the
shifted star product
defined in
Section

7.2
gives
{\mathbf{T}}^{A,a}
the structure of a monoidal supercategory.

We establish the following in
Theorems

7.3.3
and
7.4.2
.

Theorem B
.

There is an equivalence of monoidal supercategories

\displaystyle{\mathbf{T}}^{A,a}\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{A,a},

and for all
n,d\geq 0
, there is an explicit superalgebra isomorphism

T^{A}_{a}(n,d)\xrightarrow{\cong}\bigoplus_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega(n,d)}\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}).

This result describes
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
as a diagrammatic algebra. This allows new tools and techniques to be brought to the study of
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
and its representation theory. It is perhaps worth remarking that
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
is defined in the literature as a subalgebra of
S^{A}(n,d)
. In contrast, here it appears in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
with no reference to
S^{A}(n,d)
needed.

In a similar spirit, in
Section

8
we show that the wreath product superalgebras
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
also naturally appear as endomorphism algebras in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
. Namely, we define a diagrammatic monoidal supercategory
\mathbf{Wr}^{A}
by generators and relations, prove in
Proposition

8.1.2
that it is equivalent to the full monoidal subcategory of
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
consisting of objects of the form
\left\{1^{d}:=(1,\dotsc,1)\mid d\geq 0\right\}
, and prove in
Corollary

8.2.2
that for every
d\geq 1
there is a superalgebra isomorphism:

\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}(1^{d},1^{d})\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A.

1.5.
Main results: Howe duality

A fundamental question is to determine when the defining representation
G_{n}
is full. When it is,
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
gives a complete combinatorial model for the supercategory
\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{S}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. Web-slingers know to expect fullness of
G_{n}
ought to be intimately related to the existence of a Howe duality for
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. In
Section

12
this expectation is confirmed.

If
V_{m}=A^{\oplus m}
is written as column vectors and
V_{n}=A^{\oplus n}
is written as row vectors, then there are commuting actions,

U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))\curvearrowright V_{m}\otimes_{A}V_{n}\curvearrowleft U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)),

given by left and right matrix multiplication. Hence, there are commuting actions,

(1.5.1)

U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))\curvearrowright S^{\bullet}(V_{m}\otimes_{A}V_{n})\curvearrowleft U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)).

Having a symmetric Howe duality for the pair
(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A),\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
means, very roughly, that these two actions should mutually centralize. In
Section

12.4
we formulate Howe duality in this setting and show it holds if and only if the corresponding defining representations are full.

Our strongest results in this direction are under the assumption that
\mathbbm{k}
is a field of characteristic zero. In this case fullness of the defining representation
G_{n}
is equivalent to fullness of the defining representation for the supercategory
\mathbf{Wr}^{A}
. This, in turn, is equivalent to the surjectivity of the natural map,

\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{S^{A}(n,d)}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right),

for all
d\geq 1
. We say
Schur–Weyl duality holds for
A
if this map is surjective for all
n,d\geq 1
. When
\mathbbm{k}
is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and
A
is a finite-dimensional semisimple
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra, then by the double-centralizer theorem for semisimple superalgebras it follows that Schur–Weyl duality holds. See
Theorem

11.2.2
. This already covers a number of examples of interest. The question remains to determine exactly when Schur–Weyl duality holds.

In the case when
\mathbbm{k}
is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and
A
is a finite-dimensional semisimple superalgebra, we can give a stronger version of Howe duality. Under these conditions, in
Theorem

12.5.1
we prove the following strong multiplicity-free result.

Theorem C
.

If
m,n\geq 1
and
r
is the minimum of
m
and
n
, then for all
d\geq 0
,

S^{d}\left(V_{m}\otimes_{A}V_{n}\right)\cong\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(r,d)}L_{m}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\circledast L_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*}

as
(U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)),U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)))
-bisupermodules.
Here
L_{t}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})
denotes a certain simple
\mathfrak{gl}_{t}(A)
-supermodule indexed by an explicit set of multipartitions of
d
,
\Lambda^{A}_{+}(r,d)
.

1.6.
Future directions

In a sequel to this paper we plan to focus on the case where
A
is a Frobenius algebra and study the
affine
web category
\mathbf{AffWeb}^{A,a}
. This is a diagrammatic monoidal supercategory given by generators and relations as in
Definition

3.1.1
coupled with an additional affine generator coupon. Much like
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}
can be viewed as a thick-strand calculus which encompasses the wreath algebra
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
,
\mathbf{AffWeb}^{A,a}
is a thick-strand calculus which encompasses the affine wreath product algebra
\mathcal{A}_{n}(A)
defined in
[
38
]
. We expect
\mathbf{AffWeb}^{A,a}
to play an essential role in establishing certain Morita equivalence results in general which are known to hold for
\mathcal{A}_{n}(A)
under restrictions on the characteristic of the ground field (such as in
[
29
]
).

1.7.
Acknowledgments

A portion of this research was completed during the AIM SQuaRE collaboration
‘Superalgebra deformations of web categories’
. The authors wish to thank the American Institute of Mathematics for their support and hospitality.

2.
Preliminaries

2.1.
Ground rings, superalgebras, and supercategories

2.1.1.
Supermodules and supercategories

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be a characteristic zero domain with field of fractions
\mathbbm{K}
. For
R\in\{\mathbbm{k},\mathbbm{K}\}
, write
R\text{-}{\mathbf{sMod}}
for the category of left
R
-supermodules, and
R\text{-}{\mathbf{smod}}
for the full subcategory of finitely generated
R
-supermodules. Here the prefix “super” indicates that we are working in the
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}=\mathbbm{Z}/2\mathbbm{Z}
-graded setting. For brevity we often leave the prefix super implicit. We view
R
as
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-graded and concentrated in parity
\bar{0}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
and an
R
-supermodule is simply a
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-graded
R
-module. Given a
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-graded object
X=X_{\bar{0}}\oplus X_{\bar{1}}
we write
\bar{x}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
if
x\in X_{\bar{x}}
. We sometimes say
x
is
even
(resp.,
odd
) if
\bar{x}=\bar{0}
(resp.,
\bar{x}=\bar{1}
). Given a free
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule
M
of finite rank, we write
\dim_{\mathbbm{k}}(M)
for the rank of
M
and
\operatorname{grdim}_{\mathbbm{k}}(M)=p|q
for the graded rank of
M
; that is, when the rank of
M_{\bar{0}}
is
p
and the rank of
M_{\bar{1}}
is
q
.

We presume the reader is familiar with superalgebras, supermodules, (monoidal) supercategories, and the like. In particular, a supercategory is a category which is enriched over a category of supermodules (e.g.,
R\text{-}{\mathbf{sMod}}
). We generally follow the conventions of
[
7
]
for (monoidal) supercategories, superfunctors, and the diagrammatic calculus for (monoidal) supercategories.

One convention is worth making explicit: we choose to write supermodule homomorphisms on the opposite side of the action. For example, if
M
and
N
are left
A
-supermodules, then a supermodule homomorphism
f:M\rightarrow N
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map which satisfies
(am)f=a(m)f
for all
a\in A
,
m\in M
. If we instead chose to write them on the left, then a homogeneous supermodule homomorphism
g:M\rightarrow N
would be a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map which satisfies
g(am)=(-1)^{\bar{a}\bar{g}}ag(m)
for all homogeneous
a\in A
,
m\in M
. Given a homogeneous
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map
f:M\rightarrow N
, define
g:M\rightarrow N
by
g(x)=(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{x}}(x)f
. An easy check verifies this gives a bijection between the two conventions and there is no loss in choosing one over the other.

Given a set of objects
X
in a monoidal supercategory, we write
X^{\otimes d}
for the set of all
d
-fold tensor products of objects from
X
. Given an object
x
in a monoidal supercategory we sometimes write
x^{d}
or
x^{\otimes d}
for the
d
-fold tensor product of the object with itself.

2.1.2.
Locally unital superalgebras

We say that a
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra
A
is
locally unital
(see
[
10
, Section 5]
) if there exists a designated system
I
of mutually orthogonal even idempotents such that
A=\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}jAi
. Given a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra
A
, a locally unital left
A
-supermodule is a left
A
-supermodule which satisfies
M=\bigoplus_{i\in I}iM
. There is an obvious notion of locally unital for right supermodules and bisupermodules. Whenever a superalgebra is locally unital we assume its supermodules are also locally unital.

Given such
A
and
I
we may define an associated small
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory
\mathbf{A}
such that
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{A})=I
and
\mathbf{A}(i,j)=jAi
, with composition of morphisms
f\circ g
given by multiplication
fg
.
In the other direction, given a small
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory
\mathbf{A}
with
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{A})=I
, we may define a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra
A=\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}\mathbf{A}(i,j)
with designated system of idempotents
\{i\mid i\in I\}
and multiplication given by linearly extending morphism composition.
This association
A\leftrightarrow\mathbf{A}
gives a correspondence between locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebras and small
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategories.

2.1.3.
Representations of supercategories

A
(left) representation
of a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory
\mathbf{A}
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear functor
F:\mathbf{A}\rightarrow{\mathbbm{k}}\text{-}{\mathbf{Mod}}
. Supernatural transformations provide the morphisms between representations of
\mathbf{A}
. We write
\mathbf{A}\text{-Rep}
for the supercategory of representations of
\mathbf{A}
.

The correspondence between locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebras and small
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategories extends to representations. Namely, given a left representation
F:\mathbf{A}\rightarrow{\mathbbm{k}}\text{-}{\mathbf{Mod}}
,
\bigoplus_{i\in I}F(i)
is naturally a left
A
-supermodule. Conversely, if
M
is a locally unital left
A
-supermodule with decomposition
M=\bigoplus_{i\in I}iM
as
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodules, then there is an associated representation
F_{M}:\mathbf{A}\rightarrow{\mathbbm{k}}\text{-}{\mathbf{Mod}}
given on objects by
F_{M}(i)=iM
and on morphisms by
F_{M}(a)(m)=am
for
a\in\mathbf{A}(i,j)=jAi
and
m\in iM
.

2.2.
Good pairs

Definition 2.2.1
.

Let
A
be a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra with distinguished idempotent set
I
. Let
I\subseteq a\subseteq A_{\bar{0}}
be an even subalgebra of
A
. We say that
(A,a)_{I}
is a
good pair
provided that for all
i,j\in I
, there exists a homogeneous
\mathbbm{k}
-basis
{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
for
jAi
such that
{}_{j}\mathtt{b}_{i}:={}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}\cap a
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for
jai
, and
i\in{}_{i}\mathtt{b}_{i}\subseteq{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{i}
.

We remark that this definition of good pair is slightly stronger than that in
[
31
, §2A]
, which mandates only that
A/a
and
a
be
\mathbbm{k}
-free. Our definition includes the supposition that
a/\mathbbm{k}I
is
\mathbbm{k}
-free as well. This additional requirement holds in all interesting examples known to the authors.

In particular, note if
(A,a)_{I}
is a good pair, then
a
is a locally unital algebra with distinguished idempotent set
I
. When we work with a good pair we will always presume to have fixed a basis
\mathtt{B}=\bigsqcup_{i,j\in I}{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
,
\mathtt{b}=\bigsqcup_{i,j\in I}{}_{j}\mathtt{b}_{i}
as described above. We additionally fix some total order
<
on
\mathtt{B}
. It will be convenient to write
A^{(1)}=A
and
A^{(z)}=a
for
z>1
.

If
(A,a)_{I}
,
(A,a^{\prime})_{I}
are good pairs, we write
(A,a^{\prime})_{I}\subseteq(A,a)_{I}
if
(a,a^{\prime})_{I}
is a good pair. In particular, for any good pair
(A,a)_{I}
, we always have a chain of good pairs

(A,\mathbbm{k}I)_{I}\subseteq(A,a)_{I}\subseteq(A,A_{\overline{0}})_{I}
.

2.3.
Combinatorics

2.3.1.
Counting and sets

We use the generalized binomial coefficient:

\displaystyle{n\choose k}:=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!}\in\mathbbm{Z},

for any
n\in\mathbbm{Z}
,
k\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
. Given integers
a,b
with
a\leq b
, let
[a,b]=\{a,a+1,\dotsc,b\}
. Given sets
X
and
Y
, we write
X^{Y}
for the set of tuples indexed by
Y
consisting of elements from
X
.

2.3.2.
Compositions

For
\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{t})\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}^{t}
, we will set

\displaystyle|\mathbf{x}|=t,\qquad\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert=\sum_{k=1}^{t}x_{k},\qquad\mathbf{x}!=\prod_{k=1}^{t}(x_{k}!).

Set

\displaystyle\Omega(n,d)=\{\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert=d\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Omega=\bigsqcup_{n,d\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}}\Omega(n,d).

2.3.3.
Colored compositions

For
n,d\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
and a set
I
, an
n
-part
I
-colored composition of
d
is the data of a composition
\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\Omega(n,d)
, and a tuple
\mathbf{i}=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})\in I^{n}
, which we write as
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=(i_{1}^{(x_{1})},\ldots,i_{n}^{(x_{n})})
. For two such
I
-colored compositions, we will set
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{x})}
provided
i_{t}=j_{t}
whenever
x_{t}\neq 0
; i.e., the coloring of the zero components of a composition is irrelevant. Set

\displaystyle\Omega_{I}(n,d)=\{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=(i_{1}^{(x_{1})},\ldots,i_{n}^{(x_{n})})\mid\mathbf{i}\in I^{n},\,\mathbf{x}\in\Omega(n,d)\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Omega_{I}=\bigsqcup_{n,d\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}}\Omega_{I}(n,d).

We consider
\Omega_{I}
as a monoid under concatenation, with identity the empty composition
()\in\Omega_{I}(0,0)
. We define the monoid of
reduced

I
-colored compositions
\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
by imposing the following additional relation on
\Omega_{I}
:
()=(i^{(0)})
for all
i\in I
. In other words, we have
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}
in
\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
provided the colored compositions are identical after deleting all the zero components. We write

\displaystyle\widehat{\Omega}_{I}(n,d)=\{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=(i_{1}^{(x_{1})},\ldots,i_{n}^{(x_{n})})\mid\mathbf{i}\in I^{n},\,\mathbf{x}\in\Omega(n,d)\}\subseteq\widehat{\Omega}_{I}.

Example 2.3.1
.

If
I=\{\alpha,\beta\}
, then
\alpha^{(2)}\beta^{(0)}\beta^{(3)}=\alpha^{(2)}\alpha^{(0)}\beta^{(3)}
in both
\Omega_{I}
and
\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
, while
\alpha^{(2)}\beta^{(0)}\beta^{(3)}=\alpha^{(2)}\beta^{(3)}
in
\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
but not in
\Omega_{I}
.

Recall that a
partition
(resp.,
multi-partition
) of
d
is a composition of
d
with weakly decreasing parts (resp., a tuple of partitions whose total sum is
d
). Starting in
Section

11
we will introduce a veritable zoo of partitions and multi-partitions. We defer their introduction until then.

3.
The
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
category

3.1.
Defining the
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
category

Let
(A,a)_{I}
be a good pair.

Definition 3.1.1
.

Let
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
be the strict monoidal
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory defined as follows.
We have
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I})=\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
. The monoidal structure on objects in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
is inherited from the monoid
\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
; in particular the objects of
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
are monoidally generated by objects
i^{(x)}
for
i\in I
,
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, with
i^{(0)}
equating to the unit object
\mathbbm{1}\in\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
for all
i\in I
.

The generating morphisms of
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
are given by the diagrams:

(3.1.1)

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x+y)}

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x+y)}

\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(y)}

\scriptstyle f
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(z)}
\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(z)}

for
i,j\in I
,
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
z\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}
,
f\in jA^{(z)}i
, where diagrams are to be read from bottom to top. We call these morphisms ‘
split
’, ‘
merge
’, ‘
crossing
’ and ‘
coupon
’ respectively. Splits, merges and crossings have parity
\bar{0}
, and the parity of the
f
coupon is
\bar{f}
. We say a strand labeled by
i^{(x)}
has
color

i
and
thickness

x
. We refer to strands of thickness 1 as
thin
strands, otherwise we call them
thick
. Recall that
A^{(1)}=A
and
A^{(z)}=a
for
z>1
. Consequently, thick strands may only be decorated by coupons in the even subalgebra
a
, whereas thin strands may be decorated with arbitrary coupons in
A
.

Going forward, we will use the following conventions:

•

Strands of thickness 0 (and any coupons thereon) are to be deleted;

•

Diagrams containing a strand of negative thickness are to be read as zero.

The relations imposed on the morphisms in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
are given in
Eq.

3.1.2
-
Eq.

3.1.12
:

Web-associativity.
For all
i\in I
,
x,y,z\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
:

(3.1.2)

\displaystyle\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\textstyle{{}}$}}}}}}}}}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 34.45842pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-34.45842pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-35.6199pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\hbox to68.92pt{\vbox to71.24pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 40.53047pt\lower-15.1338pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

Remark 3.1.2
.

The relations
Eqs.

3.1.5
,
3.1.6
, and
3.1.7
are imposed in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
only for distinct combinations of colors in order to allow for a more minimal presentation. It will be established in
Corollary

4.2.7
that these relations in fact hold in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
for arbitrary combinations of colors.

Remark 3.1.3
.

In the common situation where
I=\{1\}
(and hence
A
is a unital algebra as in the introduction), the relations need not be extensive as they appear. All strands in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}
will be monotonically colored and there is no contribution from relations
Eqs.

3.1.5
,
3.1.6
, and
3.1.7
which stipulate distinctly colored strands. However, monotonic versions of these relations nonetheless hold in this category, as noted in
Remark

3.1.2
.

Remark 3.2.1
.

Again, in the situation when
I=\{1\}
we may use
Eq.

3.2.2
to
define
the sole monotone crossing morphism in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}
in terms of split and crossing morphisms, and hence do not require any crossing generators in our presentation.

4.
Implied relations in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}

In this section we establish a number of useful relations in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
, as well as the assertion from
Section

3.2
that
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
has an alternate presentation.

4.1.
Equivalence of presentations.

For clarity, throughout this section we will let
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
designate the category defined in
Definition

3.1.1
, and
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I,\textup{alt}}
designate the category defined in
Section

3.2
. It will be established in
Corollary

4.1.3
that these categories are isomorphic.

Lemma 4.1.1
.

The relations
Eqs.

3.2.1
and
3.2.2
hold in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
.

Lemmas

4.1.1
and
4.1.2
together imply

Corollary 4.1.3
.

There is an isomorphism
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}\cong\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I,\textup{alt}}
given by the identity on objects and diagrams.

From this point forward we will work with
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
as defined in
Definition

3.1.1
but also freely use relations
Eqs.

3.2.1
and
3.2.2
thanks to
Lemma

4.1.1
.

4.2.
Monotone relations in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}

As the statements throughout this subsection deal with monotone diagrams (where all strands are colored by the same
i
for some
i\in I
), for the sake of space in proofs we will often write
x
in place of
i^{(x)}
, etc. Because the idempotents and coupons do not play a role here, the relations in this section are analogous to those which have appeared in previous work; e.g.,
[
11
,
35
,
37
,
40
]
for the quantum setting, and
[
8
]
for the non-quantum setting. In particular, most results which appear here can be extracted from existing work in the literature, but we choose to provide full proofs for the reader’s reference.

for any
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
. We prove the lemma statement by induction on
n=r+s
. The claim is trivial for
n=0,1
, so let
n\geq 2
and assume the claim holds for all
n^{\prime}<n
. We have

\displaystyle L(r,s)\;

\displaystyle\begin{subarray}{c}\textup{\lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{DiagSwitchRel}}\\
=\\
\,\end{subarray}\;R(r,s)-\sum_{w\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}}\binom{a-b+r-s}{w}L(r-w,s-w)

\displaystyle=R(r,s)-\sum_{w\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}}\binom{a-b+r-s}{w}\sum_{u\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}}\binom{-a+b-r+s}{u}R(r-w-u,s-w-u)

\displaystyle=R(r,s)-\sum_{t\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}}\sum_{w=1}^{t}\binom{a-b+r-s}{w}\binom{-a+b-r+s}{t-w}R(r-t,s-t)

\displaystyle=R(r,s)+\sum_{t\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}}\binom{-a+b-r+s}{t}R(r-t,s-t),

where the second equality follows by the induction assumption, the last equality follows from the Chu–Vandermonde identity. This completes the proof.
∎

Considering the coefficient in the last term and using the substitution
t:=a-s
, we may write:

\displaystyle\sum_{s-r=a-b}(-1)^{a-s}\binom{b+s}{r}\binom{a}{s}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}(-1)^{t}\binom{b+a-t}{a}\binom{a}{t}=1.

The last equality follows from an application of Euler’s finite difference theorem (see
[
22
, (10.13)]
). This completes the proof.
∎

\displaystyle\;\begin{subarray}{c}\textup{ \lx@cref{creftype\lx@tilde refnum}{KnotholeRel}}\\
=\\
\,\end{subarray}\;\sum_{\ \begin{subarray}{c}s-r=a-b\\
s^{\prime}-r^{\prime}=b-a\\
t\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{a+b-s-s^{\prime}}\binom{s+s^{\prime}-t}{s^{\prime}+a-b}\binom{s+s^{\prime}-t}{s}\binom{s+s^{\prime}}{t}R(s+s^{\prime}-t,s+s^{\prime}-t),

where we use the fact that
s+s^{\prime}=r+r^{\prime}
and
r^{\prime}=s^{\prime}-a+b
in the last equality, and the notation of
Eq.

4.2.1
. Writing
m:=s+s^{\prime}-t
,
k:=s+s^{\prime}+a-b
,
c:=b-a
, we may rewrite this as

(4.2.2)

\displaystyle\sum_{k,m\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}}(-1)^{k}\binom{c+k}{m}\sum_{s=0}^{k}\binom{m}{k-s}\binom{m}{s}R(m,m).

Now we may use the binomial identities

\displaystyle\binom{c+k}{m}=\sum_{u=0}^{m}\binom{c}{m-u}\binom{k}{u}\qquad\qquad\textup{and}\qquad\qquad\sum_{s=0}^{k}\binom{m}{k-s}\binom{m}{s}=\binom{2m}{k}

to rewrite
Eq.

4.2.2
as

\displaystyle\sum_{m\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}}\sum_{u=0}^{m}\binom{c}{m-u}\sum_{k=0}^{2m}(-1)^{k}\binom{2m}{k}\binom{k}{u}R(m,m)

\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt=\sum_{m\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}}\sum_{u=0}^{m}\binom{c}{m-u}\sum_{k=0}^{2m}(-1)^{k}\binom{2m}{u}\binom{2m-u}{k-u}R(m,m)

\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt=\sum_{m\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}}\sum_{u=0}^{m}\binom{2m}{u}\binom{c}{m-u}\sum_{\ell=0}^{2m-u}(-1)^{(\ell+u)}\binom{2m-u}{\ell}R(m,m)

\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt=R(0,0),

since the binomial theorem implies

\sum_{\ell=0}^{2m-u}(-1)^{\ell}\binom{2m-u}{\ell}=0

whenever
m>0
.
∎

Now, fixing
L,R\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, we consider the coefficient
\kappa(L,R)
of

\scriptstyle c
\scriptstyle a
\scriptstyle b
\scriptstyle a+b
\scriptstyle c
\scriptstyle R
\scriptstyle L

in the sum above. Using the substitutions

A=L-R-a+c-s,\,B=c-s^{\prime}
, we have

\displaystyle\kappa(L,R)

\displaystyle=(-1)^{L+R+a}\sum_{B=0}^{b-R}\sum_{A=0}^{b-R}(-1)^{A+B}\binom{L-R-A+B}{B}\binom{L-R-A}{b-R-B}\binom{b-R}{A}

\displaystyle=\sum_{B=0}^{b-R}\sum_{A=0}^{b-R}(-1)^{a+A+B}\binom{b-R}{B}\binom{L-R-A+B}{b-R}\binom{b-R}{A}

\displaystyle=(-1)^{L+R+a}\sum_{B=0}^{b-R}(-1)^{B}\binom{b-R}{B}\sum_{A=0}^{b-R}(-1)^{A}\binom{L-R-A+B}{b-R}\binom{b-R}{A}.

An application of Euler’s finite difference theorem (see
[
22
, (10.13)]
) shows that

\displaystyle\sum_{A=0}^{b-R}(-1)^{A}\binom{L-R-A+B}{b-R}\binom{b-R}{A}=1,

so

\displaystyle\kappa(L,R)

\displaystyle=(-1)^{L+R+a}\sum_{B=0}^{b-R}(-1)^{B}\binom{b-R}{B}=(-1)^{L+a+b}\delta_{b,R},

by the binomial theorem. Therefore, we have

We may encapsulate
Lemmas

4.2.4
,
4.2.5
, and
4.2.6
with the following corollary:

Corollary 4.2.7
.

The relations
Eqs.

3.1.5
,
3.1.6
, and
3.1.7
hold for arbitrary
i,j,k,\ell,m\in I
,
x,y,z\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
.

Proof.

That the claim holds for
Eq.

3.1.6
,
Lemma

4.2.5
, and the left side of
Eq.

3.1.5
is immediate from
Lemmas

4.2.4
,
4.2.5
, and
4.2.6
. The right side of
Eq.

3.1.5
holds when
i=j=k
by
Lemma

4.2.6
. To establish the right side of
Eq.

3.1.5
when
|\{i,j,k\}|=2
, we note that any same-color crossings may be rewritten as combinations of splits and merges via
Eq.

3.2.2
, and then
Eqs.

3.1.6
and
3.1.7
may be used to pull these splits and merges across the differently-colored strand, and then rewritten as same-colored crossings again to achieve the result.
∎

5.
The defining representation

5.1.
The twist map

Let
M,N\in\mathbbm{k}\text{-}{\mathbf{sMod}}
. Recall that for short we write
M\otimes N
for
M\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}N
. We have the
twist map
,

(5.1.1)

\displaystyle\tau_{M,N}:M\otimes N\rightarrow N\otimes M,

given by

\displaystyle\tau_{M,N}(m\otimes n)=(-1)^{\overline{m}\cdot\overline{n}}n\otimes m,

for homogeneous
m\in M
,
n\in N
. The tensor operation and the twist make
\mathbbm{k}\text{-}{\mathbf{sMod}}
into a symmetric monoidal supercategory.

We have a right action of the symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
on
M^{\otimes d}
given by signed permutations:

\displaystyle(m_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes m_{d}).\tau=(-1)^{\langle\tau;(m_{1},\ldots,m_{d})\rangle}m_{\tau(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes m_{\tau(d)}

where

\displaystyle\langle\tau;(m_{1},\ldots,m_{d})\rangle:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq r<s\leq d\\
\tau(r)>\tau(s)\end{subarray}}\overline{m}_{r}\overline{m}_{s}.

5.2.
Symmetric powers

Let
M\in\mathbbm{k}\text{-}{\mathbf{sMod}}
. The
tensor superalgebra

M^{\bullet}=\bigoplus_{x=0}^{\infty}M^{\otimes x}
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra under the product
\otimes
.
Let
J\subseteq M^{\bullet}
be the ideal generated by elements of the form

\displaystyle m_{1}\otimes m_{2}-(-1)^{\overline{m}_{1}\overline{m}_{2}}m_{2}\otimes m_{1},\qquad\textup{and}\qquad m_{3}\otimes m_{3},

ranging over all homogeneous
m_{1},m_{2}\in M
, and all
m_{3}\in M_{\bar{1}}
. The
symmetric superalgebra
is
S^{\bullet}M:=M^{\bullet}/J
.
Let
\sigma:M^{\bullet}\rightarrow S^{\bullet}M
denote the canonical quotient map of
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodules.
For
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, denote the
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule

S^{x}M:=\sigma(M^{\otimes x})
, so that
S^{\bullet}M=\bigoplus_{x=0}^{\infty}S^{x}M
.
Note in particular that
S^{1}M\cong M
and
S^{0}M\cong\mathbbm{k}
.

The symmetric superbialgebra
S^{\bullet}M
has associative product
\nabla:S^{\bullet}M\otimes S^{\bullet}M\rightarrow S^{\bullet}M
, coassociative coproduct
\Delta:S^{\bullet}M\rightarrow S^{\bullet}M\otimes S^{\bullet}M
, and projections
p_{x}:S^{\bullet}M\rightarrow S^{x}M
and inclusions
\iota_{x}:S^{x}M\rightarrow S^{\bullet}M
for all
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
.

5.2.1.
The split map

We define the
split map

{}_{M}\textup{spl}^{x,y}_{x+y}:S^{x+y}M\rightarrow S^{x}M\otimes S^{y}M
by

\displaystyle{}_{M}\textup{spl}^{x,y}_{x+y}=(p_{x}\otimes p_{y})\circ\Delta\circ\iota_{x+y}.

Explicitly,

(5.2.1)

\displaystyle{}_{M}\textup{spl}^{x,y}_{x+y}(m_{1}\cdots m_{x+y})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}T=\{t_{1}<\cdots<t_{x}\}\\
U=\{u_{1}<\cdots<u_{y}\}\\
T\cup U=\{1,\ldots,x+y\}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\varepsilon(T,U)}m_{t_{1}}\cdots m_{t_{x}}\otimes m_{u_{1}}\cdots m_{u_{y}},

for all homogeneous
m_{1},\ldots,m_{x+y}\in M
, where
\varepsilon(T,U)\in\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
is defined by

\displaystyle\varepsilon(T,U)=\#\{(t,u)\in T\times U\mid t>u,\,\overline{m}_{t}=\overline{m}_{u}=\bar{1}\}.

5.2.2.
The merge map

We may similarly define the
merge map

{}_{M}\textup{mer}_{x,y}^{x+y}:S^{x}M\otimes S^{x}M\rightarrow S^{x+y}M

by

{}_{M}\textup{mer}_{x,y}^{x+y}:=p_{x+y}\circ\nabla\circ(\iota_{x}\otimes\iota_{y}).

Explicitly,

(5.2.2)

\displaystyle{}_{M}\textup{mer}_{x,y}^{x+y}(m_{1}\cdots m_{x}\otimes m_{1}^{\prime}\cdots m_{y}^{\prime})=m_{1}\cdots m_{x}m_{1}^{\prime}\cdots m_{y}^{\prime},

for all
m_{1},\ldots,m_{x},m_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,m_{y}^{\prime}\in M
.

5.3.
The superalgebra
M_{n}(A)
and the Lie superalgebra
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)

Fix
n\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
. Let
A
be a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra with distinguished idempotent set
I
. The matrix algebra
M_{n}(A)=M_{n}(\mathbbm{k})\otimes A
is also naturally a
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra. For
r,s\in[1,n]
,
f\in A
let
E_{r,s}^{f}:=E_{r,s}\otimes f
, the matrix where the
(r,s)
-entry is
f
and all others are zero. For homogeneous
f\in A
we have
\overline{E^{f}_{r,s}}=\overline{f}
. We write
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
for
M_{n}(A)
viewed as a Lie superalgebra using the supercommutator bracket. That is,
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)=M_{n}(A)
as
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodules and

\displaystyle[E_{r,s}^{f},E_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime}}^{f^{\prime}}]=\delta_{s,r^{\prime}}E_{r,s^{\prime}}^{ff^{\prime}}-(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{f}^{\prime}}\delta_{s^{\prime},r}E_{r^{\prime},s}^{f^{\prime}f}

for all
r,s,r^{\prime},s^{\prime}\in[1,n]
and homogeneous
f,f^{\prime}\in A
.
We write
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
for the universal enveloping superalgebra of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
.

When
I
is a finite set
A
is unital. In this case, let
\mathfrak{h}=\mathfrak{h}_{n}
be the
\mathbbm{k}
-submodule of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
generated by
\left\{E_{r,r}^{1}\mid 1\leq r\leq n\right\}
. Let
X(T_{n})=\bigoplus_{r=1}^{n}\mathbbm{Z}\varepsilon_{r}
be the free abelian group on generators
\varepsilon_{1},\dotsc,\varepsilon_{n}
and let

\Lambda_{n}=\left\{\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\in X(T_{n})\mid\lambda_{i}\geq 0\text{ for $i=1,\dotsc,n$}\right\}.

Given a left
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-module
M
, a vector
u\in M
has
weight

\lambda=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\in X(T_{n})
if
E_{i,i}^{1}u=\lambda_{i}u
for all
1\leq i\leq n
. The set of all vectors in
M
of weight
\lambda
is the
\lambda

weight space
of
M
. There are obvious right module versions of these definitions, as well.

5.4.
Colored symmetric power modules for
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)

For
i\in I
, write
{}_{i}V=\bigoplus_{j\in I}iAj\subseteq A
, and
{}_{i}V_{n}=({}_{i}V)^{\oplus n}
.
For
f\in{}_{i}V,r\in[1,n]
, we will write
v_{r}^{f}
to denote
f
in the
r
th component of
{}_{i}V_{n}
.

There is a right action of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
on
{}_{i}V_{n}
by right matrix multiplication on row vectors, so that

\displaystyle v_{r}^{f}\cdot E_{s,t}^{g}=\delta_{r,s}v_{t}^{fg}

for all
r,s,t\in[1,n]
,
f\in{}_{i}V
,
g\in A
.
The coproduct on
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
given by
\Delta(u)=1\otimes u+u\otimes 1
for
u\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
makes the category
\textup{mod-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
of right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules into a monoidal supercategory. Namely, for all
M,N\in\textup{mod-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
the action of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
on
M\otimes N
is given on homogeneous elements by

\displaystyle(m\otimes n)\cdot u=(-1)^{\overline{u}\,\overline{n}}mu\otimes n+m\otimes nu.

Let
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}
. We will denote the
x
th symmetric power
S^{x}({}_{i}V_{n})
by
S^{x}_{i}V_{n}
.
Then, via the coproduct of
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
,
S^{x}_{i}V_{n}\in\textup{mod-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
with the action given on homogeneous elements by

\displaystyle v_{r_{1}}^{f_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{f_{x}}\cdot E_{s,t}^{g}=\sum_{u=1}^{x}(-1)^{\bar{g}(\bar{f}_{u+1}+\cdots+\bar{f}_{x})}\delta_{r_{u}s}v_{r_{1}}^{f_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{u-1}}^{f_{u-1}}v_{t}^{f_{u}g}v_{u+1}^{f_{u+1}}\cdots v_{x}^{f_{x}}.

For all
f\in jA^{(x)}i
, we have a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map

L_{x}^{f}:S^{x}_{i}V_{n}\rightarrow S^{x}_{j}V_{n}

given by

(5.4.1)

\displaystyle L_{x}^{f}(v_{r_{1}}^{g_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{g_{x}})=v_{r_{1}}^{fg_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{fg_{x}}

for all
r_{t}\in[1,n]
,
g_{t}\in{}_{i}V
,
t\in[1,x]
. Note that when
x\geq 2
,
\bar{f}=\bar{0}
, so there is no need to worry about signs.

We write
\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{S}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
for the full monoidal subcategory of right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-modules generated by the objects
S^{x}_{i}V_{n}
, for all
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
i\in I
, so that

\displaystyle\operatorname{Ob}(\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{S}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))=\left\{S^{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathbf{i}}V_{n}:=S^{x_{1}}_{i_{1}}V_{n}\otimes\cdots\otimes S^{x_{t}}_{i_{t}}V_{n}\mid t\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0},\mathbf{x}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}^{t},\mathbf{i}\in I^{t}\right\}.

It is straightforward to check that the maps
\tau_{S_{i}^{x}V_{n},S_{j}^{y}V_{n}}
,
{}_{{}_{i}V_{n}}\textup{spl}_{x+y}^{x,y}
,
{}_{{}_{i}V_{n}}\textup{mer}_{x+y}^{x,y}
,
L_{x}^{f}
as defined in
Eqs.

5.1.1
,
5.2.1
,
5.2.2
, and
5.4.1
are even homomorphisms of right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules.

5.5.
The defining representation of
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}

\displaystyle G_{n}:\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{S}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)

G_{n}i^{(x)}=S^{x}_{i}V_{n}

on generating morphisms, for all
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
i,j\in I
, and
f\in jA^{(x)}i
.

Proof.

We simply check that images of relations
Eq.

3.1.2
–
Eq.

3.1.12
are preserved by the functor
G_{n}
. This is routine. In particular, relations
Eqs.

3.1.2
,
3.2.1
, and
3.2.2
can be checked as in
[
15
, Theorem 6.1.1]
(where full details are included in the arXiv version of that paper). Relations
Eq.

3.1.5
–
Eq.

3.1.7
are straightforward, as are
Eqs.

3.1.11
and
3.1.12
, noting that
\bar{f}=\bar{0}
for
f
-coupons on thick strands.

The left side of
Eq.

3.1.8
is clear. For the right side, we have

\displaystyle L_{x}^{\alpha f}(v_{r_{1}}^{g_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{g_{x}})

\displaystyle=v_{r_{1}}^{\alpha fg_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{\alpha fg_{x}}=\alpha^{x}v_{r_{1}}^{fg_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{fg_{x}}=\alpha^{x}L_{x}^{f}(v_{r_{1}}^{g_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{g_{x}}),

for all
\alpha\in\mathbbm{k}
,
f\in jA{i}
,
r_{t}\in[1,n]
,
g_{t}\in{}_{i}V
,
t\in[1,x]
, as desired.

The left side of
Eq.

3.1.9
is clear. The right side is clear for
x=1
, so assume
x>1
, and therefore
\bar{f}=\overline{g}=\bar{0}
. Then
for all

r_{t}\in[1,n]
,
h_{t}\in{}_{i}V
,
t\in[1,x]
, we have:

\displaystyle L^{f+g}_{x}(v_{r_{1}}^{h_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{h_{x}})

\displaystyle=v_{r_{1}}^{(f+g)h_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{(f+g)h_{x}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{t=0}^{x}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}B=\{b_{1}<\cdots<b_{t}\}\\
C=\{c_{1}<\cdots<c_{x-t}\}\\
B\cup C=[1,x]\end{subarray}}v_{r_{1}}^{(\delta_{1\in B}f+\delta_{1\in C}g)h_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{(\delta_{x\in B}f+\delta_{x\in C}g)h_{x}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{t=0}^{x}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}B=\{b_{1}<\cdots<b_{t}\}\\
C=\{c_{1}<\cdots<c_{x-t}\}\\
B\cup C=[1,x]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\varepsilon(B,C)}v_{r_{b_{1}}}^{fh_{b_{1}}}\cdots v_{r_{b_{t}}}^{fh_{b_{t}}}v_{r_{c_{1}}}^{gh_{c_{1}}}\cdots v_{r_{c_{x-t}}}^{gh_{c_{x-t}}},

where

\displaystyle\varepsilon(B,C)=\#\{(b,c)\in B\times C\mid b>c,\bar{h}_{b}=\bar{h}_{c}=\bar{1}\}.

It is easily seen, using the formulas
Eqs.

5.2.1
and
5.2.2
, that this last line is equal to

\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{x}{}_{{}_{j}V_{n}}\textup{mer}_{t,x-t}^{x}\circ(L_{t}^{f}\otimes L_{x-t}^{g})\circ{}_{{}_{i}V_{n}}\textup{spl}^{t,x-t}_{x}(v_{r_{1}}^{h_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{h_{x}}),

as desired.

Finally, for
Eq.

3.1.10
, let
i,j\in I
,
f\in jA_{\bar{1}}i
. Then for
r_{1},r_{2}\in[1,n]
,
h_{1},h_{2}\in{}_{i}V
, we have

\displaystyle{}_{{}_{j}V_{n}}\textup{mer}_{1,1}^{2}\circ(L_{1}^{f}\otimes L_{1}^{f})\circ{}_{{}_{i}V_{n}}\textup{spl}^{1,1}_{2}(v_{r_{1}}^{h_{1}}v_{r_{2}}^{h_{2}})

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\bar{h}_{1}}v_{r_{1}}^{fh_{1}}v_{r_{2}}^{fh_{2}}+(-1)^{\bar{h}_{2}(\bar{h}_{1}+1)}v_{r_{2}}^{fh_{2}}v_{r_{1}}^{fh_{1}}

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\bar{h}_{1}}v_{r_{1}}^{fh_{1}}v_{r_{2}}^{fh_{2}}+(-1)^{\bar{h}_{1}+1}v_{r_{1}}^{fh_{1}}v_{r_{2}}^{fh_{2}}=0,

completing the proof.
∎

in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(i^{(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n})},i^{(x_{1})}\cdots i^{(x_{n})})

and

\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(i^{(x_{1})}\cdots i^{(x_{n})},i^{(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n})})
, respectively. The diagrams should be interpreted as
n-1
vertically composed splits (or merges). By
Eq.

3.1.2
the resulting morphism is independent of the split (or merge) order.

For
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=i_{1}^{(x_{1})}\cdots i_{t}^{(x_{t})}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I})
define
\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}}=(i_{1}^{(1)})^{x_{1}}\cdots(i_{t}^{(1)})^{x_{t}}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I})
, and

\displaystyle Y_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}

\displaystyle:=y_{i_{1}}^{(1,\ldots,1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes y_{i_{t}}^{(1,\ldots,1)}\in\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}})

\displaystyle Z_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}

\displaystyle:=z_{i_{1}}^{(1,\ldots,1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes z_{i_{t}}^{(1,\ldots,1)}\in\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})})

Then for
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I})
, we have linear maps:

\displaystyle exp_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}:\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{j}^{\mathbf{y}}),\qquad f\mapsto Y_{\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}\circ f\circ Z_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}

\displaystyle con_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}:\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{j}^{\mathbf{y}})\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}),\qquad f\mapsto Z_{\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}\circ f\circ Y_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}

We refer to these maps a
explosion
and
contraction
, respectively.
The next lemma follows by repeated application of
Eq.

3.1.4
.

Lemma 6.1.1
.

For all
f\in\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
, we have

\displaystyle con_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}\circ exp_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}(f)=\mathbf{x}!\,\mathbf{y}!\,f.

We will say a finitely supported function
\mu:{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}\rightarrow\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
is a
restricted
{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
-composition
provided that
\mu(b)\leq 1
whenever
\overline{b}=\bar{1}
. We write
|\mu|=\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}\mu(b)\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
.
Then for such
\mu
, enumerating
\textup{supp}(\mu)=\{b_{1}<\cdots<b_{d}\}
, we define the following morphisms in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(i^{(|\mu|)},j^{(|\mu|)})
:

6.3.
A spanning set for morphisms

Let
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=i_{1}^{(x_{1})}\cdots i_{t}^{(x_{t})},\,\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}=j_{1}^{(y_{1})}\cdots j_{u}^{(y_{u})}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I})
. Let
\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
be the collection of tuples
\boldsymbol{\mu}=(\mu_{r,s})_{r\in[1,t],s\in[1,u]}
, where each
\mu_{r,s}
is a restricted
{}_{j_{s}}\mathtt{B}_{i_{r}}
-composition, and we have

\displaystyle\sum_{s\in[1,u]}|\mu_{r,s}|=x_{r}\;\;\;(\forall r\in[1,t])\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{r\in[1,t]}|\mu_{r,s}|=y_{s}\;\;\;(\forall s\in[1,u]).

For
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
, we define an associated diagram
\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}\in\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{y})})
by setting

.

\displaystyle\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\diamond}=[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{b}}\eta^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}.

6.2.2

6.4.
Action on colored symmetric power modules

Lemma 6.4.1
.

Let
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=i_{1}^{(x_{1})}\cdots i_{t}^{(x_{t})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}=j_{1}^{(y_{1})}\cdots j_{u}^{(y_{u})}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I})
, and
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
. Then the map

\displaystyle G_{n}(\eta^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}):S^{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathbf{i}}V\rightarrow S^{\mathbf{y}}_{\mathbf{j}}V

is given by

(6.4.1)

\displaystyle G_{n}(\eta^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}):\bigotimes_{\alpha=1}^{t}\prod_{\gamma=1}^{x_{\alpha}}v_{\ell_{\gamma}^{(\alpha)}}^{f_{\gamma}^{(\alpha)}}

\displaystyle\mapsto[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}\sum_{T}(-1)^{\sigma_{1}(T)+\sigma_{2}(T)+\sigma_{3}(T)}\bigotimes_{\beta=1}^{u}\prod_{\alpha=1}^{t}\prod_{c\in\mathtt{B}}^{<}\prod^{<}_{\gamma\in T_{\alpha,\beta}^{c}}v_{\ell_{\gamma}^{(\alpha)}}^{cf_{\gamma}^{(\alpha)}}

for all
\ell_{\gamma}^{(\alpha)}\in[1,n]
,
f_{\gamma}^{(\alpha)}\in{}_{i_{\alpha}}V
, where the sum ranges over all tuples of sets
T=(T_{r,s}^{b})_{b\in\mathtt{B},r\in[1,t],s\in[1,u]}
such that
T_{r,s}^{b}\subseteq[1,x_{r}]
,
|T_{r,s}^{b}|=\mu_{r,s}(b)
and
\bigsqcup_{s,b}T_{r,s}^{b}=[1,x_{r}]
, and

\displaystyle\sigma_{1}(T)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r^{\prime}<r\in[1,t]\\
s\in[1,u]\end{subarray}}\sum_{\gamma\in[1,x_{r^{\prime}}]}\overline{\mu}_{r,s}(b)\bar{b}\bar{f}^{(r^{\prime})}_{\gamma}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b,b^{\prime}\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,t]\\
s^{\prime}<s\in[1,u]\end{subarray}}\sum_{\gamma\in T^{b^{\prime}}_{r,s^{\prime}}}\overline{\mu}_{r,s}(b)\bar{b}\bar{f}_{\gamma}^{(r)}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b^{\prime}<b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,t]\\
s\in[1,u]\end{subarray}}\sum_{\gamma\in T^{b^{\prime}}_{r,s}}\overline{\mu}_{r,s}(b)\bar{b}\bar{f}_{\gamma}^{(r)};

\displaystyle\sigma_{2}(T)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r\in[1,t]\\
s^{\prime}<s\in[1,u]\\
\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\in[1,x_{r}]\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in T^{b}_{r,s}\\
\gamma^{\prime}\in T^{b^{\prime}}_{r,s^{\prime}}\end{subarray}}\bar{f}_{\gamma}^{(r)}\bar{f}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{(r)};\qquad\qquad\sigma_{3}(T)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b,b^{\prime}\in\mathtt{B}\\
r<r^{\prime}\in[1,t]\\
s^{\prime}<s\in[1,u]\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in T^{b}_{r,s}\\
\gamma^{\prime}\in T^{b^{\prime}}_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime}}\end{subarray}}(\bar{b}+\bar{f}_{\gamma}^{(r)})(\bar{b}^{\prime}+\bar{f}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{(r^{\prime})}).

Proof.

The formula follows directly from
Theorem

5.5.1
and the formulas
Eqs.

5.1.1
,
5.2.1
,
5.2.2
, and
5.4.1
. The sign
(-1)^{\sigma_{1}(T)}
arises via the coupon morphisms in
\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}
, the sign
(-1)^{\sigma_{2}(T)}
arises via the split morphisms, and the sign
(-1)^{\sigma_{3}(T)}
arises via the
Z
morphism. The scalar
[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}
arises from consideration of
Eq.

6.2.1
and the following calculation:

\displaystyle{}G_{n}\left(\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 12.11285pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-12.11285pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-29.47171pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\hbox to24.23pt{\vbox to58.94pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 12.11285pt\lower-8.30507pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

6.5.
Spanning results for
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}

Proposition 6.5.1
.

The morphisms
\{\eta^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{y})})\}
comprise a
\mathbbm{k}
-spanning set for
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}\left(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{y})}\right)
.

Proof.

Let
F
be a diagram in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{y})})
. Then we may rewrite
F
as a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear combination of diagrams composed of the generating splits, merges, crossings and coupons, where:

•

no merge occurs below any split (via
Eq.

3.1.3
);

•

no crossing occurs below any split (via
Eqs.

3.1.6
and
3.1.7
);

•

no crossing occurs below any coupon (via
Eq.

3.1.12
);

•

no coupon occurs above any merge or below any split (via
Eq.

3.1.11
);

•

there is at most one coupon on any given strand (via
Eq.

3.1.9
);

•

all coupons are elements of
\mathtt{B}
(via
Eqs.

3.1.8
and
3.1.9
);

Applying relations in this manner, and together with
Eq.

3.1.2
and
Lemma

4.2.3
, we may express
F
as a
\mathbbm{k}

6.6.
Basis results for
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}

Proposition 6.6.1
.

Let
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=i_{1}^{(x_{1})}\cdots i_{t}^{(x_{t})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}=j_{1}^{(y_{1})}\cdots j_{u}^{(y_{u})}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I})
, and assume
n\geq\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert=\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert
. Then the morphisms
\{\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})\}
have linearly independent images under the functor
G_{n}
and, moreover,
G_{n}
defines an injective map

\displaystyle G_{n}:\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})\rightarrow{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)}(S^{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathbf{i}}V,S^{\mathbf{y}}_{\mathbf{j}}V).

Proof.

Choose some enumeration of tuples

\displaystyle\{(b_{1},r_{1},s_{1}),\ldots,(b_{z},r_{z},s_{z})\}=\{(b,r,s)\mid r\in[1,t],s\in[1,u],b\in{}_{j_{s}}\mathtt{B}_{i_{r}},\mu_{r,s}(b)>0\}.

Note that by definition of
\boldsymbol{\mu}
we have
n\geq z
, so we may define associated elements

\displaystyle v^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^{t}\prod_{m=1}^{z}(v_{m}^{i_{\ell}})^{\delta_{r_{m},\ell}\mu_{\ell,s_{m}}(b_{m})}\in S^{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathbf{i}}V,

and

\displaystyle w^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^{u}\prod_{m=1}^{z}(v_{m}^{b_{m}})^{\delta_{s_{m},\ell}\mu_{r_{m},\ell}(b_{m})}\in S^{\mathbf{y}}_{\mathbf{j}}V.

For all
y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
j\in I
,
S^{y}_{j}V
has a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis consisting of restricted monomials in
v_{k}^{b}
, ranging over
k\in[1,n]
,
i\in I
, and
b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
. Here,
restricted
means that the multiplicity of
v_{k}^{b}
in the monomial is less than or equal to one when
\bar{b}=\bar{1}
. Fixing such a basis for each
S^{y}_{j}V
, this gives a basis
W
of tensor products of monomials for
S^{\mathbf{y}}_{\mathbf{j}}V
. Up to sign,
w^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
is an element of
W
, so we have a map
p_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}:S^{\mathbf{y}}_{\mathbf{j}}V\rightarrow\mathbbm{k}w^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
given by linear projection along
W
. Now it follows from
Lemma

6.4.1
that

\displaystyle p_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\circ G(\eta_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}{a})(v^{\boldsymbol{\mu}})=\pm\delta_{\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\nu}}[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}w^{\boldsymbol{\mu}},

for all
\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
.
Thus the images under
G_{n}
of morphisms
\{\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{y})})\}
are linearly independent.
∎

The next result follows immediately.

Corollary 6.6.2
.

The functors
\{G_{n}\mid n\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}\}
are asymptotically locally faithful on
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
. That is, for any fixed morphism space in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
, the functor
G_{n}
defines an injective map for
n\gg 0
.

Propositions

6.5.1
and
6.6.1
also yield the following result.

Corollary 6.6.3
.

The morphisms
\{\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})\}
comprise a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
.

6.7.
A remark on arbitrary commutative rings

Recalling that
\mathbbm{k}
is a characteristic zero domain, let
\mathbbm{L}
be an arbitrary commutative ring of characteristic
p\geq 0
equipped with ring homomorphism
\mathbbm{k}\rightarrow\mathbbm{L}
. Letting
A_{\mathbbm{L}}:=\mathbbm{L}\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}A,a_{\mathbbm{L}}:=\mathbbm{L}\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}a
, we may follow
Definition

3.1.1
to construct an
\mathbbm{L}
-linear monoidal supercategory
{\mathbf{Web}}^{A_{\mathbbm{L}},a_{\mathbbm{L}}}_{I}
. As all relations are defined integrally, this category is isomorphic to
\mathbbm{L}\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
, and thus the morphism set of
Corollary

6.6.3
comprises an
\mathbbm{L}
-basis for morphism spaces in
{\mathbf{Web}}^{A_{\mathbbm{L}},a_{\mathbbm{L}}}_{I}
.

More generally if
(A^{\prime},a^{\prime})_{I}
is a good pair of
\mathbbm{L}
-superalgebras which are not necessarily a scalar extension of
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebras, we may still construct the
\mathbbm{L}
-linear monoidal supercategory
{\mathbf{Web}}^{A^{\prime},a^{\prime}}_{I}
as in
Definition

3.1.1
. In this setting
Proposition

6.5.1
holds, but there is now no guarantee of a basis result analogous to
Corollary

6.6.3
.

6.8.
Good subpairs

In this subsection we assume we have a good subpair
(A,a^{\prime})_{I}\subseteq(A,a)
. There is then an inclusion functor
\iota_{a^{\prime},a}:{\mathbf{Web}}^{A,a^{\prime}}_{I}\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
given by the identity on objects and diagrams.

.

For all
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I})

\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})

\displaystyle\iota_{a^{\prime},a}(\eta^{a^{\prime}}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}})=[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{b}\backslash\mathtt{b}^{\prime}}\,\eta^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}.

\boldsymbol{\mu}

\scriptstyle b^{\scriptstyle a}

and

respectively.
When

or

\scriptstyle b^{\scriptstyle a}

Lemma

Corollary 6.8.2
.

The functor
\iota_{a^{\prime},a}:{\mathbf{Web}}^{A,a^{\prime}}_{I}\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
is faithful, and for all
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I})
, the image of
{\mathbf{Web}}^{A,a^{\prime}}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
under
\iota_{a^{\prime},a}
is the full-rank
\mathbbm{k}
-submodule

\mathbbm{k}\{[\boldsymbol{\mu}]_{\mathtt{b}\backslash\mathtt{b}^{\prime}}^{!}\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})\}\subseteq\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}).

That is,
{\mathbf{Web}}^{A,a^{\prime}}_{I}
may be identified as a
\mathbbm{k}
-form in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
.

Remark 6.8.3
.

In particular, one may use
Corollary

6.8.2
to identify
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
with the
\mathbbm{k}
-form in
{\mathbf{Web}}^{A,A_{\bar{0}}}_{I}
spanned by morphisms of the form
[\boldsymbol{\mu}]_{\mathtt{B}_{\bar{0}}\backslash\mathtt{b}}^{!}\eta^{A_{\bar{0}}}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
. One may compare this feature with the definition of the Schurification of
(A,a)
described in
Section

7.2
.

6.9.
