on generating morphisms.

Proof.

It is straightforward to check that
\iota_{I}
is a well-defined functor. In consideration of
Eq.

6.9.1
and
Corollary

6.6.3
as applied to
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
and
{\mathbf{Web}}_{\{1\}}^{A,a}
, it is also straightforward to check that
\iota_{I}
induces a bijection on
\mathbbm{k}
-bases for morphism spaces, completing the proof.
∎

7.
Connection to Schurification

7.1.
The algebra
W^{A,a}_{n,d}

We have come to one of our primary motivations: the connection between
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
and the generalized Schur algebra (or, ‘Schurification’)
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
defined in
[
31
]
. Throughout this section, we assume that
(A,a)_{I}
is a good pair, and
I
is a finite set. We write
1=\sum_{i\in I}i
for the unit in
A
and
a
.
For
\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{t})\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}^{t}
we write
1^{(\mathbf{x})}:=1^{(x_{1})}\cdots 1^{(x_{t})}\in\Omega_{\{1\}}
.

For
n,d\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega(n,d)
, we set
W^{A,a}_{n,d}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}(1^{(\mathbf{x})},1^{(\mathbf{y})})
. Then we set

(7.1.1)

\displaystyle W^{A,a}_{n,d}:=\bigoplus_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega(n,d)}W^{A,a}_{n,d}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})

and view
W^{A,a}_{n,d}
as a unital superalgebra, as follows. For
\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}^{\prime}\in\Omega(n,d)
,
f\in W^{A,a}_{n,d}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}),f^{\prime}\in W^{A,a}_{n,d}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})
, we set
ff^{\prime}=\delta_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime}}f\circ f^{\prime}\in W^{A,a}_{n,d}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{y})
, where the composition is taken in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}
.
The unit in
W^{A,a}_{n,d}
is

\mathbbm{1}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega(n,d)}\textup{Id}_{1^{(\mathbf{x})}}.

By
Corollary

6.6.3

W^{A,a}_{n,d}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})
has
\mathbbm{k}
-basis
\{\eta^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(1^{(\mathbf{x})},1^{(\mathbf{y})})\}
.

7.2.
The Schurification of
(A,a)

In this section we follow
[
31
]
to define the generalized Schur algebra
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
and refer the interested reader to that paper for more detail. The tensor product
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra
M_{n}(A)^{\otimes d}
has a signed permutation action of the symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
as described in
Section

5.1
. We write

\displaystyle S^{A}(n,d):=(M_{n}(A)^{\otimes d})^{\mathfrak{S}_{d}}

for the sub-superalgebra of
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
-invariants.

Let
d_{1},d_{2}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, with
\xi_{k}\in S^{A}(n,d_{k})
for
k=1,2
. Let
\mathscr{D}^{d_{1},d_{2}}
be a set of right coset representatives for
(\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{d_{2}})\backslash\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}+d_{2}}
. Then we define the associative
star product
:

\displaystyle\xi_{1}*\xi_{2}:=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathscr{D}^{d_{1},d_{2}}}(\xi_{1}\otimes\xi_{2})^{\sigma}\in S^{A}(n,d_{1}+d_{2}).

If
U=\{u_{1}<\ldots<u_{t}\}
is a finite indexing set equipped with total order
<
, we denote

\displaystyle\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}^{<}_{u\in U}\xi_{u}=\xi_{u_{1}}*\cdots*\xi_{u_{t}}.

We have ‘left’ and ‘right’-sided injective algebra homomorphisms
{\tt L}_{n}^{n+m},{\tt R}_{n}^{n+m}:M_{n}(A)\rightarrow M_{n+m}(A)
given by
{\tt L}_{n}^{n+m}(E^{b}_{r,s})=E^{b}_{r,s}
and
{\tt R}_{n}^{n+m}(E^{b}_{r,s})=E^{b}_{r+m,s+m}
, which induce algebra homomorphisms
{\tt L}_{n}^{n+m},{\tt R}_{n}^{n+m}:S^{A}(n,d)\rightarrow S^{A}(n+m,d)
. For all
\xi_{1}\in S^{A}(n_{1},d_{1})
,
\xi_{2}\in S^{A}(n_{2},d_{2})
, we define the
shifted
star product:

\displaystyle\xi_{1}\bar{*}\,\xi_{2}:={\tt L}_{n_{1}}^{n_{1}+n_{2}}(\xi_{1})*{\tt R}_{n_{2}}^{n_{1}+n_{2}}(\xi_{2})\in S^{A}(n_{1}+n_{2},d_{1}+d_{2}).

For
\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega(n,d)
,
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(1^{(\mathbf{x})},1^{(\mathbf{x})})
we set

\displaystyle\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}:=[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}\left(\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}_{r=1}^{n}\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}_{s=1}^{n}\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}_{b\in\mathtt{B}}^{<}(E_{s,r}^{b})^{\otimes\mu_{r,s}(b)}\right)\in S^{A}(n,d),

viewing
(E_{s,r}^{b})^{\otimes\mu_{r,s}(b)}\in S^{A}(n,\mu_{r,s}(b))
. While our notation in this paper is slightly different, it is straightforward to check that if
\mathbf{b}=(b_{1},\ldots,b_{d})\in\mathtt{B}^{d},\mathbf{r}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{d}),\mathbf{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{d})\in[1,n]^{d}
are such that

\displaystyle\#\{t\in[1,d]\mid b_{t}=b,r_{t}=r,s_{t}=s\}=\mu_{r,s}(b),\qquad\textup{ for all }r,s\in[1,n],b\in\mathtt{B},

then we have that
\widetilde{\eta}^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
is equal to
\pm\eta_{\mathbf{b},\mathbf{r},\mathbf{s}}
, as defined in
[
31
, §3B]
. Then we define

\displaystyle T^{A}_{a}(n,d):=\mathbbm{k}\{\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}\mid\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega(n,d),\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(1^{(\mathbf{x})},1^{(\mathbf{y})})\}\subseteq S^{A}(n,d).

Lemma 7.2.1
.

[
31
, Lemma 3.10, Proposition 3.12]

T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
is a unital sub-superalgebra of
S^{A}(n,d)
, with
\mathbbm{k}
-basis

\{\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}\mid\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega(n,d),\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(1^{(\mathbf{x})},1^{(\mathbf{y})})\}
.

7.3.
Connecting algebras

For fixed
n\geq 1
, set
V_{n}=A^{\oplus n}
. Viewing this as column vectors of height
n
with entries in
A
, we consider this as a left
M_{n}(A)
-supermodule via matrix multiplication.

Lemma 7.3.1
.

There is a well-defined
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra map
\tau:W^{A,a}_{n,d}\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)
given by

(7.3.1)

\displaystyle\tau(\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}):\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{r_{\gamma}}^{f_{\gamma}}\mapsto[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}\sum_{T}(-1)^{\sigma(T)}\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{s_{\gamma}^{T}}^{b_{\gamma}^{T}f_{\gamma}}.

for all
\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega(n,d)
,
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(1^{(\mathbf{x})},1^{(\mathbf{y})})
.
Here the sum ranges over all
T=(T_{r,s}^{b})
such that
T_{r,s}^{b}\subseteq\{\gamma\in[1,d]\mid r_{\gamma}=r\}
,
\bigsqcup_{b,s}T^{b}_{r,s}=\{\gamma\in[1,d]\>|\>r_{\gamma}=r\}
, and
|T_{r,s}^{b}|=\mu_{r,s}(b)
. For
\gamma\in[1,d]
, we let
s_{\gamma}^{T}\in[1,n]
,
b_{\gamma}^{T}\in\mathtt{B}
be the unique elements such that
\gamma\in T_{r_{\gamma},s_{\gamma}^{T}}^{b_{\gamma}^{T}}
. Finally, the sign is given by

\displaystyle\sigma(T)=\sum_{1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\bar{f}_{\gamma}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
r_{\gamma^{\prime}}<r_{\gamma}\end{subarray}}\bar{b}_{\gamma}^{T}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
r_{\gamma^{\prime}}=r_{\gamma}\\
s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}<s_{\gamma}^{T}\end{subarray}}\bar{b}_{\gamma}^{T}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
r_{\gamma^{\prime}}=r_{\gamma}\\
s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}=s_{\gamma}^{T}\\
b_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}<b_{\gamma}^{T}\end{subarray}}\bar{b}_{\gamma}^{T}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}.

Proof.

There is an injective
\mathbbm{k}
-module homomorphism:

(7.3.2)

\displaystyle\chi:V_{n}^{\otimes d}\rightarrow\bigoplus_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega(n,d)}S^{\mathbf{x}}V_{n},\qquad\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{r_{\gamma}}^{f_{\gamma}}\mapsto(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{f}\rangle}\bigotimes_{\alpha=1}^{n}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in[1,d]\\
r_{\gamma}=\alpha\end{subarray}}^{<}v_{\gamma}^{f_{\gamma}}\in S^{\mathbf{y}}V_{n},

where
\mathbf{r}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{d})\in[1,n]^{d}
,
\mathbf{f}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d})\in A^{d}
,
y_{\alpha}=\#\{\gamma\mid r_{\gamma}=\alpha\}
, and

\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{f}\rangle:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
r_{\gamma^{\prime}}<r_{\gamma}\end{subarray}}\bar{f}_{\gamma}\bar{f}_{\gamma^{\prime}}.

Here and below the symbol
\prod^{<}_{u\in U}
indicates that the product should be taken in increasing order in accordance with the order
<
on the set
U
.

Then we have

(7.3.3)

\displaystyle G_{n}(\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a})\circ

\displaystyle\chi\left(\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{r_{\gamma}}^{f_{\gamma}}\right)=(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{f}\rangle}G_{n}(\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a})\left(\bigotimes_{\alpha=1}^{n}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in[1,d]\\
r_{\gamma}=\alpha\end{subarray}}^{<}v_{\gamma}^{f_{\gamma}}\right)

(7.3.4)

\displaystyle=[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{f}\rangle}\sum_{T}(-1)^{\sigma_{1}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{2}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{3}^{\prime}(T)}\bigotimes_{s=1}^{n}\prod_{r=1}^{n}\prod_{b\in\mathtt{B}}^{<}\prod_{\gamma\in T_{r,s}^{b}}^{<}v_{\gamma}^{b^{T}_{\gamma}f_{\gamma}}

(7.3.5)

\displaystyle=[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{f}\rangle}\sum_{T}(-1)^{\sigma_{1}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{2}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{3}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{4}^{\prime}(T)}\bigotimes_{s=1}^{n}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma\in[1,d]\\
s_{\gamma}^{T}=s\end{subarray}}^{<}v_{\gamma}^{b^{T}_{\gamma}f_{\gamma}}

(7.3.6)

\displaystyle=[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{f}\rangle}\sum_{T}(-1)^{\sigma_{1}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{2}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{3}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{4}^{\prime}(T)+\langle(s_{1}^{T},\ldots,s_{d}^{T}),(b_{1}^{T}f_{1},\ldots,b_{d}^{T}f_{d})\rangle}\chi\left(\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{s_{\gamma}^{T}}^{b_{\gamma}^{T}f_{\gamma}}\right).

In the above expressions,

\displaystyle\sigma_{1}^{\prime}(T)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
r_{\gamma}=r_{\gamma^{\prime}}\\
s_{\gamma^{\prime}}<s_{\gamma}\end{subarray}}\bar{f}_{\gamma}\bar{f}_{\gamma^{\prime}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
r_{\gamma}=r_{\gamma^{\prime}}\\
s_{\gamma}^{T}=s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\\
b_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}<b_{\gamma}^{T}\end{subarray}}\bar{f}_{\gamma}\bar{f}_{\gamma^{\prime}},

\displaystyle\sigma_{2}^{\prime}(T)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\in[1,d]\\
r_{\gamma}<r_{\gamma^{\prime}}\end{subarray}}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\bar{f}_{\gamma}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\in[1,d]\\
r_{\gamma}=r_{\gamma^{\prime}}\\
s_{\gamma}^{T}<s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\end{subarray}}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\bar{f}_{\gamma}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\in[1,d]\\
r_{\gamma}=r_{\gamma^{\prime}}\\
s_{\gamma}^{T}=s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\\
b_{\gamma}^{T}<b_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\end{subarray}}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\bar{f}_{\gamma},

\displaystyle\sigma_{3}^{\prime}(T)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\in[1,d]\\
r_{\gamma}<r_{\gamma^{\prime}}\\
s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}<s_{\gamma}^{T}\end{subarray}}(\bar{b}_{\gamma}^{T}+\bar{f}_{\gamma})(\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}+\bar{f}_{\gamma^{\prime}}),

\displaystyle\sigma_{4}^{\prime}(T)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
s_{\gamma}^{T}=s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\\
r_{\gamma^{\prime}}<r_{\gamma}\end{subarray}}(\bar{b}_{\gamma}^{T}+\bar{f}_{\gamma})(\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}+\bar{f}_{\gamma^{\prime}}).

The equality
Eq.

7.3.4
follows from
Eq.

6.4.1
, where
\sigma_{1}^{\prime}(T),\sigma_{2}^{\prime}(T),\sigma_{3}^{\prime}(T)
are the values
\sigma_{1}(T),\sigma_{2}(T),\sigma_{3}(T)
reindexed in terms of
\gamma\in[1,d]
. The equality
Eq.

7.3.5
follows from reordering the monomials in each tensor factor so that subscript indices are in increasing order, which incurs the sign associated with
\sigma_{4}^{\prime}(T)
. The equality
Eq.

7.3.6
is a direct application of
Eq.

7.3.2
.
It is straightforward, if tedious, to verify that for all
T
we have

\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{f}\rangle+\sigma_{1}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{2}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{3}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{4}^{\prime}(T)+\langle(s_{1}^{T},\ldots,s_{d}^{T}),(b_{1}^{T}f_{1},\ldots,b_{d}^{T}f_{d})\rangle+\sigma(T)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
r_{\gamma}=r_{\gamma^{\prime}}\\
s_{\gamma}^{T}=s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\\
b_{\gamma}^{T}=b_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\end{subarray}}b_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\bar{f}_{\gamma}.

But by the definition of
\boldsymbol{\mu}
, if
r_{\gamma}=r_{\gamma}^{\prime}
,
s_{\gamma}^{T}=s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}
,
b_{\gamma}^{T}=b_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}
, then we must have
\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}=\bar{0}
. Therefore

\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{f}\rangle+\sigma_{1}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{2}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{3}^{\prime}(T)+\sigma_{4}^{\prime}(T)+\langle(s_{1}^{T},\ldots,s_{d}^{T}),(b_{1}^{T}f_{1},\ldots,b_{d}^{T}f_{d})\rangle=\sigma(T).

Writing
\chi^{-1}
for the inverse map
\chi(V_{n}^{\otimes d})\rightarrow V_{n}^{\otimes d}
, it follows then that taking
\tau(f):=\chi^{-1}\circ G_{n}(f)\circ\chi
for any nonzero
f\in W^{A,a}_{n,d}
satisfies the claim.
∎

Lemma 7.3.2
.

The left multiplication action of
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
on
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
gives a
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra map
\widetilde{\tau}:T^{A}_{a}(n,d)\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathbbm{k}}(V_{n}^{\otimes d})
, with

(7.3.7)

\displaystyle\widetilde{\tau}(\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}):\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{r_{\gamma}}^{f_{\gamma}}\mapsto[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}\sum_{T}(-1)^{\sigma(T)}\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{s_{\gamma}^{T}}^{b_{\gamma}^{T}f_{\gamma}}.

for all
\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega(n,d)
,
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(1^{(\mathbf{x})},1^{(\mathbf{y})})
, where
T
and
\sigma(T)
are as in
Lemma

7.3.1
.

Proof.

We have

(7.3.8)

\displaystyle\widetilde{\tau}(\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a})\left(\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{r_{\gamma}}^{f_{\gamma}}\right)

\displaystyle=[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}\left(\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}_{r=1}^{n}\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}_{s=1}^{n}\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}_{b\in\mathtt{B}}^{<}(E_{s,r}^{b})^{\otimes\mu_{r,s}(b)}\right)\cdot\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{r_{\gamma}}^{f_{\gamma}}

(7.3.9)

\displaystyle=[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}\left(\sum_{T}(-1)^{\widetilde{\sigma}_{1}(T)}\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}E_{s_{\gamma}^{T},r_{\gamma}}^{b_{\gamma}^{T}}\right)\cdot\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{r_{\gamma}}^{f_{\gamma}}

(7.3.10)

\displaystyle=[\boldsymbol{\mu}]^{!}_{\mathtt{B}\backslash\mathtt{b}}\sum_{T}(-1)^{\widetilde{\sigma}_{1}(T)+\widetilde{\sigma}_{2}(T)}v_{s_{\gamma}^{T}}^{b_{\gamma}^{T}f_{\gamma}},

where

\displaystyle\widetilde{\sigma}_{1}(T)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
r_{\gamma^{\prime}}<r_{\gamma}\end{subarray}}\bar{b}_{\gamma}^{T}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
r_{\gamma^{\prime}}=r_{\gamma}\\
s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}<s_{\gamma}^{T}\end{subarray}}\bar{b}_{\gamma}^{T}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d\\
r_{\gamma^{\prime}}=r_{\gamma}\\
s_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}=s_{\gamma}^{T}\\
.b_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}<b_{\gamma}^{T}\end{subarray}}\bar{b}_{\gamma}^{T}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}

\displaystyle\widetilde{\sigma}_{2}(T)

\displaystyle=\sum_{1\leq\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}\leq d}\bar{b}_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{T}\bar{f}_{\gamma}.

The equality
Eq.

7.3.9
follows by deleting all terms in

\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}_{r=1}^{n}\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}_{s=1}^{n}\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}_{b\in\mathtt{B}}^{<}(E_{s,r}^{b})^{\otimes\mu_{r,s}(b)}
which act as zero on
\bigotimes_{\gamma=1}^{d}v_{r_{\gamma}}^{f_{\gamma}}
. Noting that
\widetilde{\sigma}_{1}(T)+\widetilde{\sigma}_{2}(T)=\sigma(T)
, the result follows.
∎

Theorem 7.3.3
.

We have an isomorphism of superalgebras

\displaystyle w:W^{A,a}_{n,d}\xrightarrow{\sim}T^{A}_{a}(n,d),\qquad\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}\mapsto\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a},

for all
\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega(n,d)
,
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(1^{(\mathbf{x})},1^{(\mathbf{y})})
.

Proof.

By
Lemmas

7.3.1
and
7.3.2
, we have
\tau(\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}{a})=\widetilde{\tau}(\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a})
for all
\boldsymbol{\mu}
, so it follows from
Corollary

6.6.3
and
Lemma

7.2.1
that
\tau(W^{A,a}_{n,d})=\widetilde{\tau}(T^{A}_{a}(n,d))
.
We have an inclusion
\iota:T^{A}_{a}(n,d)\hookrightarrow S^{A}(n,d)
, and a map
\widetilde{\tau}^{\prime}:S^{A}(n,d)\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathbbm{k}}(V_{n}^{\otimes d})
induced by the left action of
S^{A}(n,d)
on
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
. By
[
19
, Lemma 5.7]
,
\widetilde{\tau}^{\prime}
is injective. Thus
\widetilde{\tau}=\widetilde{\tau}^{\prime}\circ\iota
is injective, so it follows that
\widetilde{\tau}(T^{A}_{a}(n,d))\cong T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
. Writing
\widetilde{\tau}^{-1}
for the inverse superalgebra map
\widetilde{\tau}(T^{A}_{a}(n,d))\xrightarrow{\sim}T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
, we thus have a superalgebra map
\widetilde{\tau}^{-1}\circ\tau:W^{A,a}_{n,d}\rightarrow T_{a}^{A}(n,d)
which gives a bijection
\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}\mapsto\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}
on bases, proving the result.
∎

There is a natural right action of the wreath product superalgebra
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
on
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
, where
A
acts on
V_{n}=A^{\oplus n}
diagonally and
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
acts by permutation of tensor factors.

Corollary 7.3.4
.

We have

\displaystyle W^{A,A_{\bar{0}}}_{n,d}\cong S^{A}(n,d)\cong\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}(V_{n}^{\otimes d}).

Proof.

The left isomorphism follows by
Theorem

7.3.3
, since
T^{A}_{A_{\bar{0}}}(n,d)=S^{A}(n,d)
, as explained in
[
31
, Remark 3.17]
. The right isomorphism is due to
[
19
, Lemma 5.7]
.
∎

7.4.
Monoidal equivalence

Recall that
(A,a)_{I}
is a good pair, with
I
finite and
1=\sum_{i\in I}i
. For any
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=i_{1}^{(x_{1})}\cdots i_{n}^{(x_{n})}\in\Omega_{I}(n,d)
, define

(7.4.1)

\displaystyle\xi_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}=(E^{i_{1}}_{1,1})^{\otimes x_{1}}*\cdots*(E^{i_{n}}_{n,n})^{\otimes x_{n}}\in T^{A}_{a}(n,d).

We remark that, if
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})})
is defined by
\mu_{r,s}(b)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\delta_{r,k}\delta_{s,k}\delta_{b,i_{k}}x_{k}
for all
r,s,b
, then it follows that
\xi_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}=\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{a}
. The set
\{\xi_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}\mid\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}\in\Omega_{I}(n,d)\}
is a collection of orthogonal idempotents in
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
, and we have
1_{T^{A}_{a}(n,d)}=\sum_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}\in\Omega_{I}(n,d)}\xi_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}
if
I=\{1\}
.

7.4.1.
The category
{\mathbf{T}}^{A,a}_{I}

We define a monoidal supercategory
{\mathbf{T}}^{A,a}_{I}
as follows.
Set
\operatorname{Ob}({\mathbf{T}}^{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathbcal{a}})=\Omega_{I}
, with the monoidal structure on objects inherited from
\Omega_{I}
. For
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}\in\Omega_{I}
, define morphism spaces by

\displaystyle{\mathbf{T}}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})=\xi_{\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}T^{A}_{a}(n,d)\xi_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}\subseteq T^{A}_{a}(n,d)

provided
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}\in\Omega_{I}(n,d)
for some
n,d
, and set
{\mathbf{T}}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})=0
otherwise.
Composition of morphisms is given by multiplication in
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
, and the monoidal structure on morphisms is given by the shifted star product
\bar{*}
. It is straightforward to check (see for instance
[
31
, §5C]
) that this yields a well-defined monoidal supercategory.

Remark 7.4.1
.

If
I=\{1\}
, then, considered as algebras, we have

\displaystyle\widetilde{{\mathbf{T}}}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}=\bigoplus_{1^{(\mathbf{x})},1^{(\mathbf{y})}\in\Omega_{\{1\}}(n,d)}\xi_{1^{(\mathbf{y})}}T^{A}_{a}(n,d)\xi_{1^{(\mathbf{x})}}=\bigoplus_{n,d\geq 0}T^{A}_{a}(n,d),

so
{\mathbf{T}}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}
serves as an umbrella for all of the Schurifications of
(A,a)
. More generally,
\widetilde{{\mathbf{T}}}^{A,a}_{I}
is an idempotent truncation of
\bigoplus_{n,d\geq 0}T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
.

Theorem 7.4.2
.

We have an equivalence of monoidal supercategories

\displaystyle\chi:{\mathbf{T}}^{A,a}_{I}\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}

given by the identity on objects, and
\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\mapsto\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
on morphisms.

Proof.

The isomorphisms
w
of
Theorem

7.3.3
and
\iota_{I}
of
Theorem

6.9.1
yield an isomorphism

\displaystyle{\mathbf{T}}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})=\widetilde{\eta}_{\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}T^{A}_{a}(n,d)\widetilde{\eta}_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}\xrightarrow{w^{-1}}\eta_{\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}W^{A,a}_{n,d}\eta_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}={}_{I}\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})\xrightarrow{\iota_{I}^{-1}}\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})

for every
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}\in\Omega_{I}
which sends
\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\mapsto\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
, so the functor
\chi
is well-defined and fully faithful. That
\chi
respects monoidal structure follows from the following observation. Letting
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}),\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{k}^{(\mathbf{z})},\mathbf{m}^{(\mathbf{w})})
, for some
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})},\in\Omega_{I}(n_{1},d_{1})
,
\mathbf{k}^{(\mathbf{z})},\mathbf{m}^{(\mathbf{w})}\in\Omega_{I}(n_{2},d_{2})
, define
\boldsymbol{\omega}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}\mathbf{k}^{(\mathbf{z})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}\mathbf{m}^{(\mathbf{w})})
by setting
\omega_{r,s}(b)=\mu_{r,s}(b)
for
r,s\in[1,n_{1}]
, and
\omega_{r+n_{1},s+n_{1}}(b)=\nu_{r,s}(b)
for
r,s\in[1,n_{2}]
. Then it is straightforward to check that

\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\bar{*}\,\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}=\widetilde{\eta}_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}
and
\eta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\otimes\eta_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}=\eta_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}
, yielding the result.
∎

8.
The wreath category

8.1.
The wreath category, I

Now, we return to the assumption that
(A,a)_{I}
is a good pair, where
I
is not necessarily finite.

.

i

\mathbf{Wr}_{A}

\scriptstyle j

\scriptstyle i
\scriptstyle j

\scriptstyle f
\scriptstyle i
\scriptstyle j

for
i,j\in I
,
f\in jAi
. Crossings have parity
\bar{0}
, and the parity of the
f

\bar{f}
. Morphisms satisfy the following relations:

Let
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I,\textup{thin}}
be the full monoidal subcategory of
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}
consisting of the ‘thin strands’; that is, the full subcategory generated by the objects
\{i^{(1)}\mid i\in I\}
, so that

\displaystyle\operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I,\textup{thin}})=\left\{i_{1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes i_{t}^{(1)}\mid t\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0},i_{1},\ldots,i_{t}\in I\right\}.

Proposition 8.1.2
.

There is an isomorphism of monoidal supercategories,

\iota_{\textup{Wr}}:\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I,\textup{thin}},

given by
i\mapsto i^{(1)}
on generating objects, and

\displaystyle\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\textstyle{}$}}}}}}}}}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 14.29456pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-14.29456pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-24.24017pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\hbox to28.59pt{\vbox to48.48pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 14.29456pt\lower-12.85902pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}

for some

,

, and where for all

,
Z
consists only of crossings and carries the
k
th strand below to the
\omega(k)
th strand above.
But, by

, the images of such morphisms comprise a

-basis for
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I,\textup{thin}}(\iota_{\textup{Wr}}\mathbf{i},\iota_{\textup{Wr}}\mathbf{j})
, so
\iota_{\textup{Wr}}
is an isomorphism.
∎

8.2.
The wreath category, II

We give another formulation of the wreath product category. Fix
d\geq 0
. Let
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}^{A}_{I}(d)
be the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory defined as follows. The objects are the elements of the set

\left\{\mathbf{i}=1_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}}\otimes i_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes i_{d}\mid i_{1},\dotsc,i_{d}\in I\right\}.

For objects
\mathbf{i}
and
\mathbf{j}
, let

\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}^{A}_{I}(d)(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})=\bigoplus_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}}\sigma\otimes j_{\sigma 1}Ai_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes j_{\sigma d}Ai_{d}.

Composition is given on homogeneous morphisms by the rule

(\sigma\otimes f_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes f_{d})\circ(\tau\otimes g_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes g_{d})=(-1)^{\langle\tau;(f_{1},\dotsc,f_{d})\rangle}\sigma\tau\otimes(f_{\tau(1)}g_{1})\otimes\dotsb\otimes(f_{\tau(d)}g_{d}),

where the sign is according to the signed place permutation action as in
Section

5.1
.
Let

\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}^{A}_{I}=\bigoplus_{d\geq 0}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}^{A}_{I}(d).

This is a monoidal supercategory via concatenation. Namely, given
d_{1},d_{2}\geq 0
let
\iota=\iota_{d_{1},d_{2}}:\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{d_{2}}\hookrightarrow\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}+d_{2}}
be the embedding which identifies
\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}}\times\mathfrak{S}_{d_{2}}
as a Young subgroup of
\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}+d_{2}}
in the obvious way. Then the tensor product of objects
\mathbf{i}=1_{\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}}}\otimes i_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes i_{d_{1}}
and
\mathbf{j}=1_{\mathfrak{S}_{d_{2}}}\otimes j_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes j_{d_{2}}
is given by

\mathbf{i}\otimes\mathbf{j}=1_{\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}+d_{2}}}\otimes i_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes i_{d_{1}}\otimes j_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes j_{d_{2}}.

The tensor product of morphisms is given by

(\sigma\otimes f_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes f_{d_{1}})\otimes(\tau\otimes g_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes g_{d_{2}})=\iota(\sigma,\tau)\otimes f_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes f_{d_{1}}\otimes g_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes g_{d_{2}}.

Theorem 8.2.1
.

There is an equivalence of monoidal
k
-linear supercategories

\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}\cong\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}^{A}_{I}.

Proof.

Let
s_{1}\in\mathfrak{S}_{2}
be the nontrivial element. A check of the relations given in
Definition

8.1.1
shows there is a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear monoidal functor
H:\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}^{A}_{I}
defined as follows. On generating objects it is defined by
H(i)=1_{\mathfrak{S}_{1}}\otimes i
for all objects
i
of
A
. On morphisms, if
f\in jAi
, then on the generating morphisms of
\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}
the functor is given by

H\left(\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 14.29456pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-14.29456pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-24.24017pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\hbox to28.59pt{\vbox to48.48pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 14.29456pt\lower-12.85902pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

It is evident that this functor is essentially surjective and full. Combining
Propositions

8.1.2
and
6.6.3
yields bases for the morphism spaces of
\mathbf{Wr}_{A}
. Applying
H
to these bases yields bases for the morphism spaces of
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}^{A}_{I}
. Thus
H
is an equivalence of categories.
∎

For each
d\geq 0
consider the full subcategory
\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}(d)
of
\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}
consisting of all objects

I^{\otimes d}:=\left\{\mathbf{i}=i_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes i_{d}\mid i_{1},\dotsc,i_{d}\in I\right\}.

Since each of the morphisms in
\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}
preserve the number of objects in a tensor product we have the decomposition

\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}=\bigoplus_{d\geq 0}\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}(d).

Correspondingly, for each
d\geq 0
there is a superalgebra

\operatorname{Wr}^{A}_{I}(d)=\bigoplus_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}(d))}{\rm Hom}_{\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}}\left(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\right).

Let
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
denote the wreath product superalgebra. Since
A
has a distingished set of idempotents
I
, there is a corresponding set of distinguished idempotents for
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
:

1_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}}\otimes I^{\otimes d}=\left\{1_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}}\otimes i_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes i_{d}\mid i_{1},\dotsc,i_{d}\in I\right\}.

The equivalence in the previous theorem restricts to define an equivalence
\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}(d)\cong\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}^{A}_{I}(d)
for every
d\geq 0
and yields the following result.

Corollary 8.2.2
.

For every
d\geq 0
, there is an even isomorphism of idempotented superalgebras,

\psi_{A,d}:\operatorname{Wr}^{A}_{I}(d)\rightarrow\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A.

9.
Fullness of representations

9.1.
Defining representations

Write
\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
for the full monoidal subcategory of right
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-supermodules of the form
{}_{i_{1}}V_{n}\otimes\dotsb\otimes{}_{i_{d}}V_{n}
for some
d\geq 0
and
i_{1},\dotsc,i_{d}\in I
. For a fixed
d
, let
\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)(d)
denote the full subcategory consisting of objects in the aforementioned form with precisely
d
terms in the tensor product.

We consider the following functors to be the defining representation of the diagrammatic category in question:

\displaystyle G_{n}:\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{S}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A),

\displaystyle F_{n}:=G_{n}\circ\iota_{\textup{Wr}}:\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A),

\displaystyle F_{n}^{d}:\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}(d)\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)(d),

where
G_{n}
is from
Theorem

5.5.1
and
\iota_{\textup{Wr}}
is from
Proposition

8.1.2
.
It is evident that the functors
G_{n}
,
F_{n}
, and
F_{n}^{d}
are essentially surjective.

9.2.
Fullness for the web category

The following result allows a reduction to thin strands when working over a field of characteristic zero.

Proposition 9.2.1
.

Assume
\mathbbm{k}
is a field of characteristic zero. For a given
n\geq 0
, the functor,

G_{n}:\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{S}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A),

is full if and only if the functor,

F_{n}:\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A),

is full.

Proof.

For the proof, let
\widehat{G}_{n}:\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I,\textup{thin}}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
be the restriction of
G_{n}
. Since
\iota_{Wr}
is an equivalence,
F_{n}
will be full if and only if
\widehat{G}_{n}
is full. If
G_{n}
is full then clearly the restriction
\widehat{G}_{n}
to a full subcategory is still full. On the other hand, assume
\widehat{G}_{n}
is full. A standard argument using the explosion and contraction maps of
Section

6.1
shows
G_{n}
must also be full. Namely, the explosion and contraction maps along with
Lemma

6.1.1
establishes a commutative diagram as in
[
15
, Lemma 6.7.1]
and the argument used in the proof of
[
15
, Theorem 6.7.2]
then readily adapts to this setting.
∎

9.3.
Fullness for the wreath category

Consider

(9.3.1)

\bigoplus_{\mathbf{i}\in\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}(d)}F^{d}_{n}(\mathbf{i})=\bigoplus_{\mathbf{i}=i_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes i_{d}\in I^{\otimes d}}i_{1}V_{n}\otimes\dotsb\otimes i_{d}V_{n}\cong V_{n}^{\otimes d}.

This is a left
\operatorname{Wr}^{A}_{I}(d)
-supermodule and, via
\psi_{A,d}
from
Corollary

8.2.2
, a left
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodule. This action coincides with the action on
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
, where
A^{\otimes d}
acts diagonally by left multiplication and
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
acts by signed permutation of tensor factors. Furthermore, this action commutes with the right action by
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
given by right matrix multiplication (where we write
V_{n}=A^{\oplus n}
as row vectors).

Let

\rho^{A}_{n,d}:\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)

be the corresponding representation.
We call a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map
f:V_{n}^{\otimes d}\rightarrow V_{n}^{\otimes d}

finite
with respect to
I
if there is a finite set
J\subseteq I^{\otimes d}
such that
f(F^{d}_{n}(\mathbf{i}))=0
whenever
\mathbf{i}\not\in J
and the image of
f
lies in
\bigoplus_{\mathbf{j}\in J}F^{d}_{n}(\mathbf{j})
. We write
\operatorname{End}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)^{\text{fin}}
for the
\mathbbm{k}
-subsuperalgebra of all finite maps and note that it contains the image of
\rho_{n,d}^{A}
.

Proposition 9.3.1
.

For any fixed
n\geq 0
, the functor

F_{n}:\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)

is full if and only if the superalgebra map

\rho^{A}_{n,d}:\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)^{\textup{\text{fin}}}

is surjective for all
d\geq 0
.

Proof.

We first claim that if there is a nonzero morphism from an object of
\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)(d_{1})
to an object of
\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)(d_{2})
, then
d_{1}=d_{2}
. For any finite set of elements in
A
there is an
e\in A
given by a sum of distinguished idempotents which acts as the identity on those elements when right multiplied. In turn, given a fixed vector in an object of
\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)(d)
there is an
e\in A
such that
\sum_{r=1}^{n}E_{r,r}^{e}\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
acts on that vector by the scalar
d\in\mathbbm{k}
. Now, say there is an object
X
of
\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)(d_{1})
and an object
Y
of
\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)(d_{2})
with a nonzero
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism
f:X\rightarrow Y
. Choose
x\in X
so that
f(x)\neq 0
. Then there exists
e\in A
such that
\sum_{r=1}^{n}E_{r,r}^{e}
scales
x
by
d_{1}
and scales
f(x)
by
d_{2}
. It follows that
d_{1}=d_{2}
, as claimed.

From the previous paragraph it follows there is a decomposition

\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)=\bigoplus_{d\geq 0}\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)(d).

Thus the functor
F_{n}
is full if and only if the functor
F^{d}_{n}
is full for every
d\geq 0
.
However, from the discussion at the beginning of this section, this happens if and only if the induced superalgebra map

\rho_{n,d}^{A}:\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)^{\text{fin}}

is surjective.
∎

Combining
Theorems

11.2.2
,
9.2.1
, and
9.3.1
gives the following situation where the defining representations
G_{n}
and
F_{n}
are known to be full.

Proposition 9.3.2
.

If
\mathbbm{k}
is a field of characteristic zero and
A
is a finite-dimensional semisimple superalgebra, then the functors

\displaystyle G_{n}

\displaystyle:\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{I}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{S}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A),

\displaystyle F_{n}

\displaystyle:\mathbf{Wr}^{A}_{I}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{T}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A),

are full.

10.
The category
\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))

10.1.
The category
\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))

In this section we assume
(A,a)_{I}
is a good pair,
I
is finite, and
1=\sum_{i\in I}i
.
Let
\Lambda_{n}
be the free
\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
-module of rank
n
on basis
\{\varepsilon_{r}\mid r\in[1,n]\}
. For
\lambda\in\Lambda_{n}
we write
\lambda_{r}
for the coefficient of
\varepsilon_{r}
in
\lambda
.

Definition 10.1.1
.

Let
\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
be the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory consisting of objects
\Lambda_{n}
, and of morphisms generated by symbols

\displaystyle\{\mu E_{r,s}^{f}\lambda:\lambda\rightarrow\mu\mid r,s\in[1,n],\;\lambda,\mu\in\Lambda,\;\mu+\varepsilon_{s}=\lambda+\varepsilon_{r},\;f\in A\}.

We will often omit the symbols
\lambda
and
\mu
, writing
E_{r,s}^{f}
when the domain/codomain of the morphism is general or clear by context.
The parities of morphisms are given by
\overline{E_{r,s}^{f}}=\bar{f}
.
Morphisms in
\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
are subject to the following relations, for all admissible
\lambda\in\Lambda_{n}
,
r,s,p,q\in[1,n]
, and homogeneous
f,g\in A
:

(1)

E^{kf}_{r,s}=kE^{f}_{r,s}
for all
k\in\mathbbm{k}
.

(2)

E^{f+g}_{r,s}=E^{f}_{r,s}+E^{g}_{r,s}
.

(3)

E^{1}_{r,r}\lambda=\lambda_{r}\textup{id}_{\lambda}
.

(4)

E_{p,q}^{f}E_{r,s}^{g}-(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{g}}E_{r,s}^{g}E_{p,q}^{f}=\delta_{q,r}E_{p,s}^{fg}-(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{g}}\delta_{p,s}E_{r,q}^{gf}.

(5)

(E^{f}_{r,s})^{2}=\delta_{r,s}E^{f^{2}}_{r,s}
if
\bar{f}=\bar{1}
.

Remark 10.1.2
.

If
\mathbbm{k}
is a ring where 2 is invertible, relation (5) is redundant, as
2(E^{f}_{r,s})^{2}=2\delta_{r,s}E^{f^{2}}_{r,s}
is implied by (4) when
\bar{f}=\bar{1}
.

10.2.
A functor from
\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
to
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\},n}

Let
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\},n}
be the full subcategory of
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}
consisting of objects
1^{(\lambda_{1})}\cdots 1^{(\lambda_{n})}
, for
\lambda=\sum\lambda_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\in\Lambda_{n}
. In this section, as all strands are monotonically colored by
1
, for sake of space we will often write
x
for the object
1^{(x)}\in\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}
, and
\lambda
for the object
1^{(\lambda_{1})}\cdots 1^{(\lambda_{n})}
in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\}}
.

We occasionally omit the
\lambda
subscript and write
e_{[r,s]}^{(f,t)}
when the domain is general or clear from context.

Theorem 10.2.1
.

For each
n\geq 0
there is a functor

W_{n}:\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\},n}

given on objects by

W_{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\right)=1^{(\lambda_{1})}\dotsb 1^{(\lambda_{i})}

and on morphisms by

W_{n}\left(E_{r,s}^{f}\lambda\right)=e_{[r,s],\lambda}^{(f,1)}.

Proof.

We check that the defining relations in
Definition

10.1.1
are preserved by
W_{n}
. Indeed, (1) follows from
Eq.

3.1.8
, (2) follows from
Eq.

3.1.9
, (3) follows from
Eq.

3.1.4
, (4) follows from
Eqs.

3.1.2
,
3.1.3
, and
3.1.9
, and (5) follows from
Eqs.

3.1.3
and
3.1.10
.
∎

Lemma 10.2.2
.

Let
k\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}

is in
S^{n}_{k}(\lambda,\nu)
.

Proof.

We may assume that
y^{\prime}
is itself a composition of
m
many morphisms in
Y_{1}^{n}
.
First, note that if
t=0
, the claim holds trivially, and if
m=0
, then
y=e_{[r,s],\lambda}^{(f,t)}\in Y^{n}_{k}
, so we now make an inductive assumption that
m>0,t>0
and the claim holds when
m^{\prime}<m
or
t^{\prime}<t
.

As
m>0
, we may write
y^{\prime}=y^{\prime\prime}e_{[v,u]}^{(g,\ell)}
for some
v,u\in[1,n]
,
1\leq\ell\leq k
,
g\in A^{(\ell)}
, where
y^{\prime\prime}
is a composition of
m-1
morphisms from
Y_{k}^{n}
. If
v\neq s
, then
e_{[v,u]}^{(g,\ell)}
moves freely down below the split on the
s
th strand in
y
. Then the induction assumption on
m
may be used to complete the proof of the claim. So we now assume that
v=s
, so
y^{\prime}=y^{\prime\prime}e_{[s,u]}^{(g,\ell)}
, and we may write, using
Eqs.

3.1.2
,
3.1.11
, and
3.1.12
:

Finally, applications of
Eqs.

3.1.2
and
3.1.11
allow us to write such diagrams as
\mathbbm{k}
-linear combinations of diagrams of the form

\scriptstyle\cdots
\scriptstyle\cdots
\scriptstyle\cdots
\scriptstyle\cdots
y^{\prime\prime}
\scriptstyle\lambda_{1}
\scriptstyle\lambda_{s}
\scriptstyle\lambda_{u}
\scriptstyle\lambda_{n}
\scriptstyle\nu_{1}
\scriptstyle\nu_{r}
\scriptstyle\nu_{n}
\scriptstyle t^{\prime}
\scriptstyle t^{\prime\prime}
\scriptstyle\ell^{\prime}
\scriptstyle f
\scriptstyle f\hskip-0.56905ptg
\scriptstyle g

where
t^{\prime}+t^{\prime\prime}=t
and
\ell^{\prime}+t^{\prime\prime}=\ell
. If
t^{\prime}=0
or
t^{\prime\prime}=0
, then such diagrams are in
S^{n}_{k}(\lambda,\nu)
by the induction assumption on
m
. If
t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime}>0
, then applying the induction assumption on
t
to the
t^{\prime}
-thick strand, and subsequently to the
t^{\prime\prime}
-thick strand shows that such diagrams are in
S^{n}_{k}(\lambda,\nu)
. This completes the induction step and the proof of the lemma.
∎

Theorem 10.2.3
.

Morphisms in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\},n}
are generated under composition by the set
Y^{n}_{\infty}
in
Eq.

10.2.1
. If
\mathbbm{k}
is a field of characteristic zero, then morphisms in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\},n}
are generated under composition by the set

\displaystyle\widetilde{Y}_{1}^{n}:=\left\{e_{[r,s],\lambda}^{(1,1)}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda_{n},r,s\in[1,n]\right\}\cup\left\{e_{[r,r],\lambda}^{(f,1)}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda_{n},r\in[1,n],f\in A\right\}\subseteq Y^{n}_{1}.

Proof.

For the first claim, we have that morphism spaces in
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\},n}
are spanned by elements of the form
\eta^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
by
Proposition

6.5.1
.
We show that such spanning elements belong to the set
S^{n}_{\infty}
by induction on
d=|\lambda|
.
Let
\eta^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
for some
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\lambda,\nu)
, with
|\lambda|=d
. If
d=0
, then
\eta^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
is the identity morphism. Thus we may assume
d>0
, and that the claim holds for all
d^{\prime}<d
. Then there exists some
r,s\in[1,n]
,
b\in\mathcal{B}
such that
\mu_{s,r}(b)>0
, and so, pulling the strand with the coupon
b
and thickness
\mu_{s,r}(b)
off to the right in
\eta^{a}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
, we may write
