\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}$}}}}}}}}}.

Note that the central part of this last diagram is
e_{[r,r],\lambda-\varepsilon_{r}}^{(f,t-1)}
, which is in
S_{1}^{n}
by the induction assumption. But then
e_{[r,r],\lambda}^{(f,t)}\in S_{1}^{n}
by
Lemma

10.2.2
.

Thus we have that
\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\},n}
is generated under composition by
Y_{1}^{n}
when
\mathbbm{k}
is a field of characteristic zero. To show that it is generated by the smaller set
\widetilde{Y}_{1}^{n}
, we note that for all
f\in A
,
r,s\in[1,n]
, we have

\displaystyle e_{[r,s]}^{(f,1)}=e_{[r,s]}^{(1,1)}e_{[s,s]}^{(f,1)}-e_{[s,s]}^{(f,1)}e_{[r,s]}^{(1,1)},

by an application of
Eq.

3.1.3
.
∎

The following is an immediate corollary of the previous result.

Corollary 10.2.4
.

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be a field of characteristic zero. Then the functor

W_{n}:\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{A,a}_{\{1\},n}

is full for all
n\geq 0

11.
Polynomial representations and Schur–Weyl duality

11.1.
Polynomial representations

In this section we assume
(A,a)_{I}
is a good pair,
I
is finite, and
1=\sum_{i\in I}i
. Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a field equipped with a unital ring homomorphism
\mathbbm{k}\rightarrow\mathbbm{K}
.

Recall from
Section

9.3
that
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
is a
(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A,U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-bisupermodule. Thus, after base change, there is a superalgebra homomorphism

\zeta^{d}_{n,\mathbbm{K}}:U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A_{\mathbbm{K}}))\rightarrow S^{A}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}.

Lemma 11.1.1
.

If
\mathbbm{K}
is characteristic zero, then the homomorphism
\zeta^{d}_{n,\mathbbm{K}}
is surjective.

Proof.

Consider the good pair
(A,\mathbbm{k}1)_{\{1\}}
. First, observe that
S^{\mathbbm{k}1}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}=S(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
is the ordinary Schur algebra. It is well known that the corresponding map
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(\mathbbm{K}))\rightarrow S(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
is surjective and thus the restriction of
\zeta^{d}_{n,\mathbbm{K}}
to the subalgebra
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(\mathbbm{K}1))\subseteq U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
,

\zeta^{d}_{n,\mathbbm{K}}:U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(\mathbbm{K}1))\rightarrow S^{\mathbbm{k}1}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}},

is surjective.

From the definition of
T^{A}_{\mathbbm{k}1}(n,d)
given in
Section

7.2
and the fact that
\mathbbm{K}
has characteristic zero it follows that
S^{A}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}=T^{A}_{\mathbbm{k}1}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
. By
[
31
, Theorem 2]
,
T^{A}_{\mathbbm{k}1}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
is generated as a superalgebra by
\left\{\zeta^{d}_{n}(x)\mid x\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A_{\mathbbm{K}})\right\}
along with the subsuperalgebra
S^{\mathbbm{k}1}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
. Since both of these sets are in the image of
\zeta^{d}_{n}
, the result follows.
∎

By inflation through
\zeta^{d}_{n,\mathbbm{K}}
we can view the category of right
S^{A}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}
-supermodules as a subcategory of right
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A_{\mathbbm{K}}))
-supermodules which we call the
polynomial representations of degree
d
. When
\mathbbm{K}
is characteristic zero the previous result implies this is a full subcategory. We will freely identify these categories without comment in what follows.

11.2.
Schur–Weyl duality

Recall from
Section

9.3
that the image of
\rho^{A}_{n,d}
lies in the finite part of the centralizer of
S^{A}(n,d)
:

(11.2.1)

\rho^{A}_{n,d}:\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{S^{A}(n,d)}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)^{\text{fin}}.

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be an algebraically closed field of characteristic different from two equipped with a unital ring homomorphism
\mathbbm{k}\rightarrow\mathbbm{K}
. Upon base change to
\mathbbm{K}
there is a superalgebra map

(11.2.2)

\rho^{A_{\mathbbm{K}}}_{n,d}:\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A_{\mathbbm{K}}\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{S^{A}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}}\left(V_{n,\mathbbm{K}}^{\otimes d}\right)^{\text{fin}}=\operatorname{End}_{T^{A}_{a}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}}\left(V_{n,\mathbbm{K}}^{\otimes d}\right)^{\text{fin}}.

We remark that
\mathbbm{k}
is an integral domain,
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
is a free
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule, and
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-lattice of
S^{A}(n,d)
. From this it follows that
\operatorname{End}_{S^{A}(n,d)}(V_{n}^{\otimes d})=\operatorname{End}_{T^{A}_{a}(n,d)}(V_{n}^{\otimes d})
and, hence, after base change, the equality of endomorphism algebras given in
Eq.

11.2.2
holds. We say
Schur–Weyl duality holds for
A
over
\mathbbm{K}
if
\rho^{A_{\mathbbm{K}}}_{n,d}
is surjective for all
n,d\geq 0
. By
Proposition

9.3.1
this is equivalent to the functor
F_{n}
being full for all
n\geq 0
.

Remark 11.2.1
.

The results of
[
19
, Section 5.3]
show
\rho^{A_{\mathbbm{k}}}_{n,d}
is surjective whenever
n\geq d
and
|I|<\infty
.

Determining when Schur–Weyl duality holds is an interesting question which is beyond the scope of this paper. The following result verifies it in a situation which cover many cases of interest.

Theorem 11.2.2
.

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero equipped with a unital ring homomorphism
\mathbbm{k}\rightarrow\mathbbm{K}
. If
A_{\mathbbm{K}}
is a finite-dimensional semisimple
\mathbbm{K}
-superalgebra, then Schur–Weyl duality holds for
A
over
\mathbbm{K}
.

Proof.

Since
A_{\mathbbm{K}}
is semisimple it follows from
Remark

11.4.2
that
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A_{\mathbbm{K}}
is also semisimple. Since
S^{A}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{K}}\cong\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A_{\mathbbm{K}}}\left(V_{n,\mathbbm{K}}^{\otimes d}\right)
by
[
19
, Lemma 5.7]
, Schur–Weyl duality holds by the double centralizer theorem for finite-dimensional semisimple superalgebras (e.g., see
[
12
, Proposition 3.5]
).
∎

11.3.
Representations of finite-dimensional semisimple superalgebras

For the remainder of this section we assume
\mathbbm{k}
is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and that
A
is finite-dimensional and semisimple. We remind the reader that we allow all (not just parity preserving) supermodule homomorphisms and that our convention is to write maps on the side opposite to the action.

We give a brief overview of the representation theory of finite-dimensional superalgebras. Details can be found in, for example,
[
9
,
12
,
27
]
. We will discuss what happens for left supermodules and the reader can make the obvious translations to right supermodules and bisupermodules. Given an
A
-supermodule
M
, write
\Pi M
for the parity shift of
M
. For short we sometimes write
M^{p|q}=M^{\oplus p}\oplus(\Pi M)^{\oplus q}
. A simple
A
-supermodule
S
is
type
\mathtt{M}
if it remains irreducible as an
A
-
module
(ie., if
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-gradings are ignored). A simple supermodule
S
is of type
\mathtt{M}
if and only if
\operatorname{End}_{A}(S)
is
1|0
-dimensional. Otherwise,
S\cong T\oplus\Pi T
for some simple
A
-module
T
. In this case
S
is said to be of type
\mathtt{Q}
. A simple supermodule
S
is of type
\mathtt{Q}
if and only if
\operatorname{End}_{A}(S)
is
1|1
-dimensional, in which case
S
admits an odd involution. As another characterization, a simple supermodule
S
is of type
\mathtt{Q}
if
S
and
\Pi S
are isomorphic via an even map and of type
\mathtt{M}
if they are only isomorphic via an odd map.

Correspondingly, there are two types of finite-dimensional simple superalgebras: the superalgebra of linear endomorphisms of an
m|n
-dimensional superspace
V
,
M(V)
; and the superalgebra of linear endomorphisms of an
n|n
-dimensional superspace
V
which preserve an odd involution,
Q(V)
. In both cases
V
is the unique simple supermodule and is of type
\mathtt{M}
and type
\mathtt{Q}
, respectively. More generally, if
A
is a semisimple finite-dimensional associative unital superalgebra, then the Artin–Wedderburn theorem for superalgebras states that

(11.3.1)

A\cong\left(\bigoplus_{V\text{ of type $\mathtt{M}$}}M(V)\right)\oplus\left(\bigoplus_{V\text{ of type $\mathtt{Q}$}}Q(V)\right)

as superalgebras where the direct sum is over a complete, irredundant set of simple supermodules for
A
. If
V
is of type
\mathtt{M}
, then upon choosing a suitably ordered homogeneous basis of
m
even and
n
odd vectors we can write

(11.3.2)

M(V)\cong M_{m|n}(\mathbbm{k})=\left\{\left(\begin{matrix}W&X\\
Y&Z\end{matrix}\right)\right\}.

where
W
,
X
,
Y
, and
Z
are matrices over
\mathbbm{k}
with
W
being
m\times m
,
X
being
m\times n
,
Y
being
n\times m
, and
Z
being
n\times n
. Then
V\cong\mathbbm{k}^{m|n}
with
M(V)
acting by left multiplication. If
V
is of type
\mathtt{Q}
, then upon choosing a suitably ordered homogenous basis of
n
even and
n
odd vectors which are interchanged by the odd involution we have
Q(V)\cong Q_{n}(\mathbbm{k})
being matrices of the form
Eq.

11.3.2
with the additional condition that
W=Z
and
X=Y
. Again
V\cong\mathbbm{k}^{n|n}
.

If
A
and
B
are associative superalgebras and
S
and
T
are simple
A
- and
B
-supermodules, respectively, then the tensor product
S\otimes T
is an
A\otimes B
-supermodule. If both
S
and
T
are of type
\mathtt{M}
, then
S\otimes T
is a simple
A\otimes B
-supermodule of type
\mathtt{M}
. If exactly one of
S
and
T
are of type
\mathtt{Q}
, then
S\otimes T
is a simple
A\otimes B
-supermodule of type
\mathtt{Q}
. If both
S
and
T
are of type
\mathtt{Q}
, then
S\otimes T\cong(S\circledast T)\oplus\Pi(S\circledast T)
for a simple
A\otimes B
-supermodule
S\circledast T
of type
\mathtt{M}
(we make an arbitrary fixed choice of the simple subsupermodule denoted
S\circledast T
). We extend notation by declaring
S\circledast T
to be the simple
A\otimes B
-supermodule
S\otimes T
in the other cases. Applying this construction and ranging over all possible simple supermodules
S
and
T
yields a complete, irredundant set of simple
A\otimes B
-supermodules.

For a finite-dimensional semisimple superalgebra
A
, let
\Xi_{A}
be an index set for the simple left
A
-supermodules and write
S^{\alpha}
for the simple labeled by
\alpha\in\Xi_{A}
. For definiteness which will simplify notation later, we sometimes fix an order on
\Xi_{A}
and write
\Xi_{A}=\left\{1,\dotsc,\ell\right\}
according to that order.
Define a function

\delta:\Xi_{A}\rightarrow\{0,1\}

by
\delta(\alpha)=0
if
S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{M}
and
\delta(\alpha)=1
if
S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{Q}
.

Applying the tensor product rule discussed above shows that

(11.3.3)

\left\{S^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}:=S^{\alpha_{1}}\circledast S^{\alpha_{2}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast S^{\alpha_{d}}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{d})\in\Xi_{A}^{d}\right\}

is a complete, irredundant set of simple
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodules. Furthermore, if we define

\delta(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\begin{cases}0,\text{ if $\sum_{k=1}^{d}\delta(\alpha_{k})$ is even};\\
1,\text{ if $\sum_{k=1}^{d}\delta(\alpha_{k})$ is odd},\end{cases}

then
S^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
is of type
\mathtt{M}
if
\delta(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=0
and of type
\mathtt{Q}
if
\delta(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=1
.

Given an element
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}
and an
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodule
M
, let
{}^{\sigma}M=M
as a
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule with
A^{\otimes d}
action given by
(a_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes a_{d}).m=((a_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes a_{d})\sigma)m
, where
\sigma
acts on
A^{\otimes d}
by signed place permutation. There is an even isomorphism of
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodules,

{}^{\sigma}\left(S^{\alpha_{1}}\otimes S^{\alpha_{2}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{\alpha_{d}}\right)\cong S^{\alpha_{\sigma(1)}}\otimes S^{\alpha_{\sigma(2)}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{\alpha_{\sigma(d)}}.

Hence, after possibly replacing some of the simple supermodules in
Eq.

11.3.3
with their parity shifts, there is an even isomorphism of
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodules,

(11.3.4)

{}^{\sigma}S^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\cong S^{\sigma\cdot\boldsymbol{\alpha}},

for all
\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\Xi_{A}^{d}
and all
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}
, where
\sigma
acts on the left on
\Xi_{A}^{d}
by place permutation.

11.4.
Representations of wreath product superalgebras

For nonnegative integers
n
and
d
, let

\Lambda^{0}_{+}(n,d)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Lambda^{1}_{+}(n,d)

be the set of partitions of
d
with at most
n
nonzero parts, and the set of strict partitions of
d
with at most
n
nonzero parts, respectively. Recall that a partition is
strict
if it has no nonzero repeated parts.
For fixed
d\geq 0
, set

\Lambda^{0}_{+}(d)=\bigcup_{n\geq 0}\Lambda^{0}_{+}(n,d)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Lambda^{1}_{+}(d)=\bigcup_{n\geq 0}\Lambda^{1}_{+}(n,d).

Define
\delta(\lambda)=0
for all
\lambda\in\Lambda^{0}_{+}(d)
. Given any partition
\lambda
, let
\ell(\lambda)
be the number of nonzero parts in
\lambda
. For
\lambda\in\Lambda^{1}_{+}(d)
, define

\delta(\lambda)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{ if $\ell(\lambda)$ is even};\\
1,&\text{ if $\ell(\lambda)$ is odd}.\end{cases}

Recall that we have a fixed total order on
\Xi_{A}
and use it to identify
\Xi_{A}
with
\left\{1,\dotsc,\ell\right\}
. Given a sequence of nonnegative integers
\mathbf{n}=(n_{1},\dotsc,n_{\ell})
indexed by
\Xi_{A}
and a fixed
d\geq 0
, let

\Lambda^{A}_{+}(\mathbf{n},d)=\left\{\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})\;\left|\;\lambda^{(\alpha)}\in\Lambda^{\delta(\alpha)}_{+}(n_{\alpha},d_{\alpha}),\sum_{\alpha=1}^{\ell}d_{\alpha}=d\right.\right\}

be the set of
\Xi_{A}
-indexed multi-partitions of
d
where the partition
\lambda^{(\alpha)}
has at most
n_{\alpha}
nonzero parts, and
\lambda^{(\alpha)}
is strict whenever
S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{Q}
. Set

\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)=\bigcup_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}^{\Xi_{A}}}\Lambda^{A}_{+}(\mathbf{n},d).

Define

\delta:\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)\rightarrow\{0,1\}

by

\delta(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})=\begin{cases}0,&\text{ if $\sum_{\alpha=1}^{\ell}\delta(\lambda^{(\alpha)})$ is even};\\
1,&\text{ if $\sum_{\alpha=1}^{\ell}\delta(\lambda^{(\alpha)})$ is odd}.\end{cases}

If
A
is semisimple, then
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
is semisimple for all
d\geq 0
. Thus the representation theory of
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
comes down to describing the simple supermodules. These were given by Rosso–Savage in
[
36
, Proposition 4.3]
and shown to be indexed by
\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)
. As we will need a description of these simple supermodules which is somewhat different than theirs, we provide an alternate proof.

We will use without comment the following observation. Let
M
be a
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodule. If, when it is viewed as a
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodule via restriction,
M
contains a submodule isomorphic to
S^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}:=S^{\alpha_{1}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast S^{\alpha_{d}}
for some
\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{d})\in\Xi_{A}^{d}
, then it also contains
\sigma S^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\cong{}^{\sigma}S^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\cong S^{\sigma\cdot\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
for any
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}
. A similar statement obviously applies to supermodules for the Young subalgebras of
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
.

11.4.1.
Simple supermodules for Young subalgebras

Let
S=S^{\alpha}
be a simple
A
supermodule. Let
e\in A
be a minimal even idempotent such that
Ae\cong S
. By the tensor product rule given in
Section

11.3
,
S^{\circledast d}
is a simple supermodule for
A^{\otimes d}
and
e^{\otimes d}(S^{\beta_{1}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast S^{\beta_{d}})\neq 0
if and only if
\beta_{1}=\dotsb=\beta_{d}=\alpha
.

Let
\mathcal{e}
denote the even idempotent
1_{\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}}\otimes e^{\otimes d}\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
. Recalling the theory of idempotent truncation (e.g., see
[
23
, Section 6.2]
or
[
9
, Section 2]
), there is an exact functor

F_{\mathcal{e}}:\mathbf{smod}\text{-}\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\rightarrow\mathbf{smod}\text{-}\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A)\mathcal{e}

given by
F_{\mathcal{e}}M=\mathcal{e}M
. This functor defines a type-preserving bijection between the simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodules not annihilated by
F_{\mathcal{e}}
and the simple
\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A)\mathcal{e}\cong\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr(eAe)
-supermodules. From the previous paragraph we see that for a simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodule
T
,
F_{\mathcal{e}}T\neq 0
if and only if
T
contains a simple
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodule which is isomorphic to
S^{\circledast d}
.

Contemplating the matrix form of
A
given in
Section

11.3
shows that if
S
is of type
\mathtt{M}
, then
eAe\cong\mathbbm{k}
and
\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A)\mathcal{e}\cong\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr(eAe)\cong\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}
, where we view
\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}
as a superalgebra concentrated in parity
\bar{0}
. For
\lambda\in\Lambda^{0}_{+}(d)
let
D^{\lambda^{(\alpha)}}
be the simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodule for which
F_{e}D^{\lambda^{(\alpha)}}
is evenly isomorphic to the simple
\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}
-module
T^{0,\lambda^{(\alpha)}}
(viewed as a supermodule concentrated in parity
\bar{0}
) labeled by the partition
\lambda
. Then the set

\left\{D^{\lambda^{(\alpha)}}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda_{+}^{0}(d)\right\}

is a complete, irredundant set of simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodules which contain an
A^{\otimes d}
-submodule isomorphic to
S^{\circledast d}
. Furthermore, they are of type
\mathtt{M}
whenever
\delta(\lambda)=0
(i.e., always).

On the other hand, if
S
is of
\mathtt{Q}
, then
eAe\cong\operatorname{Cl}_{1}
and
\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A)\mathcal{e}\cong\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr(eAe)\cong\operatorname{Ser}_{d}
, the Sergeev superalgebra. For
\lambda\in\Lambda^{1}_{+}(d)
let
D^{\lambda^{(\alpha)}}
be the simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodule for which
F_{e}D^{\lambda^{(\alpha)}}
is evenly isomorphic to the simple
\operatorname{Ser}_{d}
-supermodule,
T^{1,\lambda^{(\alpha)}}
, labeled by the strict partition
\lambda
. Then the set

\left\{D^{\lambda^{(\alpha)}}\mid\lambda\in\Lambda_{+}^{1}(d)\right\}

is a complete, irredundant set of simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodules which contain a submodule isomorphic to
S^{\circledast d}
when viewed as a
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodule. Furthermore,
D^{\lambda^{(\alpha)}}
is of type
\mathtt{M}
if
\delta(\lambda)=0
and is of type
\mathtt{Q}
if
\delta(\lambda)=1
.

Now, fix a composition of
d
,
\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},\dotsc,d_{\ell})
with parts labeled by
\Xi_{A}
. Let
\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}=\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}}\times\dotsb\times\mathfrak{S}_{d_{\ell}}
be the corresponding Young subgroup of
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
and let
\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A=\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\otimes A^{\otimes d}
be the corresponding Young subalgebra of
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
. Given
\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)
such that
(\lVert\lambda^{(1)}\rVert,\dotsc,\lVert\lambda^{(\ell)}\rVert)=\mathbf{d}
, we can apply the tensor product rule from
Section

11.3
to
\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A\cong(\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}}\wr A)\otimes\dotsb\otimes(\mathfrak{S}_{d_{\ell}}\wr A)
to see that

D^{\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\lambda^{(\ell)}}

is a simple
\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A
-supermodule. Furthermore, it is of type
\mathtt{M}
if
\delta(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})=0
and of type
\mathtt{Q}
if
\delta(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})=1
.

Finally, observe that
D=D^{\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\lambda^{(\ell)}}
contains a simple
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodule isomorphic to
S^{\mathbf{d}}:=(S^{1})^{\circledast d_{1}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast(S^{\ell})^{\circledast d_{\ell}}
. Indeed, since the sum of all subsupermodules isomorphic to
S^{\mathbf{d}}
will be stable under the action of
\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A
, it follows that
every
simple
A^{\otimes d}
-subsupermodule of
D
is isomorphic to
S^{\mathbf{d}}
. Conversely, any simple
\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A
-supermodule which contains a simple
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodule isomorphic to
S^{\mathbf{d}}
is isomorphic to
D^{\mu^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\mu^{(\ell)}}
for some
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(d)
which satisfies
(\lVert\mu^{(1)}\rVert,\dotsc,\lVert\mu^{(\ell)}\rVert)=(d_{1},\dotsc,d_{\ell})
,

11.4.2.
Simple supermodules for wreath product superalgebras

For
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)
, let
\mathbf{d}=(\lVert\mu^{(1)}\rVert,\dotsc,\lVert\mu^{(\ell)}\rVert)
and let
\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\wr A=\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A
. Set

(11.4.1)

\left\{D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\wr A}(D^{\mu^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\mu^{(\ell)}})\mid\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)\right\}.

We claim this is a complete, irredundant set of simple supermodules for
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
.

Before proving the claim we make one observation which will be helpful in the proof. Fix
\boldsymbol{\mu}=(\mu^{(1)},\dotsc,\mu^{(\ell)})\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)
and let
\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},\dotsc,d_{\ell})=({\lVert\mu^{(1)}\rVert},\dotsc,{\lVert\mu^{(\ell)}\rVert})
. As discussed in the previous subsection,
D^{\mu^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\mu^{(\ell)}}
will then be a direct sum of copies of
S^{\mathbf{d}}=(S^{1})^{\circledast d_{1}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast(S^{\ell})^{\circledast d_{\ell}}
when viewed as an
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodule. Therefore, since

(11.4.2)

D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=\bigoplus_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}/\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}\sigma\otimes(D^{\mu^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\mu^{(\ell)}})\cong\bigoplus_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}/\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}{}^{\sigma}(D^{\mu^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\mu^{(\ell)}})

is a decomposition as
A^{\otimes d}
-supermodules, it follows that
S^{\beta_{1}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast S^{\beta_{d}}
appears as an
A^{\otimes d}
-summand of
D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
if and only if
(\beta_{1},\dotsc,\beta_{d})\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}\cdot(1^{\lVert\mu^{(1)}\rVert},\dotsc,\ell^{\lVert\mu^{(\ell)}\rVert})
.

Proposition 11.4.1
.

Let
A
be a finite-dimensional semisimple superalgebra. Then, the set

\left\{D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\mid\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(d)\right\}

is a complete irredundant set of simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodules and
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
is of type
\mathtt{M}
if
\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=0
and is of type
\mathtt{Q}
if
\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=1
.

Proof.

First, let
M
be a simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodule. We can choose a composition of
d
indexed by
\Xi_{A}
,
\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},\dotsc,d_{\ell})
, for which
S^{\mathbf{d}}=(S^{1})^{\circledast d_{1}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast(S^{\ell})^{\circledast d_{\ell}}
appears as an
A^{\otimes d}
-subsupermodule of
M
. Since
\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A
is a semisimple superalgebra, the discussion at the end of
Section

11.4.1
implies there is a
\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)
with
(\lVert\lambda^{(1)}\rVert,\dotsc,\lVert\lambda^{(\ell)}\rVert)=\mathbf{d}
for which
D^{\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\lambda^{(\ell)}}
appears as a
\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\wr A=\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A
-subsupermodule of
M
. Frobenius reciprocity along with the simplicity of
M
implies there is a homogenous surjective
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodule homomorphism

D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\twoheadrightarrow M.

In short, every simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodule is the quotient of
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
for some
\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)
.

Next, we show
Eq.

11.4.1
forms an irredundant set of simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodules by studying
{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}})
. First, obviously for there to be nontrivial homomorphisms it must be that
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
and
D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
have
A^{\otimes d}
composition factors in common. From
Eq.

11.4.2
it follows that
(\lVert\lambda^{(1)}\rVert,\dotsc,\lVert\lambda^{(\ell)}\rVert)=(\lVert\mu^{(1)}\rVert,\dotsc,\lVert\mu^{(\ell)}\rVert)
. Assume this is the case and let
\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},\dotsc,d_{\ell})
be this composition of
d
. By Frobenius reciprocity we have

(11.4.3)

{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}})\cong{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A}(D^{\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\lambda^{(\ell)}},D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}).

By considering
A^{\otimes d}
composition factors and
Eq.

11.4.2
it follows that the image of a
\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A
-supermodule homomorphism
D^{\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\lambda^{(\ell)}}\rightarrow D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
must have its image contained within the subspace
1_{\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}}\otimes D^{\mu^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\mu^{(\ell)}}
. That is,

(11.4.4)

{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A}(D^{\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\lambda^{(\ell)}},D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}})\cong{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A}(D^{\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\lambda^{(\ell)}},D^{\mu^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\mu^{(\ell)}}).

Combining
Eqs.

11.4.3
and
11.4.4
along with the discussion in
Section

11.4.1
demonstrates that
{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}})=0
whenever
\boldsymbol{\lambda}\neq\boldsymbol{\mu}
. When
\boldsymbol{\lambda}=\boldsymbol{\mu}
this endomorphism space has graded dimension
1|0
whenever
\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=0
and graded dimension
1|1
whenever
\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=1
. By Schur’s Lemma it follows that the set

\left\{D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\mid\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)\right\}

is an irredundant set of simple
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodules and the type is as asserted. The first paragraph implies this is also a complete set of simple supermodules. This proves the claim.
∎

Remark 11.4.2
.

While we will not use this fact, it is worth noting that the above construction gives the simple supermodules for
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
whenever
A
is a finite-dimensional superalgebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Write
J(B)
for the Jacobson radical of a superalgebra
B
. By
[
9
, Lemma 2.6]
this is a homogeneous ideal and coincides with the Jacobson radical of
B
as an algebra. The arguments of
[
14
, Section 3]
show that

(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A)/J(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A)\cong\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr\left(A/J(A)\right).

From this we see the semisimplicity condition can be dropped.

Since dualizing is a contravariant equivalence between left- and right-supermodules which preserves type, the following is immediate.

Corollary 11.4.3
.

The set

\left\{D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda},*}:=(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})^{*}\mid\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)\right\}

is a complete, irredundant set of simple right
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodules. The supermodule
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda},*}
is of type
\mathtt{M}
if
\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=0
and of type
\mathtt{Q}
if
\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=1
.

11.5.
Schur–Weyl–Berele–Regev–Sergeev duality

In this section we recall some well-known strong multiplicity-free decompositions.

Fix
M,N\geq 0
and
d\geq 1
. Let

\Lambda_{+}(M|N,d)^{\text{hook}}=\left\{\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dotsc,\lambda_{M+N})\in\Lambda_{+}^{0}(M+N,d)\mid\lambda_{M+1}\leq N\right\}.

That is, these are the partitions
\lambda
of
d
with not more than
M+N
parts that also satisfy
\lambda_{M+1}\leq N
(the so-called
hook condition
).

Let
W_{M|N}=\mathbbm{k}^{M|N}
. For any
d\geq 1
, let
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
act on the right on
W_{M|N}^{\otimes d}
by signed place permutation and let

S(M|N,d)=\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}}\left(W_{M|N}^{\otimes d}\right)

be the type
A
Schur superalgebra. For a partition
\lambda\in\Lambda_{+}^{0}(d)
recall we write
T^{0,\lambda}
for the simple left
\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}
-supermodule labeled by
\lambda
; it is viewed as a type
\mathtt{M}
supermodule concentrated in parity
\bar{0}
.

Applying the double centralizer theorem for semisimple superalgebras (e.g., see
[
12
, Theorem 3.10]
), there is a decomposition into simple
(S(M|N,d),\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d})
-bisupermodules:

(11.5.1)

W_{M|N}^{\otimes d}\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{+}(M|N,d)^{\text{hook}}}L_{\mathfrak{gl}(M|N)}(\lambda)\circledast(T^{0,\lambda})^{*}.

The set

\left\{L_{\mathfrak{gl}(M|N)}(\lambda)\mid\lambda\in\Lambda_{+}(M|N,d)^{\text{hook}}\right\}

is a complete, irredundant set of simple
S(M|N,d)
-supermodules. Every
L_{\mathfrak{gl}(M|N)}(\lambda)
is of type
\mathtt{M}
. Correspondingly, for every
\lambda\in\Lambda_{+}(M|N,d)^{\text{hook}}
we declare
\delta(\lambda)=0
.
type

Next, fix
N\geq 0
and
d\geq 1
. Set
\Lambda_{+}(N,d)^{\text{strict}}
to be the set of all strict partitions of
d
with not more than
N
parts. Let
W_{N}=\mathbbm{k}^{N|N}
. There is a right action of
\operatorname{Ser}_{d}
, the Sergeev superalgebra, on
(W_{N})^{\otimes d}
. Let

Q(N,d)=\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{Ser}_{d}}\left(W_{N}^{\otimes d}\right)

be the type
Q
Schur superalgebra. For a strict partition
\lambda
of
d
recall we write
T^{1,\lambda}
for the simple left
\operatorname{Ser}_{d}
-supermodule labeled by
\lambda
. For strict partitions define

\delta(\lambda)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{ if $\ell(\lambda)$ is even};\\
1,&\text{ if $\ell(\lambda)$ is odd}.\end{cases}

The supermodule
T^{1,\lambda}
is of type
\mathtt{M}
if
\delta(\lambda)=0
and of type
\mathtt{Q}
if
\delta(\lambda)=1
.

Applying the double centralizer theorem for semisimple superalgebras (e.g., see
[
12
, Theorem 3.46]
), there is a decomposition into simple
(Q(N,d),\operatorname{Ser}_{d})
-bisupermodules:

(11.5.2)

W_{N}^{\otimes d}\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{+}(N,d)^{\text{strict}}}L_{\mathfrak{q}(N)}(\lambda)\circledast(T^{1,\lambda})^{*}.

The set

\left\{L_{\mathfrak{q}(N)}(\lambda)\mid\lambda\in\Lambda_{+}(N,d)^{\text{strict}}\right\}

is a complete, irredundant set of simple
Q(N,d)
-supermodules. The supermodules
L_{\mathfrak{q}(N)}(\lambda)
and
T^{1,\lambda}
have the same type; namely, they are of type
\mathtt{M}
if
\delta(\lambda)=0
and of type
\mathtt{Q}
if
\delta(\lambda)=1
.

11.6.
Polynomial representations and generalized Schur–Weyl duality

We next study how the previous section generalizes when
A
is an arbitrary finite-dimensional semisimple superalgebra. The double centralizer theorem for semisimple superalgebras (see
[
12
, Proposition 3.5]
) combined with the classification of simple right
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodules given in
Corollary

11.4.3
yields the following strong multiplicity-free result.

Proposition 11.6.1
.

If
A
be a finite-dimensional semisimple superalgebra, then there is a subset

\mathbb{X}^{A}(n,d)\subseteq\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)

such that there is a decomposition

V_{n}^{\otimes d}\cong\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\mathbb{X}^{A}(n,d)}L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\circledast D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda},*}

into simple
(S^{A}(n,d),\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A)
-bisupermodules.

The set

\left\{L(\boldsymbol{\lambda}):=L_{n}^{A}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\mid\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\mathbb{X}^{A}(n,d)\right\}

is a complete, irredundant set of simple
S^{A}(n,d)
-supermodules. The supermodule
L(\boldsymbol{\lambda})
is of type
\mathtt{M}
if
\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=0
and of type
\mathtt{Q}
if
\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=1
.

The obvious problem is to determine the set
\mathbb{X}^{A}(n,d)
. We do this next. For each
\alpha\in\Xi_{A}
, say
S^{\alpha}
has graded dimension
m_{\alpha}|n_{\alpha}
. For a fixed
n\geq 1
, let
M_{\alpha}=nm_{\alpha}
and
N_{\alpha}=nn_{\alpha}
. For each
\alpha\in\Xi_{A}
, and fixed
n\geq 1
and
d\geq 0
, let

\Lambda^{\alpha}_{+}(n,d)=\begin{cases}\Lambda_{+}(M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha},d)^{\text{hook}},&\text{ if $\delta(\alpha)=0$};\\
\Lambda_{+}(N_{\alpha},d)^{\text{strict}},&\text{ if $\delta(\alpha)=1$}.\end{cases}

For each
\alpha\in\Xi_{A}
and fixed
n\geq 1
, let

\Lambda^{\alpha}_{+}(n,\bullet)=\bigcup_{d\geq 0}\Lambda_{+}^{\alpha}(n,d).

In other words, elements of
\Lambda^{\alpha}_{+}(n,\bullet)
are partitions which have a limited number of nonzero parts where the limit depends on
S^{\alpha}
and
n
, and which are hook partitions if
S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{M}
and are strict partitions if
S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{Q}
.

Finally,
for fixed
n\geq 1
and
d\geq 0
, set

\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,d)=\left\{\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})\in\prod_{\alpha\in\Xi_{A}}\Lambda^{\alpha}_{+}(n,\bullet)\;\left|\;\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\lVert\lambda^{(i)}\rVert=d\right.\right\}.

In other words,
\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,d)
is the set of multipartitions of
d
indexed by the set
\Xi_{A}
where each
\lambda^{(\alpha)}
has a limited number of nonzero parts where the limit depends on
S^{\alpha}
and
n
, and which is a hook partition if
S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{M}
and is a strict partition if
S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{Q}
. For a fixed composition of
d
with parts indexed by
\Xi_{A}
,
\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},\dotsc,d_{\ell})
, let

\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,\mathbf{d})=\left\{\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,d)\;\left|\;\lVert\lambda^{(\alpha)}\rVert=d_{\alpha}\text{ for $\alpha\in\Xi_{A}$}\right.\right\}.

Obviously,
\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,\mathbf{d})\subseteq\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,d)\subseteq\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)
and

\bigcup_{\mathbf{d}}\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,\mathbf{d})=\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,d),

where the union is over all compositions of
d
indexed by
\Xi_{A}
.

The next result confirms
\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,d)
is the set we seek.

Theorem 11.6.2
.

If
A
is a finite-dimensional semisimple
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra, then for all
n\geq 1
and
d\geq 0
,

\mathbb{X}^{A}(n,d)=\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,d).

That is, the set

\left\{L(\boldsymbol{\lambda}):=L_{n}^{A}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\;\left|\;\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,d)\right.\right\}

is a complete, irredundant set of simple
S^{A}(n,d)
-supermodules. The supermodule
L_{n}^{A}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})
is of type
\mathtt{M}
if
\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=0
and of type
\mathtt{Q}
if
\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=1
.

Proof.

First, since
A\cong A^{*}
as
(A,A)
-bisupermodules, we have

\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)^{*}\cong V_{n}^{\otimes d}

as left
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodules. In particular,
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda},*}
appears as a summand of
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
as a right
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodule if and only if
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
appears in
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
as a left
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodule.

Now let
\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(d)
and let
\mathbf{d}=(\lVert\lambda^{(1)}\rVert,\dotsc,\lVert\lambda^{(\ell)}\rVert)=(d_{1},\dotsc,d_{\ell})
be the corresponding composition of
d
. In light of
Proposition

11.6.1
and the first paragraph, it suffices to compute the dimension of

{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}\left(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)\cong{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\wr A}\left(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\lambda^{(\ell)}},V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right),

where the isomorphism is parity preserving and follows from Frobenius reciprocity.

For
\alpha\in\Xi_{A}
, fix a minimal even idempotent
e_{\alpha}\in A
so that
Ae_{\alpha}\cong S^{\alpha}
as left
A
-supermodules. Set

\mathcal{e}=1_{\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}}\otimes e_{1}^{\otimes d_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes e_{\ell}^{\otimes d_{\ell}}\in\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{d}}\wr A.

A direct calculation verifies that

\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\wr A)\mathcal{e}\cong\left(\mathfrak{S}_{d_{1}}\wr(e_{1}Ae_{1})\right)\otimes\dotsb\otimes\left(\mathfrak{S}_{d_{\ell}}\wr(e_{\ell}Ae_{\ell})\right).

Contemplating the description of
A
as matrices given after
Eq.

11.3.1
shows that for all
\alpha\in\Xi_{A}
,

e_{\alpha}Ae_{\alpha}\cong\begin{cases}\mathbbm{k},&\text{ if $\delta(\alpha)=0$};\\
\operatorname{Cl}_{1},&\text{ if $\delta(\alpha)=1$}.\end{cases}

For short, let
\mathfrak{S}^{0}_{d}=\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}
and
\mathfrak{S}^{1}_{d}=\operatorname{Ser}_{d}
. Then,

\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\wr A)\mathcal{e}\cong\mathfrak{S}^{\delta(1)}_{d_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes\mathfrak{S}^{\delta(\ell)}_{d_{\ell}}.

For
z=0,1
and
\mu\in\Lambda_{+}^{z}(d)
, let
T^{z,\mu}
be the simple
\mathfrak{S}^{z}_{d}
-supermodule labeled by
\mu
using the labeling choice given in
Section

11.4
.

Using the theory of idempotent trunction (e.g., see
[
23
, Section 6.2]
or see
[
9
, Section 2]
for the super version), since
\mathcal{e}D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\neq 0
it must be a simple
\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\wr A)\mathcal{e}
-supermodule of the same type as
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
and, moreover, there is an isomorphism

{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\wr A}\left(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)\cong{\rm Hom}_{\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\wr A)\mathcal{e}}\left(\mathcal{e}D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},\mathcal{e}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)\right).

Since
\mathcal{e}
is even the isomorphism is parity preserving. It follows from the discussion in
Section

11.4
that

\mathcal{e}D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=e_{1}^{\otimes d_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes e_{\ell}^{\otimes d_{\ell}}\left(D^{\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast D^{\lambda^{\ell}}\right)\cong T^{\delta(1),\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast T^{\delta(\ell),\lambda^{(\ell)}}.

Thus we are reduced to determining the multiplicity of
T^{\delta(1),\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast T^{\delta(\ell),\lambda^{(\ell)}}
in
\mathcal{e}\left({V}_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)
as
\mathcal{e}\left(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\right)\mathcal{e}\cong\mathfrak{S}^{\delta(1)}_{d_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes\mathfrak{S}^{\delta(\ell)}_{d_{\ell}}
-supermodules.

For each
\alpha\in\Xi_{A}
, say
S^{\alpha}
has graded dimension
m_{\alpha}|n_{\alpha}
. Then,

(11.6.1)

\displaystyle\mathcal{e}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)

\displaystyle=\left(e_{1}V_{n}\right)^{\otimes d_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes\left(e_{\ell}V_{n}\right)^{\otimes d_{\ell}}

(11.6.2)

\displaystyle=\left((e_{1}A)^{\oplus n}\right)^{\otimes d_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes\left((e_{\ell}A)^{\oplus n}\right)^{\otimes d_{\ell}}

(11.6.3)

\displaystyle=\left((\mathbbm{k}^{m_{1}|n_{1}})^{\oplus n}\right)^{\otimes d_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes\left((\mathbbm{k}^{m_{\ell}|n_{\ell}})^{\oplus n}\right)^{\otimes d_{\ell}}.

Let us analyze this supermodule by first studying the tensor factor corresponding to a fixed
\alpha\in\Xi_{A}
.

The first case is if
\delta(\alpha)=0
,
S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{M}
, and
S^{\alpha}
has graded dimension
m_{\alpha}|n_{\alpha}
. Setting
M_{\alpha}=nm_{\alpha}
and
N_{\alpha}=nn_{\alpha}
, we have
(\mathbbm{k}^{m_{\alpha}|n_{\alpha}})^{\oplus n}\cong W_{M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha}}
as superspaces and
\mathfrak{S}^{0}_{d_{\alpha}}=\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d_{\alpha}}
acts on
(W_{M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha}})^{\otimes d_{\alpha}}
by signed place permutation as in
Eq.

11.5.1
. By
Eq.

11.5.1
and the observation at the start of the proof,
T^{0,\lambda^{(\alpha)}}
appears in
(W_{M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha}})^{\otimes d_{\alpha}}
if and only if
\lambda^{(\alpha)}\in\Lambda_{+}(M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha},d_{\alpha})^{\text{hook}}
; moreover, its multiplicity equals
2^{-\delta(\lambda^{(\alpha)})}\dim_{\mathbbm{k}}(L_{\mathfrak{gl}(M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha})}(\lambda^{(\alpha)}))
. For the remainder of this proof when we are in this case we sometimes write
L^{0}_{M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha}}(\lambda^{(\alpha)})
for
L_{\mathfrak{gl}(M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha})}(\lambda^{(\alpha)})
.

The second case is if
\delta(\alpha)=1
,
S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{Q}
, and
S^{\alpha}
has graded dimension
n_{\alpha}|n_{\alpha}
. Setting
N_{\alpha}=nn_{\alpha}
, we have
(\mathbbm{k}^{n_{\alpha}|n_{\alpha}})^{\oplus n}\cong\mathbbm{k}^{N_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha}}=W_{N_{\alpha}}
as superspaces and
\mathfrak{S}^{1}_{d_{\alpha}}=\operatorname{Ser}_{d_{\alpha}}
acts on
W_{N_{\alpha}}^{\otimes d_{\alpha}}
as in
Eq.

11.5.2
. By
Eq.

11.5.2
and the observation at the start of the proof,
T^{1,\lambda^{(\alpha)}}
appears in
(W_{N_{\alpha}})^{d_{\alpha}}
if and only if
\lambda^{(\alpha)}\in\Lambda_{+}(N_{\alpha},d_{\alpha})^{\text{strict}}
; moreover, its multiplicity equals
2^{-\delta(\lambda^{(\alpha)})}\dim_{\mathbbm{k}}(L_{\mathfrak{q}(N_{\alpha})}(\lambda^{(\alpha)}))
. For the remainder of this proof when we are in this case we declare
M_{\alpha}=N_{\alpha}
and sometimes write
L^{1}_{M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha}}(\lambda^{(\alpha)})
for
L_{\mathfrak{q}(N_{\alpha})}(\lambda^{(\alpha)})
.

Applying these two cases to
Eq.

11.6.1
yields the
\mathcal{e}\left(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\right)\mathcal{e}\cong\mathfrak{S}^{\delta(1)}_{d_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes\mathfrak{S}^{\delta(\ell)}_{d_{\ell}}
-supermodule isomorphism

(11.6.4)

\mathcal{e}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)\cong\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(n,\mathbf{d})}2^{-h(\boldsymbol{\lambda})}d(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\left(T^{\delta(1),\lambda^{(1)}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes T^{\delta(\ell),\lambda^{(\ell)}}\right),

where

d(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\dim_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(L^{\delta(1)}_{M_{1}|N_{1}}(\lambda^{(1)})\otimes\dotsb\otimes L^{\delta(\ell)}_{M_{\ell}|N_{\ell}}(\lambda^{(\ell)})\right)

and

h(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\delta(\lambda^{(i)}).

Recall that the function
\delta
was defined on hook and strict partitions in
Section

11.5
. Also note that the isomorphism in
Eq.

11.6.4
is parity preserving.

Finally, applying the tensor product rule from
Section

11.3
to
Eq.

11.6.4
yields the following decomposition as
\mathcal{e}\left(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\right)\mathcal{e}\cong\mathfrak{S}^{\delta(1)}_{d_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes\mathfrak{S}^{\delta(\ell)}_{d_{\ell}}
-supermodules:

\mathcal{e}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)\cong\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda^{(1)},\dotsc,\lambda^{(\ell)})\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(n,\mathbf{d})}2^{\lfloor h(\boldsymbol{\lambda})/2\rfloor-h(\boldsymbol{\lambda})}d(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\left(T^{\delta(1),\lambda^{(1)}}\circledast\dotsb\circledast T^{\delta(\ell),\lambda^{(\ell)}}\right).

Combined with the earlier reductions, we conclude that the multiplicity of
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda},*}
in
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
is nonzero if and only if
\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(n,d)
. When it is nonzero the multiplicity equals
2^{\lfloor h(\boldsymbol{\lambda})/2\rfloor-h(\boldsymbol{\lambda})}d(\boldsymbol{\lambda})
. The assertions of the theorem follow from this and
Proposition

11.6.1
.
∎

Remark 11.6.3
.

Given a finite-dimensional semisimple superalgebra
B
, a
B
-supermodule
M
, and a simple
B
-supermodule
S
, the
graded multiplicity
of
S
in
M
is defined to be
p|q
if the
S
-isotypic component of
M
is isomorphic via a parity preserving map to
S^{\oplus p}\oplus(\Pi S)^{\oplus q}
. If the reader attends to the graded dimensions in the previous proof they will find that the graded multiplicity of
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
in
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
is equal to

\displaystyle 2^{\lfloor h(\boldsymbol{\lambda})/2\rfloor-h(\boldsymbol{\lambda})}\operatorname{grdim}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(L^{\delta(1)}_{M_{1}|N_{1}}(\lambda^{(1)})\otimes\dotsb\otimes L^{\delta(\ell)}_{M_{\ell}|N_{\ell}}(\lambda^{(\ell)})\right)

\displaystyle=2^{-\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})}\operatorname{grdim}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(L^{\delta(1)}_{M_{1}|N_{1}}(\lambda^{(1)})\circledast\dotsb\circledast L^{\delta(\ell)}_{M_{\ell}|N_{\ell}}(\lambda^{(\ell)})\right).

Therefore,

\operatorname{grdim}_{\mathbbm{k}}L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})=\operatorname{grdim}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(L^{\delta(1)}_{M_{1}|N_{1}}(\lambda^{(1)})\circledast\dotsb\circledast L^{\delta(\ell)}_{M_{\ell}|N_{\ell}}(\lambda^{(\ell)})\right).

for all
\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(n,d)
.

This is a numerical foreshadow of the fact
S^{A}(n,d)
is isomorphic to direct sum of tensor products of Schur superalgebras of types
\mathtt{A}
and
\mathtt{Q}
. We show this next. For
\alpha\in\Xi_{A}
and
d\geq 0
, say
S^{\alpha}
has graded dimension
m_{\alpha}|n_{\alpha}
and let
M_{\alpha}=nm_{\alpha}
and
N_{\alpha}=nn_{\alpha}
. Set

S^{\alpha}(n,d)=\begin{cases}S(M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha},d),&\text{ if $\delta(\alpha)=0$};\\
Q(N_{\alpha},d),&\text{ if $\delta(\alpha)=1$}.\end{cases}

Proposition 11.6.4
.

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and let
A
be a finite-dimensional semisimple
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra. Then, for all
n\geq 1
and
d\geq 0
, there is an isomorphism of superalgebras

S^{A}(n,d)\cong\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},\dotsc,d_{\ell})\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}^{\Xi_{A}}\\
\lVert\mathbf{d}\rVert=d\end{subarray}}S^{1}(n,d_{1})\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{\ell}(n,d_{\ell}).

Proof.

Let
A=\oplus_{\alpha\in\Xi_{A}}A_{\alpha}
be the decomposition given in
Eq.

11.3.1
. By
[
31
, Lemma 4.8]
there is a superalgebra isomorphism

(11.6.5)

S^{A}(n,d)\cong\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},\dotsc,d_{\ell})\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}^{\Xi_{A}}\\
\lVert\mathbf{d}\rVert=d\end{subarray}}S^{A_{1}}(n,d_{1})\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{A_{\ell}}(n,d_{\ell}).

Thus it suffices to describe
S^{A}(n,d)
when
A
is a semisimple superalgebra with a single simple module. Assume
A
is such a superalgebra.

If
\delta(\alpha)=0
, then the simple supermodule
S=S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{M}
. Say it has graded dimension
m_{\alpha}|n_{\alpha}
, and set
M_{\alpha}=m_{\alpha}n
and
N_{\alpha}=n_{\alpha}n
. Let
e\in A
be a minimal even idempotent and set
\mathcal{e}=1_{\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}}\otimes e^{\otimes d}\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
. Using the theory of idempotent trunction (e.g., see
[
23
, Section 6.2]
or see
[
9
, Section 2]
for the super version), the functor
F_{\mathcal{e}}:\mathbf{smod}\text{-}\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A\rightarrow\mathbf{smod}\text{-}\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A)\mathcal{e}
given by
M\mapsto Me
defines a superalgebra isomorphism

\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A)\mathcal{e}}\left((V_{n}^{\otimes d})\mathcal{e}\right).

However,
\mathcal{e}(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A)\mathcal{e}\cong\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr eAe\cong\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}
as superalgebras and

(V_{n}^{\otimes d})\mathcal{e}\cong(V_{n}e)^{\otimes d}\cong((Ae)^{\oplus n})^{\otimes d}\cong(\mathbbm{k}^{m_{\alpha}|n_{\alpha}})^{\oplus n})^{\otimes d}\cong(\mathbbm{k}^{M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha}})^{\otimes d}

as right
\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}
-supermodules. Thus

S^{A}(n,d)\cong\operatorname{End}_{\mathbbm{k}\mathfrak{S}_{d}}\left((k^{M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha}})^{\otimes d}\right)=S^{\alpha}(M_{\alpha}|N_{\alpha},d).

An identical argument applies when
\delta(\alpha)=1
and the simple supermodule
S=S^{\alpha}
is of type
\mathtt{Q}
.
∎

We close this section with an observation that will be needed later.

Remark 11.6.5
.

For
B\in\left\{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A,S^{A}(n,d),U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))\right\}
there are natural left and right actions on
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
. As discussed in the proof of
Theorem

11.6.2
When
A
is semisimple, there is an isomorphism of
(A,A)
-bimodules
A^{*}\cong A
and
\left(V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right)^{*}\cong V_{n}^{\otimes d}
. For each superalgebra
B
, this isomorphism identifies the natural left action with the dual of the natural right action of
B
, and vice versa. In particular, dualizing
Proposition

11.6.1
yields

(11.6.6)

V_{n}^{\otimes d}\cong\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(n,d)}D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\circledast L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*},

where the isomorphism is as
(\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A,S^{A}(n,d))
-bisupermodules.

12.
Howe duality

Throughout this section we assume
\mathbbm{k}
is a field and that
(A,a)_{I}
is a good pair with
I
finite. In particular,
A
is unital with identity
1=\sum_{i\in I}i
.

12.1.
The symmetric space
\mathcal{S}_{m,n}

Fix
m,n\geq 1
. Let
V_{m}=A^{\oplus m}
and
V_{n}=A^{\oplus n}
be viewed as column and row vectors, respectively. Since
V_{m}
(resp.,
V_{n}
) is a right (resp., left)
A
-supermodule by multiplication, we can consider the
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule
V_{m}\otimes_{A}V_{n}
. Given
f\in A
, we write
v_{r}^{f}
for the element of
V_{m}
which is a column vector of all zeros except for
f
in the
r
th position. Likewise,
v_{r}^{f}
will also be used to denote the element of
V_{n}
which is a row vector of all zeros except for
f
in the
r
th position. For brevity we write
z_{p,q}^{f}
for
v_{p}^{1_{A}}\otimes v_{q}^{f}=v_{p}^{f}\otimes v_{q}^{1_{A}}
in
V_{m}\otimes_{A}V_{n}
.

Via matrix multiplication there is an obvious left (resp., right) action by
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
(resp.,
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
) on
V_{m}\otimes_{A}V_{n}
. The actions of
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
and
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
mutually commute. Via their coproducts,
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
and
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
have corresponding commuting actions on

\mathcal{S}_{m,n}:=S^{\bullet}\left(V_{m}\otimes_{A}V_{n}\right).

The monomial

z_{p_{1},q_{1}}^{f_{1}}\dotsb z_{p_{r},q_{r}}^{f_{r}}\in\mathcal{S}_{m,n}

has
\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)
-weight

d^{\prime}_{1}\varepsilon_{1}+\dotsb+d^{\prime}_{m}\varepsilon_{m},

where
d^{\prime}_{k}=|\left\{i\mid p_{i}=k\right\}|
. It also has
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-weight

d^{\prime\prime}_{1}\varepsilon_{1}+\dotsb+d^{\prime\prime}_{n}\varepsilon_{n},

where
d^{\prime\prime}_{\ell}=|\left\{j\mid q_{j}=\ell\right\}|
. For
\lambda\in\Lambda_{m}
and
\mu\in\Lambda_{n}
, let
\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda,\mu}
denote the set of vectors of
\mathcal{S}_{m,n}
which are simultaneously vectors of weight
\lambda
for
\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)
and weight
\mu
for
\mathfrak{gl}_{(A)}
. The
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for
\mathcal{S}_{m,n}
given by monomials shows there is a direct sum decomposition of
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodules:

\mathcal{S}_{m,n}=\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\lambda\in\Lambda_{m}\\
\mu\in\Lambda_{n}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda,\mu}.

For
\lambda\in\Lambda_{m}
and
\mu\in\Lambda_{n}
, set

(12.1.1)

\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\bullet,\mu}=\bigoplus_{\nu\in\Lambda_{m}}\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\nu,\mu}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda,\bullet}=\bigoplus_{\nu\in\Lambda_{n}}\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda,\nu}.

Then,

(12.1.2)

\mathcal{S}_{m,n}=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda_{n}}\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\bullet,\mu}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{S}_{m,n}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{m}}\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda,\bullet}.

Since the actions of
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
and
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
commute, the decompositions of
\mathcal{S}_{m,n}
given in
Eq.

12.1.2
are as
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
- and
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-supermodules, respectively.

Lemma 12.1.1
.

For each
\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\in\Lambda_{m}
, there is an isomorphism of
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-supermodules,

\mathcal{S}^{\lambda,\bullet}_{m,n}\cong S^{\lambda_{1}}(V_{n})\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{\lambda_{m}}(V_{n}),

For each
\mu=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\in\Lambda_{n}
, there is an isomorphism of
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
-supermodules,

\mathcal{S}^{\bullet,\mu}_{m,n}\cong S^{\mu_{1}}(V_{m})\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{\mu_{n}}(V_{m}),

Proof.

The first isomorphism is the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map given on monomials by

z_{1,q_{1,1}}^{f_{1,1}}\dotsb z_{1,q_{1,r_{1}}}^{f_{1,r_{1}}}z_{2,q_{2,1}}^{f_{2,1}}\dotsb z_{2,q_{2,r_{2}}}^{f_{2,r_{2}}}\dotsb z_{m,q_{m,1}}^{f_{m,1}}\dotsb z_{m,q_{m,r_{m}}}^{f_{m,r_{m}}}\\
\mapsto v_{q_{1,1}}^{f_{1,1}}\dotsb v_{q_{1,r_{1}}}^{f_{1,r_{1}}}\otimes v_{q_{2,1}}^{f_{2,1}}\dotsb v_{q_{2,r_{2}}}^{f_{2,r_{2}}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes v_{q_{m,1}}^{f_{m,1}}\dotsb v_{q_{m,r_{m}}}^{f_{m,r_{m}}}.

A check on monomials verifies this is an even isomorphism of
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-supermodules. The obvious variant gives the second isomorphism.
∎

Let

\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))=\bigoplus_{\lambda,\mu\in\Lambda_{m}}\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))(\lambda,\mu)

be the locally unital superalgebra associated to the supercategory
\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
. Note that
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
is an idempotented form of the enveloping superalgebra
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
whose weight idempotents lie in
\Lambda_{n}
. Whenever
M
is a supermodule for
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
with a direct sum decomposition into weight spaces whose weights lie in
\Lambda_{n}
there is a well-defined action of
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
and, conversely, any supermodule for
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
defines a supermodule for
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
with a weight space decomposition whose weights lie in
\Lambda_{n}
. In particular, from
Eq.

12.1.1
it follows that
\mathcal{S}_{m,n}
is a
(\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)),\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)))
-bisupermodule.

Given a left
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
-supermodule homomorphism
f:\mathcal{S}_{m,n}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{m,n}
, we say
f
is
left finite
if there is a finite set
J\subseteq\Lambda_{n}
such that
(\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\bullet,\mu})f=0
for all
\mu\not\in J
and if the image of
f
is contained in
\oplus_{\mu\in J}\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\bullet,\mu}
. Similarly, given a right
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-supermodule homomorphism
f:\mathcal{S}_{m,n}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{m,n}
, we say
f
is
right finite
if there is a finite set
J\subseteq\Lambda_{m}
such that
f(\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda,\bullet})=0
for all
\lambda\not\in J
and if the image of
f
is contained in
\oplus_{\lambda\in J}\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda,\bullet}
. In both cases we write a superscript
fin
for the set of finite maps and it should be clear from context whether they are left finite or right finite.

Since the actions of
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
and
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
on
\mathcal{S}_{m,n}
commute, the action of an element of one superalgebra defines a supermodule homomorphism for the other. Furthermore, the action of
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
and
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
is by left and right finite maps, respectively. That is, there are superalgebra maps

(12.1.3)

\displaystyle\rho^{\ell}_{m}

\displaystyle:\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))}\left(\mathcal{S}_{m,n}\right)^{\text{fin}}\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(\mathcal{S}_{m,n}\right),

(12.1.4)

\displaystyle\rho^{r}_{n}

\displaystyle:\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))}\left(\mathcal{S}_{m,n}\right)^{\text{fin}}\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(\mathcal{S}_{m,n}\right).

12.2.
Miscellanea

In this section we record various notions which will be needed in what follows. Given
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategories
\mathbf{C}
and
\mathbf{D}
, let
{\mathcal{F}\hskip-1.4457pt\mathpzc{un}}(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D})
denote the category whose objects are even superfunctors
\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\mathbf{D}
and whose morphisms are supernatural transformations. Given a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory
\mathbf{C}
, there is the
opposite supercategory

\mathbf{C}^{\text{sop}}
with the same objects as
\mathbf{C}
,
{\rm Hom}_{\mathbf{C}^{\text{sop}}}(X,Y):={\rm Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(Y,X)
, and composition
\bullet
given by the rule
f\bullet g=(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{g}}g\circ f
for all composable homogenous morphisms in
\mathbf{C}^{\text{sop}}
.
Given
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategories
\mathbf{C}
and
\mathbf{D}
, we can form the supercategory
\mathbf{C}\boxtimes\mathbf{D}
. The objects of this category are given by

\left\{(x,y)\mid\text{$x$ is an object of $\mathbf{C}$ and $y$ is an object of $\mathbf{D}$}\right\}

and the morphisms are given by

{\rm Hom}_{\mathbf{C}\boxtimes\mathbf{D}}\left((x_{1},x_{2}),(y_{1},y_{2})\right)={\rm Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(x_{1},y_{1})\otimes{\rm Hom}_{\mathbf{D}}(x_{2},y_{2}).

Composition is given on homogeneous morphisms by

(12.2.1)

(f_{1}\otimes f_{2})\circ(g_{1}\otimes g_{2})=(-1)^{\bar{f}_{2}\bar{g}_{1}}(f_{1}\circ g_{1})\otimes(f_{2}\circ g_{2}).

See
[
7
]
for details on these constructions in the super setting. The correspondence between
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategories and locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebras takes opposites to opposites, and takes tensor products to tensor products.

A
right representation
of a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory
\mathbf{A}
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear functor
F:\mathbf{A}^{\text{sop}}\rightarrow{\mathbbm{k}}\text{-}{\mathbf{Mod}}
, and a
birepresentation
of the pair
(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear functor
F:\mathbf{A}\boxtimes\mathbf{B}^{\text{sop}}\rightarrow{\mathbbm{k}}\text{-}{\mathbf{Mod}}
. We write
\mathbf{A}\text{-Rep}
,
\text{Rep-}\mathbf{A}
, and
\mathbf{A}\text{-Rep-}\mathbf{B}
for the supercategories of representations of
\mathbf{A}
, right representations of
\mathbf{A}
, and birepresentations of
(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})
, respectively. The correspondence with locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebras gives category equivalences
\mathbf{A}\text{-Rep}\cong A\text{-}\mathbf{sMod}
,
\text{Rep-}\mathbf{A}\cong\mathbf{sMod}\text{-}A
, and
\mathbf{A}\text{-Rep-}\mathbf{B}\cong(A,B)
-supermodules.

The following lemma is straightforward.

Lemma 12.2.1
.

Let
A
be a superalgebra and let
(A,a)_{I}
be a good pair. Then the following statements are true.

(1)

The map which is the identity on objects and flips diagrams across their horizontal axis defines an isomorphism of supercategories,

\left({\mathbf{Web}}^{A,a}_{I}\right)^{\text{sop}}\rightarrow{\mathbf{Web}}^{A^{\text{sop}},a^{\text{sop}}}_{I}.

(2)

The map which is the identity on objects and is the transpose,
E_{r,s}^{f}\mapsto E_{s,r}^{f}
, on generating morphisms defines an isomorphism of supercategories,

\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))^{\text{sop}}\rightarrow\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A^{\text{sop}})).

(3)

The map given on generating elements by
z_{p,q}^{f}\mapsto z_{q,p}^{f}
defines a parity preserving isomorphism of
(\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A^{\text{sop}})),\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A^{\text{sop}})))
-bisupermodules,

\mathcal{S}^{A}_{m,n}\cong\mathcal{S}^{A^{\text{sop}}}_{n,m}.

12.3.
Categorical representations from
\mathcal{S}_{m,n}

Let

(12.3.1)

\displaystyle R^{\ell}_{m}:\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))\rightarrow{\mathbbm{k}}\text{-}{\mathbf{Mod}},

(12.3.2)

\displaystyle R^{r}_{n}:\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))^{\text{sop}}\rightarrow{\mathbbm{k}}\text{-}{\mathbf{Mod}},

be the representations corresponding to the maps
\rho^{\ell}_{m}
and
\rho^{r}_{n}
, respectively. Recall the functors
G_{m}
and
W_{m}
from
Theorems

5.5.1
and
10.2.1

Lemma 12.3.1
.

For all
m\geq 0
the functors
R^{\ell}_{m}
and
G_{m}\circ W_{m}
are naturally isomorphic.

Proof.

Let
\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\in\Lambda_{m}
. Then
R^{\ell}_{m}(\lambda)=\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda,\bullet}
and

(G_{m}\circ W_{m})(\lambda)=G_{m}(1^{\lambda_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes 1^{\lambda_{m}})=S^{\lambda_{1}}(V_{n})\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{\lambda_{m}}(V_{n}).

These are isomorphic
\mathbbm{k}
-modules via the map given in
Lemma

12.1.1
.

Given
1\leq r,s\leq m
and
f\in A
, consider the generating morphism
E_{r,s}^{f}\in\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))(\lambda,\gamma)
. Then

R^{\ell}_{m}(E_{r,s}^{f}):\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda,\bullet}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\gamma,\bullet}

is the map given by the left action of the element
E_{r,s}^{f}\in\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)
.

On the other hand,

(G_{m}\circ W_{m})(E_{r,s}^{f}):S^{\lambda_{1}}(V_{n})\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{\lambda_{m}}(V_{n})\rightarrow S^{\gamma_{1}}(V_{n})\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{\gamma_{m}}(V_{n})

is given by the
\mathbbm{k}
-module homomorphism
G_{m}(e_{[r,s],\lambda}^{f,1})
. Checking on a monomial confirms this map agrees with the one in the previous paragraph via the isomorphism given in
Lemma

12.1.1
.
∎

Since
\mathcal{S}_{m,n}
is a
(\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)),\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-bisupermodule, the following result is immediate.

Lemma 12.3.2
.

Fix
m,n\geq 1
. There is a birepresentation

F_{m,n}:\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))\boxtimes\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))^{\text{sop}}\rightarrow{\mathbbm{k}}\text{-}{\mathbf{Mod}}.

It is given on an object
(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda_{m}\times\Lambda_{n}
by

F_{m.n}(\lambda,\mu)=\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda,\mu}.

On homogeneous morphisms
f\in{\rm Hom}_{\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})
,
g\in{\rm Hom}_{\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))^{\text{sop}}}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})
the map

F_{m.n}(f\otimes g):\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda_{1},\mu_{1}}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda_{2},\mu_{2}}

is given on a homogeneous
x\in\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{\lambda_{1},\mu_{1}}
by

F_{m,n}(f\otimes g)(x)=(-1)^{\bar{g}\bar{x}}f((x)g)=(-1)^{\bar{g}\bar{x}}(f(x))g.

12.4.
Categorical and finitary Howe duality

For any supercategories
\mathbf{C}
and
\mathbf{D}
, there is a functor

\iota^{\prime}:\mathbf{C}\rightarrow{\mathcal{F}\hskip-1.4457pt\mathpzc{un}}(\mathbf{D},\mathbf{C}\boxtimes\mathbf{D})

given as follows. First, for an object
x
in
\mathbf{C}
define a functor
\iota^{\prime}(x)=\iota^{\prime}_{x}:\mathbf{D}\rightarrow\mathbf{C}\boxtimes\mathbf{D}
by
\iota^{\prime}_{x}(y)=(x,y)
for all objects
y
in
\mathbf{D}
and by
\iota^{\prime}_{x}(g)=1_{x}\otimes g
for all morphisms
g\in{\rm Hom}_{\mathbf{D}}(y_{1},y_{2})
. Next we define the functor
\iota^{\prime}
on morphisms. Given any morphism
f:x_{1}\rightarrow x_{2}
in
\mathbf{C}
construct a supernatural transformation
\iota^{\prime}(f):\iota^{\prime}_{x_{1}}\Rightarrow\iota^{\prime}_{x_{2}}
by setting, for any object
y\in\mathbf{D}
, the morphism
\iota^{\prime}(f)_{y}=f\otimes 1_{y}:\iota^{\prime}_{x_{1}}(y)\rightarrow\iota^{\prime}_{x_{2}}(y)
. Making the obvious changes yields an analogous functor

\iota^{\prime\prime}:\mathbf{D}\rightarrow{\mathcal{F}\hskip-1.4457pt\mathpzc{un}}(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{C}\boxtimes\mathbf{D}).

Given a birepresentation
F:\mathbf{C}_{1}\boxtimes\mathbf{C}^{\text{sop}}_{2}\rightarrow{\mathbbm{k}}\text{-}{\mathbf{Mod}}
, there are functors
F_{*}:{\mathcal{F}\hskip-1.4457pt\mathpzc{un}}(\mathbf{C}^{\text{sop}}_{2},\mathbf{C}_{1}\boxtimes\mathbf{C}^{\text{sop}}_{2})\rightarrow\text{Rep-}\mathbf{C}_{2}
and
F_{*}:{\mathcal{F}\hskip-1.4457pt\mathpzc{un}}(\mathbf{C}_{1},\mathbf{C}_{1}\boxtimes\mathbf{C}_{2}^{\text{sop}})\rightarrow\mathbf{C}_{1}\text{-Rep}
given in both cases by
H\mapsto F\circ H
. In turn, there are functors

\displaystyle{F}_{1}=F_{*}\circ\iota^{\prime}

\displaystyle:\mathbf{C}_{1}\rightarrow\text{Rep-}\mathbf{C}_{2},

\displaystyle{F}_{2}=F_{*}\circ\iota^{\prime\prime}

\displaystyle:\mathbf{C}^{\text{sop}}_{2}\rightarrow\mathbf{C}_{1}\text{-Rep}.

We say the birepresentation
F

left centralizes
if the functor
{F}_{1}
is full, it
right centralizes
if the functor
{F}_{2}
is full, and it
has the double centralizer property
if both
{F}_{1}
and
{F}_{2}
are full. As a sanity check, the reader may wish to verify that when
\mathbf{C}_{1}
and
\mathbf{C}_{2}
both have only a single object these definitions specialize to the notion of two superalgebras having mutually centralizing actions on a bisupermodule.

Theorem 12.4.1
.

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be a field of characteristic zero. The following statements hold:

(1)

If for a given
m\geq 0
the defining representation
G_{m}
is full for
A
, then
F_{m,n}
left centralizes for all
n\geq 0
.

(2)

If for a given
n\geq 0
the defining representation
G_{n}
is full for
A^{\text{sop}}
, then
F_{m,n}
right centralizes for all
m\geq 0
.

Proof.

To prove that
F_{m,n}
left centralizes we must show that
F_{m,n,1}=F_{m,n,*}\circ\iota^{\prime}:\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))\rightarrow\text{Rep-}\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
is full. Recall that the supercategory
\text{Rep-}\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
is equivalent to the supercategory of right
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-supermodules. Under this equivalence, for any object
\lambda\in\Lambda_{m}
we have

F_{m,n,1}(\lambda)=\mathcal{S}_{m.n}^{\lambda,\bullet}.

Given objects
\lambda,\gamma\in\Lambda_{m}
, the morphism
a\in\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))(\lambda,\mu)
goes to the
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-supermodule homomorphism

F_{m,n,1}(a):\mathcal{S}_{m.n}^{\lambda,\bullet}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{m.n}^{\gamma,\bullet}

given by acting on the left with the superalgebra element
a\in\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
. That is, under the equivalence
F_{m,n,1}
goes to the functor
R^{\ell}_{m}
. Therefore, by
Lemma

12.3.1
it suffices to show
G_{m}\circ W_{m}
is full. But
W_{m}
is full by
Corollary

10.2.4
and
G_{m}
is full by assumption.

For clarity, for the remainder of the proof we use a superscript
A
to indicate the underlying algebra (e.g.,
F^{A}_{m,n}
for
F_{m,n}
). To prove that
F^{A}_{m,n}
right centralizes we must show that

F^{A}_{m,n,2}=F^{A}_{m,n,*}\circ\iota^{{}^{\prime\prime},A}:\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))^{\text{sop}}\rightarrow\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))\text{-Rep}

is full. Recall that the supercategory
\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))\text{-Rep}
is equivalent to the supercategory of left
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
-supermodules. Under this equivalence, for any object
\mu\in\Lambda_{n}
we have

F^{A}_{m,n,2}(\mu)=\mathcal{S}_{m.n}^{\bullet,\mu}.

Given objects
\mu,\nu\in\Lambda_{n}
, the morphism
b\in\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))^{\text{sop}}(\mu,\nu)
goes to the
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
-supermodule homomorphism

F^{A}_{m,n,2}(b):\mathcal{S}_{m.n}^{\bullet,\mu}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{m.n}^{\bullet,\nu}

given by acting on the right with the superalgebra element
b\in\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
.

That is, under the equivalence
F^{A}_{m,n,2}
goes to the functor
R^{r,A}_{n}
and fullness amounts to showing that any finite right
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-supermodule endomorphism of
\mathcal{S}^{A}_{m,n}
can be realized by the action on the left by an element of
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
. That is, that any finite left
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))^{\text{sop}}
-supermodule endomorphism of
\mathcal{S}^{A}_{m,n}
can be realized by the action on the right by an element of
\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))^{\text{sop}}
. Applying the identifications given in
Lemma

12.2.1
shows that fullness of
F^{A}_{m,n,2}
follows from the fullness of
R^{\ell,A^{\text{sop}}}_{n}
. This was established in the previous paragraph (replacing
A
with
A^{\text{sop}}
, of course).
∎

Combining the above with the results from
Section

9
immediately implies the following categorical version of Howe duality.

Proposition 12.4.2
.

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be a field of characteristic zero. Assume that Schur–Weyl duality holds for
A
and
A^{\text{sop}}
. Then the birepresentation

F_{m,n}:\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))\boxtimes\dot{{\bf U}}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))^{\text{sop}}\rightarrow{\mathbbm{k}}\text{-}{\mathbf{Mod}}

has the double centralizer property.

These results can also be reformulated into the following finitary Howe duality.

Proposition 12.4.3
.

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be a field of characteristic zero and let
A
be a unital
\mathbbm{k}
-linear superalgebra. Assume that Schur–Weyl duality holds for
A
or
A^{\text{sop}}
. Then, respectively, the superalgebra maps

\displaystyle\rho^{\ell}_{m}

\displaystyle:\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))}\left(\mathcal{S}_{m,n}\right)^{\text{fin}},

\displaystyle\rho^{r}_{n}

\displaystyle:\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))\rightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\dot{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))}\left(\mathcal{S}_{m,n}\right)^{\text{fin}},

are surjective.

Proof.

As discussed in the proof of
Theorem

12.4.1
, the assumptions of the theorem prove the functors
R^{\ell}_{m}
and
R^{r}_{n}
are full which, in turn, is equivalent to
\rho^{\ell}_{m}
and
\rho^{r}_{n}
being surjective.
∎

12.5.
Strong multiplicity-free decompositions

In this section we assume
\mathbbm{k}
is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and that
A
is finite-dimensional and semisimple.

For homogeneous
a_{1},\dotsc,a_{d},b_{1},\dotsc,b_{d}\in A
, define

\varepsilon((a_{1},\dotsc,a_{d}),(b_{1},\dotsc,b_{d}))=\sum_{1\leq q<p\leq d}\bar{a}_{p}\bar{b}_{q}.

Then in
A^{\otimes d}
we have

(a_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes a_{d})(b_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes b_{d})=(-1)^{\varepsilon((a_{1},\dotsc,a_{d}),(b_{1},\dotsc,b_{d}))}(a_{1}b_{1})\otimes\dotsb(a_{d}b_{d}).

Also, for
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}
recall the notation
\langle\tau;(a_{1},\dotsc,a_{d})\rangle
defined in
Section

5.1
. With these formulas a calculation shows that for all
\tau\in\mathfrak{S}_{d}
,

(12.5.1)

\left[(a_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes a_{d})(b_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes b_{d})\right]\cdot\tau=\left[(a_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes a_{d})\cdot\tau\right]\left[(b_{1}\otimes\dotsb\otimes b_{d})\cdot\tau\right].

Theorem 12.5.1
.

If
m,n\geq 1
and
r
is the minimum of
m
and
n
, then for all
d\geq 0
,

\mathcal{S}^{d}_{m,n}\cong\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda^{A}_{+}(r,d)}L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\circledast L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*}

as
(U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)),U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)))
-supermodules.

Proof.

Let
A^{\otimes d}
act by diagonal multiplication on the left on
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
and on the right on
V_{m}^{\otimes d}
. There is a
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule isomorphism

V_{m}^{\otimes d}\otimes_{A^{\otimes d}}V_{n}^{\otimes d}\xrightarrow{\cong}(V_{m}\otimes_{A}V_{n})^{\otimes d}

given on homogeneous elements by

(v_{i_{1}}^{a_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes v_{i_{d}}^{a_{d}})\otimes(v_{j_{1}}^{b_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes v_{j_{d}}^{b_{d}})\mapsto(-1)^{\varepsilon((a_{1},\dotsc,a_{d}),(b_{1},\dotsc,b_{d}))}z_{i_{1},j_{1}}^{a_{1}b_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes z_{i_{d},j_{d}}^{a_{d}b_{d}}.

Let
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
acts on the right on
(V_{m}\otimes_{A}V_{n})^{\otimes d}
via signed place permutation. It also acts on the right on
V_{m}^{\otimes d}\otimes_{A^{\otimes d}}V_{n}^{\otimes d}
by acting diagonally via simultaneous signed place permutations on
V_{m}^{\otimes d}
and
V_{n}^{\otimes d}
. That the above map is an isomorphism of
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
-supermodules follows from
Eq.

12.5.1
. Restricting this isomorphism to
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
-invariants yields the middle isomorphism:

(12.5.2)

V_{m}^{\otimes d}\otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A^{\otimes d}}V_{n}^{\otimes d}\cong\left[V_{m}^{\otimes d}\otimes_{A^{\otimes d}}V_{n}^{\otimes d}\right]^{\mathfrak{S}_{d}}\cong\left[(V_{m}\otimes_{A}V_{n})^{\otimes d}\right]^{\mathfrak{S}_{d}}=\mathcal{S}^{d}_{m,n}.

The left isomorphism is straightforward. It is also straightforward to check that the maps in
Eq.

12.5.2
are
(U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)),U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)))
-bisupermodule homomorphisms.

To further our analysis of
Eq.

12.5.2
we pause to consider, for
\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(n,d)
and
\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(m,d)
,

(L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\mu})\otimes D^{\boldsymbol{\mu},*})\otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\otimes L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*}).

As a
(U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)),U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)))
-bisupermodule it is isomorphic to a direct sum of copies of
L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\mu})\circledast L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*}
. To determine the number of summands will require knowing the dimension of
D^{\boldsymbol{\mu},*}\otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
. By tensor-Hom adjunction there is a parity preserving isomorphism of
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodules:

{\rm Hom}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(D^{\boldsymbol{\mu},*}\otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},\mathbbm{k}\right)\cong{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}\left(D^{\boldsymbol{\mu},*},D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda},*}\right)\cong{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}\left(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\right).

By Schur’s lemma the dimension of the right hand side is
2^{\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})}
if
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\cong D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
as
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A
-supermodules, and zero otherwise. Note that when there is an isomorphism,
L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*}
,
D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda},*}
,
D^{\boldsymbol{\mu},*}
,
D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}
, and
L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\mu})
all have the same type.

Taken together with the tensor product rule from
Section

11.3
this discussion shows

(L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\mu})\otimes D^{\boldsymbol{\mu},*})\otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\otimes L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*})\cong\begin{cases}2^{\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})}L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\mu})\otimes L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*}\cong 2^{2\delta(\boldsymbol{\lambda})}L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\mu})\circledast L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*},&\text{ if }D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\cong D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}};\\
0,&else.\end{cases}

Comparing multiplicities shows

(L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\mu})\circledast D^{\boldsymbol{\mu},*})\otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\circledast L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*})\cong\begin{cases}L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\mu})\circledast L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*},&\text{ if }D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\cong D^{\boldsymbol{\mu}};\\
0,&else.\end{cases}

We are now prepared to prove the statement of the theorem. Combining
Eq.

11.6.6
,
Eq.

12.5.2
,
Proposition

11.6.1
, and the previous calculation yields the following isomorphisms of
(U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)),U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)))
-bisupermodules:

\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{m,n}^{d}

\displaystyle\cong V_{m}^{\otimes d}\otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A^{\otimes d}}V_{n}^{\otimes d}

\displaystyle\cong\left(\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(m,d)}L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\mu})\circledast D^{\boldsymbol{\mu},*}\right)\otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}\left(\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(n,d)}D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\circledast L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*}\right)

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(m,d)}\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(n,d)}\left(L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\mu})\circledast D^{\boldsymbol{\mu},*}\right)\otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr A}\left(D^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\circledast L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*}\right)

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\Lambda_{+}^{A}(r,d)}L^{A}_{m}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})\circledast L^{A}_{n}(\boldsymbol{\lambda})^{*}.

∎

The decomposition of
\mathcal{S}^{d}_{m,n}
as a
(U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A)),U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)))
-bimodule given in the previous theorem immediately implies that these actions are mutually centralizing. Thus we have the following corollary.

Corollary 12.5.2
.

Assume
\mathbbm{k}
is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and
A
is a finite-dimensional semisimple superalgebra. Then for all
m,n\geq 1
, the actions of
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A))
and
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
on
\mathcal{S}^{d}_{m,n}
are mutually centralizing.

It is well-known that Howe dualities can be reformulated in the language of polynomial differential operators. They also have a number of interesting applications to the study of
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
and its representation theory when, e.g.,
A=\mathbbm{k}
or
A=\operatorname{Cl}_{1}
. See, for example,
[
12
,
26
]
. We expect that most of these will have
A
-analogues and it would be interesting to develop them.

13.
Examples

We end with a discussion of some examples of interest.

13.1.
The category of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}
-webs

If
A=a=\mathbbm{k}
then
{\mathbf{Web}}^{\mathbbm{k},\mathbbm{k}}_{\{1\}}
can be seen to be isomorphic to the category of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}
-webs defined in
[
15
]
, the
Schur category
defined in
[
8
]
, and the web category introduced in
[
11
]
. For
n,d\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, the
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra
W^{\mathbbm{k},\mathbbm{k}}_{n,d}
is isomorphic to the well-studied classical Schur algebra
S^{\mathbbm{k}}(n,d)
.

13.2.
Cyclotomic Schur algebras

Let
C_{r}
be a cyclic group of order
r
and let
A=\mathbbm{k}C_{r}
. Then
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr\mathbbm{k}C_{r}
is a complex reflection group algebra. The generalized Schur algebra
S^{A}(n,d)
is the cyclotomic Schur algebra. It and related algebras have been studied in, for example,
[
1
,
2
,
4
,
16
,
17
,
21
,
24
,
33
,
34
]
.

13.3.
The category of
\mathfrak{q}_{n}
-webs

Let
A=\operatorname{Cl}_{1}=\mathbbm{k}[c]/(c^{2}-1)
to be the Clifford superalgebra on one generator, where the
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-grading is given by declaring
\bar{c}=\bar{1}
. Then
\mathfrak{S}_{d}\wr\operatorname{Cl}_{1}
is isomorphic to the Sergeev superalgebra
\operatorname{Ser}_{d}
which, in turn, is related to the spin representations of the symmetric group. It is not difficult to verify that
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(\textup{Cl}_{1})\cong\mathfrak{q}_{n}(\mathbbm{k})
as Lie superalgebras. If we set
a=\mathbbm{k}1_{A}
and
I=\{1\}
, then there is an asymptotically faithful functor

G_{n}:{\mathbf{Web}}^{\operatorname{Cl}_{1},\mathbbm{k}}_{\left\{1\right\}}\rightarrow\textup{mod}_{\mathcal{S}}\textup{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(\operatorname{Cl}_{1}).

When
\mathbbm{k}=\mathbb{C}
a diagrammatic supercategory
\mathfrak{q}\textup{-}{\mathbf{Web}}_{\uparrow}
was introduced by Brown and the second author in
[
6
]
and a similar functor

\mathfrak{q}\textup{-}{\mathbf{Web}}_{\uparrow}\rightarrow\mathfrak{q}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})\text{-supermodules}

was defined and studied. As we next explain,
{\mathbf{Web}}^{\operatorname{Cl}_{1},\mathbbm{k}}_{{1}}
and
\mathfrak{q}\textup{-}{\mathbf{Web}}_{\uparrow}
are in fact isomorphic as
\mathbbm{k}
-linear monoidal supercategories and these two functors coincide.

The category
{\mathbf{Web}}^{\operatorname{Cl}_{1},{\mathbb{C}}}_{\{1\}}
only has monotone generators and only needs the single coupon
c
on the thin strands. On the other hand, the category
\mathfrak{q}
-
\operatorname{\mathbf{Web}}_{\uparrow}
was defined in
[
6
]
as having generating objects
\uparrow_{k}
for
k\geq 0
and three kinds of (upward oriented) diagrammatic generators: splits, merges, and dots on
\uparrow_{k}
for all
k
. We skip the list of relations and ask the reader to refer to
[
6
, Section 4.1]
. In
[
6
]
the crossing of thin strands is defined by the same formula as in
Eq.

3.2.2
, but for thick strands they are defined in terms of the single strand crossings by:

\beta_{\uparrow_{k},\uparrow_{l}}=\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 14.43457pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-14.43457pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-19.9897pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\hbox to28.87pt{\vbox to39.98pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 5.54309pt\lower-11.0982pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill}
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 24.61 24.61}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{{{}{}{{}}
}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{{{}{}{{}}
}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{{{}{}{{}}
}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
