Proposition 13.3.1
.

There is a well-defined functor
\mathcal{F}:{\mathbf{Web}}^{\operatorname{Cl}_{1},{\mathbb{C}}}_{\{1\}}\rightarrow\mathfrak{q}
-
\operatorname{\mathbf{Web}}_{\uparrow}
, sending
1^{(k)}
to
\uparrow_{k}
for
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
. On morphisms it sends the merges and splits to their counterparts in
\mathfrak{q}
-
\operatorname{\mathbf{Web}}_{\uparrow}
, the crossing in
\operatorname{Hom}(1^{(k)}1^{(\ell)},1^{(\ell)}1^{(k)})
to the element
\beta_{\uparrow k,\uparrow\ell}
, and, lastly, it sends the coupon
c
on the thin strand colored by
1
to the dot on
\uparrow_{1}
.

Proof.

Here we use the alternate presentation for
\mathbf{Web}^{\operatorname{Cl}_{1},\mathbb{C}}_{\{1\}}
given in
Section

3.2
. It is enough to show that the image of all defining relations for
\mathbf{Web}^{\operatorname{Cl}_{1},\mathbb{C}}_{\{1\}}
hold in
\mathfrak{q}
-
\operatorname{\mathbf{Web}}_{\uparrow}
. Among them,
Eq.

3.1.2
,
Eq.

3.1.5
,
Eq.

3.1.6
,
Eq.

3.1.7
,
Eq.

3.1.10
and the first part of
Eq.

3.1.9
all have obvious analogues in
\mathfrak{q}
-
\operatorname{\mathbf{Web}}_{\uparrow}
. In addition, the second part in
Eq.

3.1.9
, as well as
Eq.

3.1.11
and
Eq.

3.1.12
are vacuous since we only allow nontrivial coupons on thin strands.

Among the remaining two relations, we first argue that
Eq.

3.2.2
holds when
x=1
by arguing by induction on
y
. The base case when
x=y=1
is immediate. The induction step is given by

(13.3.1)

1

Note we omit the thickness labels when the strand is labeled by
1
. Here, the second equality follows from resolving the lower left crossing; the third equality follows from
[
6
, (4.21)]
, generalized to the thick strand case, as well as applying the induction hypothesis to the last term in
Eq.

13.3.2
. In the last equality, the fourth term in
Eq.

13.3.4
appears three times in the previous step, one from applying the association rule to the second term in
Eq.

13.3.4
, and another from applying the rung swap relation
[
6
, (4.6)]
to the third term in
Eq.

13.3.4
. These three terms appear with coefficients
-\frac{1}{\ell}
,
-\frac{2(\ell-1)}{\ell}
, and
\frac{\ell-1}{\ell}
, which sum to yield
-1
in the last step. We leave to the reader the general case where one fixes
y
as an arbitrary integer and inducts on
x
. The argument is similar and uses the above identity in the induction step.

holds by induction on

s=0
is trivial. Suppose

holds for
s-1
and arbitrary
r

Here, after a change of variables
t\mapsto t-1
in the second term, one only needs to verify that

\displaystyle\frac{s-t}{s}\binom{x-y+r-s+1}{t}+\frac{x-y-2s+r+1}{s}\binom{x-y+r-s}{t-1}=\binom{x-y+r-s}{t},

which is straightforward.
∎

.

Proof.

It is enough to check the image of all relations in
[
6
, Section 4.1]
hold in
\mathbf{Web}^{\operatorname{Cl}_{1},\mathbb{C}}_{\{1\}}
. Here we omit the explicit computations. Relations
[
6
, (4.1)-(4.2)]
are identical to the relations in
\mathbf{Web}^{\operatorname{Cl}_{1},\mathbb{C}}_{\{1\}}
. Relations
[
6
, (4.3)-(4.4)]
can be deduced from applying
Eq.

3.1.3
to the middle portion of each diagram. Relation
[
6
, (4.5)]
can be deduced from applying
Eq.

3.2.2
to the middle portion. Relation
[
6
, (4.6)]
is a special case of
Eq.

3.2.1
. The first equality in
[
6
, (4.7)]
is the result of applying
Eq.

3.1.3
to the middle right portion of each diagram on the left, and similarly the second equality holds.
[
5
, (4.8)]
follows from applying
Eq.

3.1.3
to the middle portion of the third picture. Similarly
[
6
, (4.9)]
holds.
∎

By construction the functors
\mathcal{F}
and
\mathcal{G}
are
\mathbbm{k}
-linear monoidal functors and are inverses of each other.

Theorem 13.3.3
.

There is an isomorphism of
\mathbbm{k}
-linear monoidal supercategories,

{\mathbf{Web}}^{\operatorname{Cl}_{1},\mathbbm{k}}_{\left\{1\right\}}\cong\mathfrak{q}\textup{-}{\mathbf{Web}}.

Under the isomorphism
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(\operatorname{Cl}_{1})\cong\mathfrak{q}_{n}(\mathbbm{k})
one readily checks that
V_{n}=\operatorname{Cl}_{1}^{\oplus n}\cong\mathbbm{k}^{n|n}
, the natural representation of
\mathfrak{q}_{n}(\mathbbm{k})
. Given these identifications, one could reasonably expect that the functor
G_{m}
coincides with the one given in
[
6
]
. This turns out to be true. The only wrinkle is that we consider right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(\operatorname{Cl}_{1})
-supermodules while in
[
6
]
they considered left
\mathfrak{q}_{n}(\mathbbm{k})
-supermodules. This can be resolved by suitably using opposites. We leave the straightforward details to the interested reader.

Before leaving this example we should also mention that a Howe duality was already obtained for the pair
(\mathfrak{q}_{m}({\mathbb{C}}),\mathfrak{q}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}))
by Sergeev
[
39
]
(or see
[
12
]
).

13.4.
Zigzag superalgebras and RoCK blocks

Let
G=(I,E)
be a simple connected graph with no loops. For each pair of connected vertices
i\textup{\textemdash}j
, fix
\varepsilon_{ij},\varepsilon_{ji}\in\{\pm 1\}
. Then the associated locally unital
zigzag superalgebra

\overline{Z}=\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}j\overline{Z}i
has distinguished set of orthogonal idempotents corresponding to the vertices
I
of
G
, with the following
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for each subspace:

\displaystyle j\overline{Z}i=\begin{cases}\mathbbm{k}\{i,c_{i}\}&\textup{if }i=j;\\
\mathbbm{k}\{a_{ji}\}&\textup{if }i\textup{\textemdash}j;\\
0&\textup{otherwise},\end{cases}

Multiplication is defined via the orthogonality of the idempotents
I
, coupled with the additional rules:

\displaystyle a_{kj}a_{ji}=\delta_{ik}\varepsilon_{ji}c_{i},\qquad c_{i}a_{ij}=a_{ij}c_{j}=0,\qquad c_{i}^{2}=0.

The parity of elements is defined by
\bar{i}=\bar{c}_{i}=\bar{0}
,
\bar{a}_{ij}=\bar{1}
. Taking
\bar{z}=\mathbbm{k}I
, we have a good pair
(\overline{Z},\bar{z})_{I}
. It is straightforward to check that if
G
is a tree, then different choices of signs
\varepsilon_{ij}
nonetheless yield isomorphic zigzag superalgebras.

13.4.1.
The zigzag web category

Following
Section

3.1
we may define the associated web category
{\mathbf{Web}}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I}
. For the reader’s benefit we describe a streamlined presentation of
{\mathbf{Web}}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I}
adapted to the particulars of the zigzag superalgebra.

{\mathbf{Web}}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I}
is a monoidal supercategory generated by objects
i^{(x)}
, where
i\in I
,
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, with generating morphisms

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x+y)}

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x+y)}

\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(y)}

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(1)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(1)}

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(1)}
\scriptstyle k^{\scriptstyle(1)}

for
i,j,k\in I
with
i\textup{\textemdash}k
,
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, where all morphisms are even save the rightmost, which is odd. Here we are using the circle dot in lieu of the
c_{i}
coupon, and a color-change ‘tag’ in lieu of the
a_{ki}
coupon. These morphisms are subject to relations (
3.1.2
–
3.1.7
), together with the following streamlined analogues of relations (

–
3.1.12
):

13.4.2.
RoCK blocks of symmetric groups

Let
H_{N}(q)
be the Hecke algebra of the symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{N}
over a field
\mathbbm{F}
with parameter
q\in\mathbbm{F}^{\times}
, and let
e
be the associated quantum characteristic. Let
\mathcal{B}
be a weight
d

RoCK block
of
H_{N}(q)
, see
[
20
]
.
Let
G
be the path graph
{\tt A}_{e-1}
with vertices
I=\{1,2,\ldots,e-1\}
:

\cdots
\scriptstyle 1
\scriptstyle 2
\scriptstyle 3
\scriptstyle e-2
\scriptstyle e-1

Let
(\overline{Z},\bar{z})_{I}
be the associated zigzag good pair as defined in
Section

13.4
. Let
{\mathbf{Web}}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I}
be the associated web category defined in
Section

13.4.1
, and set:

\displaystyle\textup{Web}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I,n,d}=\bigoplus_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}\in\widehat{\Omega}_{I}(n,d)}{\mathbf{Web}}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}).

In other words,
{\mathbf{Web}}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I,n,d}
is the full subcategory of
{\mathbf{Web}}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I}
consisting of objects
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}\in\widehat{\Omega}_{I}(n,d)
, and
\textup{Web}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I,n,d}
is the associated locally unital algebra, as described in
Section

2.1.2
.

Proposition 13.4.1
.

Let
n\geq d
. Then
\textup{Web}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I,n,d}
is Morita equivalent to
\mathcal{B}
.

Proof.

It is shown in
[
20
, Theorem A]
that the generalized Schur algebra
T^{\overline{Z}}_{\bar{z}}(n,d)
is Morita equivalent to
\mathcal{B}
.
For each
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}\in\widehat{\Omega}_{I}(n,d)
, choose a representative
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}_{0}
of this class in
\Omega_{I}(n,d)
. Recalling the idempotents
\xi_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}
defined in
Eq.

7.4.1
, set
\xi_{I}=\sum_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}_{0}\in\Omega_{I}(n,d)}\xi_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}_{0}}\in T^{\overline{Z}}_{\bar{z}}(n,d)
.

Let
\mathbbm{F}
be a field. As shown in
[
32
, §7.9]
, the simple
T^{\overline{Z}}_{\bar{z}}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{F}}
-modules may be labeled as follows:

\displaystyle\left\{L_{\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbbm{F}}\mid\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda^{(1)},\ldots,\lambda^{(e-1)})\textup{ an $(e-1)$-multipartition of }d\right\},

and there exist weight idempotents

\displaystyle\xi_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=\scalebox{2}{\textasteriskcentered}_{r=1}^{n}(E^{i}_{r,r})^{\otimes\lambda^{(i)}_{r}}\in T^{\overline{Z}}_{\bar{z}}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{F}},

such that
\xi_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}L_{\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbbm{F}}\neq 0
.
It is straightforward to check that for any such multipartition
\boldsymbol{\lambda}
there exist elements
\xi_{1},\xi_{2}\in T^{\overline{Z}}_{\bar{z}}(n,d)_{\mathbbm{F}}
such that
\xi_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=\xi_{1}\xi_{I}\xi_{2}
, so
we have
\xi_{I}L_{\boldsymbol{\lambda},\mathbbm{F}}\neq 0
for all multipartitions
\boldsymbol{\lambda}
as well.
Hence by
[
20
, Lemma 8.26]
, we have that

\displaystyle\xi_{I}T_{\bar{z}}^{\overline{Z}}(n,d)\xi_{I}=\bigoplus_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}_{0},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}_{0}\in\Omega_{I}(n,d)}\xi_{\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}_{0}}T^{\overline{Z}}_{\bar{z}}(n,d)\xi_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}_{0}}

is Morita equivalent to
T_{\bar{z}}^{\overline{Z}}(n,d)
. By
Theorem

7.4.2
, the functor
\chi
induces an isomorphism of algebras
\xi_{I}T_{\bar{z}}^{\overline{Z}}(n,d)\xi_{I}\cong\textup{Web}^{\overline{Z},\bar{z}}_{I,n,d}
, completing the proof.
∎

13.4.3.
Related zigzag/RoCK block conjectures

Let
n\geq d
.
Taking
(Z,z)_{I}
to be the good pair for the
extended
zigzag algebra
[
32
, §7.9]
, it is conjectured in
[
32
, Conjecture 7.58]
that
T^{Z}_{z}(n,d)
is Morita equivalent to the level
d
RoCK block of the
q
-Schur algebra
S_{q}(N,f)
. Similarly, taking
(A,a)_{I}
to be the good pair for the Brauer tree superalgebra in
[
28
, §2.2e]
, it is conjectured in
[
28
, Conjecture 1]
that
T^{A}_{a}(n,d)
is Morita (super)equivalent to the level
d
RoCK block of the Sergeev superalgebra
\operatorname{Ser}_{n}
.
If these conjectures are found to hold, then a result analogous to
Proposition

13.4.1
should hold in these settings as well. If so, this will give diagrammatic models for these RoCK blocks which are similar to those in
Section

13.4.1
.
